subject: advanced-accounting
case_facts_html:
Fly Ltd. made a sale of INR 7,00,000 to Wings International in May 2023 and recognised Trade Receivables which was initially recorded at the prevailing exchange rate on the date of sales, transaction recorded at US$ 1= ₹79.4. The Company also took a loan from U.S Company for ₹10,00000 in December 2023 which was initially recorded at the prevailing exchange rate on the date of transaction, transaction recorded at US$ 1= ₹81.1.

On 31st March 2024, exchange rate was US$ 1 = ₹83.3.
question_html:
What will be the closing balance of Trade Receivables on 31st March 2024:

  1. ₹700,000
  2. ₹7,14,978 approx
  3. ₹7,34,383 approx
  4. ₹7,50,000 approx
answer_html: Answer: (C) ₹7,34,383 approx — the trade receivable is a foreign-currency monetary asset, restated at the closing rate on the balance sheet date. USD principal = ₹7,00,000 / 79.4 = USD 8,815.82 (approx); at the closing rate of USD 1 = ₹83.3, the restated balance = 8,815.82 × 83.3 = ₹7,34,383 approx.

topics.title: The Effects of Changes in Foreign Exchange Rates
topics.subtopictitle: Foreign currency monetary item (trade receivable) restated at the closing rate on the balance sheet date
topics.label: AS 11 (3.4)

examiner_comment.text: A common error in this type of question is applying the average or historical rate instead of the closing rate to a foreign-currency monetary asset at the balance sheet date, understating the translated receivable balance.

subject: advanced-accounting
case_facts_html:
X Ltd. purchased 3,000 shares of Amazing Ltd. in December 2023 @ ₹100 each and paid brokerage @ 1%. In May 2024, Amazing Ltd. issued bonus shares at one for every three shares held by shareholders.

X Ltd. sold 1000 shares in September 2024 at ₹110 each. After issue of bonus, shares were quoted at ₹95. In December 2024, the shares were quoted at ₹70.
question_html:
What would be the carrying cost of investments in Amazing Ltd. after sale of shares as per AS 13:

  1. ₹3,03,000
  2. ₹2,27,250
  3. ₹3,00,000
  4. ₹3,30,000
answer_html: Answer: (B) ₹2,27,250 — original cost = 3,000 shares × ₹100 + 1% brokerage = ₹3,03,000. The May 2024 bonus issue (1 for 3) adds 1,000 shares at nil cost, so the weighted-average cost across the enlarged 4,000-share holding remains ₹3,03,000, i.e. ₹75.75/share. On sale of 1,000 shares in September 2024, the cost removed = 1,000 × ₹75.75 = ₹75,750, leaving the carrying cost of the remaining 3,000 shares at ₹3,03,000 − ₹75,750 = ₹2,27,250.

topics.title: Accounting for Investments
topics.subtopictitle: Weighted-average cost per share after a bonus issue, applied to shares sold
topics.label: AS 13 (3.5)

examiner_comment.text: A common mistake is treating the bonus shares as adding to the cost base of the holding, rather than spreading the original cost over the enlarged number of shares (original plus bonus) to arrive at the correct weighted-average carrying cost.

X Ltd. sold 1000 shares in September 2024 at ₹110 each. After issue of bonus, shares were quoted at ₹95. In December 2024, the shares were quoted at ₹70.

What would be the carrying cost of investments in Amazing Ltd. in quarter ending in December 2024 as per AS 13:

  2. ₹2,27,250
  3. ₹2,20,000
  4. ₹3,00,000
answer_html: Answer: (A) ₹2,10,000 — the remaining 3,000 shares carry a weighted-average cost of ₹2,27,250 (see Q2(a)); at the December 2024 market price of ₹70/share, their fair value = 3,000 × ₹70 = ₹2,10,000. subject: advanced-accounting
case_facts_html: Sun Limited has acquired 40% share in Moon Ltd. for ₹500,000 on 01.07.2023. Moon Ltd. is holding 40% stake in Star Limited. Now, sun limited can exercise significant influence on Moon Limited. Moon limited declared dividend of ₹80,000 for the Financial Year 2022-23 on 15.09.2023. For the year 2023-24, Moon Ltd. earned profit of ₹4,00,000 and declared dividend for ₹90,000 on 15.09.2024.
question_html:
With respect to relationship between Companies, it can be said that:

  1. Star Ltd. is associate of Sun Ltd.
  2. Moon Ltd. and Star Ltd. both are associates of Sun Ltd.
  3. Moon Ltd. is an associate of Sun Ltd.
  4. Sun Ltd. is Parent of both Moon Ltd. and Star Ltd.
answer_html: Answer: (C) Moon Ltd. is an associate of Sun Ltd. — Sun's direct 40% stake in Moon falls within AS 23's significant-influence range (20%-50%), making Moon an associate. Star Ltd. is not itself directly held by Sun; Moon's 40% stake in Star does not, on its own, extend associate status from Sun to Star, since Moon is only an associate (not a subsidiary) of Sun, and AS 23 does not treat an indirect holding routed through another associate as conferring significant influence.

topics.title: Accounting for Investments in Associates in Consolidated Financial Statements
topics.subtopictitle: Associate relationship via direct significant influence; an indirect stake held through another associate does not itself confer associate status
topics.label: AS 23 (2.3)

examiner_comment.text: A common error is extending "associate" status to a company held only indirectly through another associate (rather than through a subsidiary), when AS 23 does not treat such indirect holdings as conferring significant influence on their own.

subject: advanced-accounting
case_facts_html: Sun Limited has acquired 40% share in Moon Ltd. for ₹500,000 on 01.07.2023. Moon Ltd. is holding 40% stake in Star Limited. Now, sun limited can exercise significant influence on Moon Limited. Moon limited declared dividend of ₹80,000 for the Financial Year 2022-23 on 15.09.2023. For the year 2023-24, Moon Ltd. earned profit of ₹4,00,000 and declared dividend for ₹90,000 on 15.09.2024.
question_html:
What will be the carrying amount of investment in Separate Financial Statements of Sun Limited as on 31.03.2024?

  1. ₹5,00,000
  2. ₹5,80,000
  3. ₹4,68,000
  4. ₹5,32,000
answer_html: Answer: (C) ₹4,68,000 — in Sun's separate financial statements, the investment is carried at cost. The dividend of ₹80,000 declared on 15.09.2023 relates to Moon's FY2022-23 profits, a pre-acquisition period (Sun acquired its stake on 01.07.2023); Sun's 40% share of this pre-acquisition dividend (₹32,000) is treated as a recovery of the cost of investment, not as income, reducing the carrying cost to ₹5,00,000 − ₹32,000 = ₹4,68,000.

topics.label: AS 13 (3.5)

examiner_comment.text: A frequent slip is failing to identify that a dividend declared shortly after acquisition can still relate to a pre-acquisition profit period, and should reduce the cost of investment in separate financial statements rather than being credited to income.

question_html:
What will be the carrying amount of investment in Consolidated Financial Statements of Sun Limited as on 31.03.2024?

  1. ₹9,00,000
  2. ₹5,88,000
  3. ₹4,52,000
  4. ₹6,20,000
answer_html: Answer: (B) ₹5,88,000 — under the equity method for CFS, the carrying amount starts from the same pre-acquisition-dividend-adjusted cost as the separate financial statements (₹4,68,000, see Q3(b)) and is increased by Sun's 40% share of Moon's post-acquisition profit for FY2023-24, time-apportioned for the 9 months since acquisition (01.07.2023 to 31.03.2024): 40% × ₹4,00,000 × 9/12 = ₹1,20,000. Carrying amount = ₹4,68,000 + ₹1,20,000 = ₹5,88,000.

subject: advanced-accounting
case_facts_html: Sun Limited has acquired 40% share in Moon Ltd. for ₹500,000 on 01.07.2023. Moon Ltd. is holding 40% stake in Star Limited. Now, sun limited can exercise significant influence on Moon Limited. Moon limited declared dividend of ₹80,000 for the Financial Year 2022-23 on 15.09.2023. For the year 2023-24, Moon Ltd. earned profit of ₹4,00,000 and declared dividend for ₹90,000 on 15.09.2024.
question_html:
As per AS 23, the existence of significant influence by an investor is usually evidenced in one or more of the following ways: (a) participation in policy making processes; (b) interchange of managerial personnel; (c) right to receive dividend; (d) provision of essential technical information.

  1. All the statements are correct
  2. Statements (a), (b) and (c) are correct
  3. Statements (b), (c) and (d) are correct
  4. Statements (a), (b) and (d) are correct
answer_html: Answer: (D) Statements (a), (b) and (d) are correct — participation in policy-making, interchange of managerial personnel, and provision of essential technical information are all AS 23 evidences of significant influence. A mere right to receive dividend (statement c) is not, since it is a passive entitlement common to any shareholder rather than evidence of participation in decisions.

topics.label: AS 23 (2.3)

examiner_comment.text: A recurring error is treating a mere right to receive dividend as evidence of significant influence, when AS 23's list of evidencing factors is centred on participation in decisions, not the passive entitlements every shareholder holds.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html:
Cost of current investment acquired was ₹1000 but the fair value was ₹800. The Investment was recorded at ₹800. Now the fair value of Investment is Rs 1200. At what value should it be recorded and how much gain will be credited to profit and loss account.

  1. No change is required and it will continue at ₹800
  2. Current investment will be recorded at ₹1000 and gain of ₹200 will be credited to profit and loss account.
  3. Current investment will be recorded at ₹1200 and gain of ₹400 will be credited to profit and loss account.
  4. Current investment will be recorded at ₹1200 but no gain will be credited to profit and loss account.
answer_html: Answer: (B) Current investment will be recorded at ₹1,000 and gain of ₹200 will be credited to profit and loss account — under AS 13, the investment was initially carried at the lower of cost (₹1,000) and fair value (₹800), i.e. ₹800. When fair value subsequently rises to ₹1,200, the carrying amount can be written back up, but only as far as the original cost (₹1,000) — never above it, even though the new fair value is higher. The write-back from ₹800 to ₹1,000 is a gain of ₹200 credited to profit and loss.

topics.title: Accounting for Investments
topics.subtopictitle: Current investment written up only to original cost, never above cost, even if fair value later exceeds cost
topics.label: AS 13 (3.6)

examiner_comment.text: A common error is writing a current investment up to its new, higher fair value, when AS 13 caps the carrying amount of a current investment at its original cost even after a subsequent value recovery.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html:
As per AS 20 an enterprise should present/disclose the following: (a) the amounts used as the numerators in calculating basic and diluted earnings per share, and a reconciliation of those amounts to the net profit or loss for the period. (b) the weighted average number of equity shares used as the denominator in calculating basic and diluted earnings per share, and a reconciliation of these denominators to each other. (c) basic and diluted earnings per share, even if the amounts disclosed are negative (a loss per share). (d) the nominal value of shares along with the earnings per share figures.

  1. All the statements are correct
  2. Statements (a), (b) and (c) are correct
  3. Statements (b), (c) and (d) are correct
  4. Statements (a), (b) and (c) are correct
answer_html: Answer: (A) All the statements are correct — AS 20 requires disclosure of the numerator amounts and their reconciliation to net profit, the denominator (weighted average shares) and its reconciliation, both basic and diluted EPS even when negative, and the nominal value of shares alongside the EPS figures.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html:
Accounting Standard 10, Property, Plant and Equipment is applicable to:

  1. Biological Assets (other than Bearer Plants) related to agricultural activity
  2. Wasting Assets including Mineral rights, Expenditure on the exploration for and extraction of minerals, oil, natural gas and similar non-regenerative resources
  3. Inventories
  4. Bearer Plant (except produce on Bearer Plants)
answer_html: Answer: (D) Bearer Plant (except produce on Bearer Plants) — AS 10 covers bearer plants themselves (the produce growing on them is outside AS 10's scope, covered elsewhere), while biological assets generally, wasting assets/mineral rights, and inventories are all excluded from AS 10's scope.

examiner_comment.text: A common error is assuming AS 10 excludes bearer plants altogether, when only the produce growing on a bearer plant is outside its scope; the bearer plant itself is squarely within AS 10.

question_html:
A Ltd. provides after sales warranty for two years to its customers. Based on past experience, the company has the following policy for making provision for warranties on the invoice amount, on the remaining balance warranty period: Less than 1 year: 2% provision; More than 1 year: 3% provision. The company has raised invoices as under:

Invoice DateAmount (₹)

04th Oct, 20231,35,000

Calculate the provision to be made for warranty under AS-29 as at 31st March, 2023 and 31st March, 2024. Also compute amount to be debited to P & L account for the year ended 31st March, 2024.
answer_html:
Provision to be made for warranty under AS 29 'Provisions, Contingent Liabilities and Contingent Assets':

As at 31st March, 2023 = ₹60,000 × 0.02 + ₹40,000 × 0.03 = ₹1,200 + ₹1,200 = ₹2,400

As at 31st March, 2024 = ₹40,000 × 0.02 + ₹1,35,000 × 0.03 = ₹800 + ₹4,050 = ₹4,850

Amount debited to Profit and Loss Account for year ended 31st March, 2024:

Balance of provision required as on 31.03.20244,850

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html: As per provisions of AS-26, how would you deal to the following situations: (1) ₹23,00,000 paid by a manufacturing company to the legal advisor for defending the patent of a product is treated as a capital expenditure. (2) During the year 2023-24, a company spent ₹7,00,000 for publicity and research expenses on one of its new consumer products which was marketed in the same accounting year but proved to be a failure. (3) A company spent ₹25,00,000 in the past three years to develop a product, these expenses were charged to profit and loss account since they did not meet AS-26 criteria for capitalization. In the current year approval of the concerned authority has been received. The company wishes to capitalize ₹25,00,000 by disclosing it as a prior period item. (4) A company with a turnover of ₹200 crores and an annual advertising budget of ₹50,00,000 had taken up for the marketing of a new product by a company. It was estimated that the company would have a turnover of ₹20 crore from the new product. The company had debited to its Profit & Loss Account the total expenditure of ₹50,00,000 incurred on extensive special initial advertisement campaign for the new product.
answer_html:
As per AS 26 "Intangible Assets", subsequent expenditure on an intangible asset after its purchase or its completion should be recognized as an expense when it is incurred unless (a) it is probable that the expenditure will enable the asset to generate future economic benefits in excess of its originally assessed standard of performance; and (b) expenditure can be measured and attributed to the asset reliably. If these conditions are met, the subsequent expenditure should be added to the cost of the intangible asset.

  1. In the given case, the legal expenses to defend the patent of a product amounting ₹23,00,000 should not be capitalized and be charged to Profit and Loss Statement.
  2. The company is required to expense the entire amount of ₹7,00,000 in the Profit and Loss account for the year ended 31st March, 2024 because no benefit will arise in the future.
  3. As per AS 26, expenditure on an intangible item that was initially recognized as an expense by a reporting enterprise in previous annual financial statements should not be recognized as part of the cost of an intangible asset at a later date. Thus, the company cannot capitalize the amount of ₹25,00,000 and it should be recognized as expense.
  4. Expenditure of ₹50,00,000 on advertising and promotional activities should always be charged to Profit and Loss Statement. Hence, the company has done the correct treatment by debiting the sum of ₹50 lakhs to Profit and Loss Account.

examiner_comment.text: A frequent mistake is capitalising defence-of-patent legal costs or attempting to retrospectively capitalise previously expensed development costs once approval is later obtained; AS 26 bars reinstating costs already recognised as an expense in an earlier period.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html: Indicate in each case whether revenue can be recognized and when it will be recognized as per AS-9. (1) Trade discount and volume rebate received. (2) Where goods are sold to distributors or others for resale. (3) Where seller concurrently agrees to repurchase the same goods at a later date. (4) Insurance agency commission for rendering services. (5) On 11-03-2024 cloths worth ₹50,000 were sold to X mart, but due to refurbishing of their showroom being underway, on their request, clothes were delivered on 12-04-2024.
answer_html:
1. Trade discounts and volume rebates received are not encompassed within the definition of revenue, since they represent a reduction of cost. Trade discounts and volume rebates given should be deducted in determining revenue.
  2. When goods are sold to distributor or others, revenue from such sales can generally be recognized if significant risks of ownership have passed; however, in some situations the buyer may in substance be an agent and in such cases the sale should be treated as a consignment sale.
  3. For transactions, where seller concurrently agrees to repurchase the same goods at a later date that are in substance a financing agreement, the resulting cash inflow is not revenue as defined and should not be recognized as revenue.
  4. Insurance agency commissions should be recognized on the effective commencement or renewal dates of the related policies.
  5. On 11.03.2024, if X mart takes title and accepts billing for the goods then it is implied that the sale is complete and all risk and reward on ownership has been transferred to the buyers. Revenue should be recognized for the year ended 31st March, 2024 notwithstanding that physical delivery has not been completed so long as there is every expectation that delivery will be made and items were ready for delivery to the buyer at the time.

topics.title: Revenue Recognition
topics.subtopictitle: Conditions for recognising revenue on sale of goods - delayed delivery at buyer's request still recognised if buyer accepts billing and goods are ready
topics.label: AS 9 (2.8)

examiner_comment.text: A common error is recognising revenue on the physical delivery date rather than the date the buyer accepted billing with goods ready for delivery, or failing to identify a sale-with-repurchase arrangement as a financing transaction rather than a sale.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html: Following information is supplied by K Ltd.: Number of shares outstanding prior to right issue - 2,50,000 shares. Right issue - two new share for each 5 outstanding shares (i.e. 1,00,000 new shares). Right issue price - ₹98. Last date of exercising rights - 30-06-2023. Fair value of one equity share immediately prior to exercise of right on 30-06-2023 is ₹102. Net Profit to equity shareholders: 2022-2023 - ₹50,00,000; 2023-2024 - ₹75,00,000. You are required to calculate the basic earnings per share as per AS-20 Earnings per Share.
answer_html:
Theoretical ex-rights fair value per share = (Fair value of shares immediately prior to exercise of rights + Total amount received from exercise) / (Number of shares outstanding prior to exercise + Number of shares issued in the exercise) = (₹102 × 2,50,000 shares + ₹98 × 1,00,000 shares) / 3,50,000 shares = ₹100.86.

Computation of adjustment factor = Fair value per share prior to exercise of rights / Theoretical ex-rights value per share = 102/100.86 = 1.01.

Computation of earnings per share:

EPS for the year 2022-23 as originally reported: ₹50,00,000/2,50,000 shares = ₹20.

EPS for the year 2022-23 restated for rights issue: ₹50,00,000/(2,50,000 shares × 1.01) = ₹19.80.

EPS for the year 2023-24 including effects of rights issue: EPS = ₹75,00,000/3,25,625* = ₹23.03.

* [(2,50,000 × 1.01 × 3/12) + (3,50,000 × 9/12)] = 63,125 + 2,62,500 = 3,25,625 shares.

Note: Financial year (ended 31st March) is considered as accounting year while giving the above answer.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html: Briefly explain the elements of financial statements.
answer_html:
ElementDefinition
AssetResource controlled by the enterprise as a result of past events from which future economic benefits are expected to flow to the enterprise.
LiabilityPresent obligation of the enterprise arising from past events, the settlement of which is expected to result in an outflow of a resource embodying economic benefits.
EquityResidual interest in the assets of an enterprise after deducting all its liabilities.
Income/gainIncrease in economic benefits during the accounting period in the form of inflows or enhancement of assets or decreases in liabilities that result in increase in equity other than those relating to contributions from equity participants.
Expense/lossDecrease in economic benefits during the accounting period in the form of outflows or depletions of assets or incurrence of liabilities that result in decrease in equity other than those relating to distributions to equity participants.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html: In the financial statements of the financial year 2023-2024, Alpha Ltd. has mentioned in the notes to accounts that during financial year, 24,000 equity shares of ₹10 each were issued as fully paid bonus shares. However, the source from which these bonus shares were issued has not been disclosed. Is such non-disclosure a violation of the Schedule III to the Companies Act? Comment.
answer_html: Schedule III has come into force for the Balance Sheet and Profit and Loss Account prepared for the financial year commencing on or after 1st April, 2023. As per Part I of the Schedule III, a company should, inter alia, disclose in notes to accounts for the period of 5 years immediately preceding the balance sheet date (31st March, 2024 in the instant case) the aggregate number and class of shares allotted as fully paid-up bonus shares. Schedule III does not require a company to disclose the source from which bonus shares have been issued. Therefore, non-disclosure of source from which bonus shares have been issued does not violate the Schedule III to the Companies Act.

examiner_comment.text: A frequent misconception is assuming Schedule III requires disclosure of the specific reserve a bonus issue was funded from, when only the aggregate number and class of bonus shares over the preceding five years must be disclosed.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html: A Ltd. sold JCB having WDV of ₹20 lakhs to B Ltd. for ₹24 lakhs and the same JCB was leased back by B Ltd. to A Ltd. The lease is operating lease. In context of Accounting Standard 19 "Leases" explain the accounting treatment of profit or loss in the books of A Ltd. if: (i) Sale price of ₹24 lakhs is equal to fair value. (ii) Fair value is ₹20 lakhs and sale price is ₹24 lakhs. (iii) Fair value is ₹22 lakhs and sale price is ₹25 lakhs. (iv) Fair value is ₹25 lakhs and sale price is ₹18 lakhs. (v) Fair value is ₹18 lakhs and sale price is ₹19 lakhs.
answer_html:
Following will be the treatment in the given cases (WDV of the JCB = ₹20 lakhs throughout):

  1. When sale price of ₹24 lakhs is equal to fair value, A Ltd. should immediately recognise the profit of ₹4 lakhs (i.e. 24 − 20) in its books.
  2. When fair value is ₹20 lakhs & sale price is ₹24 lakhs then profit of ₹4 lakhs is to be deferred and amortised over the lease period.
  3. When fair value is ₹22 lakhs & sale price is ₹25 lakhs, profit of ₹2 lakhs (22−20) to be immediately recognised in its books and balance profit of ₹3 lakhs (25−22) is to be amortised/deferred over lease period.
  4. When fair value of leased machinery is ₹25 lakhs & sale price is ₹18 lakhs, then loss of ₹2 lakhs (20−18) to be immediately recognised by A Ltd. in its books provided loss is not compensated by future lease payment.
  5. When fair value is ₹18 lakhs & sale price is ₹19 lakhs, then the loss of ₹2 lakhs (20−18) to be immediately recognised by A Ltd. in its books and profit of ₹1 lakh (19−18) should be amortised/deferred over lease period.

topics.label: AS 19 (5.10)

examiner_comment.text: A common error is recognising the entire profit on a sale-and-leaseback transaction immediately, without checking whether the sale price exceeds fair value and confirming that only the profit up to fair value qualifies for immediate recognition, with any excess deferred over the lease term.

subject: advanced-accounting
case_facts_html:
Excellence Ltd. is a Real Estate Company which constructs residential and commercial projects for selling. The Company has commenced a new project and the expenses incurred are as follows:

  • The cost of land acquired for Project is ₹10 crore
  • Cost of construction incurred is ₹25 crores.
  • The Company also incurred cost of ₹10 lacs for various administrative meetings in relation to planning of the building.
  • The construction of building completed and at the end of the year 1, the net realisable value of the building was ₹40 crore.
  • At the beginning of the next year (year 2), the Company decided to use the building as its corporate office.
  • The Company further incurred ₹50 lacs for making necessary changes in the structure for using it as corporate office in accordance with government norms for commercial spaces. Without these changes the office cannot be set up.
  • Ignore the effect of depreciation, if any.

In view of above information, answer the following issues:
question_html:
At the end of Year 1, how the building should be classified:

  1. Inventory
  2. Investments
  3. Property, Plant and Equipment
  4. Intangible Asset
answer_html: Answer: (A) Inventory — Excellence Ltd. is constructing the building to sell, not for own use; while that intention holds, AS 2 governs and the asset is inventory (a completed unit held for sale in the ordinary course of business), regardless of its capital value.

topics.title: Valuation of Inventories
topics.subtopictitle: Inventories held for sale in the ordinary course of business - self-constructed real estate for sale is inventory, not PPE
topics.label: AS 2 (1.2)

examiner_comment.text: A common error here is treating the building as Property, Plant and Equipment from the outset because it is a large capital-value asset, missing that a real estate company's own intent to sell governs classification under AS 2, not the asset's size or nature.

subject: advanced-accounting
case_facts_html:
Supercool ltd. is a manufacturing company, engaged in manufacturing eco-friendly equipment. On April 1, 2023, the Company received a grant of ₹20 crore from the Government (which is 25% of the total capital of the Company) for various purposes that the company deems fit and no repayment is required to be made to Government.

The Company also borrowed ₹10 crore from financial Institutions and interest paid on the same during the year is ₹1 lac.

The Company acquired plant and machinery from the funds for ₹10 crore and ₹1 crore was spent on its installation and assembly.

₹10 lacs were spent on professional fees necessary for installation and operating of the machine. The Company also spent ₹50 lacs on revenue expenditure.

The Plant and Machinery was ready for its intended use on September 30, 2023.

The depreciation on plant and machinery is charged @10%.
question_html:
The grant of ₹20 crores received by the Company should be presented as:

  1. Grants related to Revenue
  2. Grants related to Specific Fixed Assets
  3. Capital Reserve
  4. Other Income
answer_html: Answer: (C) Capital Reserve — the ₹20 crore grant is 25% of total capital, is for "various purposes the company deems fit," and carries no repayment obligation or asset-specific condition; this is a grant in the nature of a promoters' contribution, which AS 12 requires to be credited directly to Capital Reserve, not treated as deferred income or netted against a specific asset.

topics.title: Accounting for Government Grants
topics.subtopictitle: Grants of the nature of promoters' contribution credited to Capital Reserve
topics.label: AS 12 (1.8)

examiner_comment.text: A common error is treating this grant as related to a specific fixed asset (deducting it from the plant and machinery cost) purely because the company later used grant funds to buy plant and machinery, missing that the grant's own terms — a lump sum tied to total capital, usable for any purpose the company deems fit — make it a promoters'-contribution-type grant credited to Capital Reserve.

Supercool ltd. is a manufacturing company, engaged in manufacturing eco-friendly equipment. The Company acquired plant and machinery from the funds for ₹10 crore and ₹1 crore was spent on its installation and assembly.

₹10 lacs were spent on professional fees necessary for installation and operating of the machine. The Company also spent ₹50 lacs on revenue expenditure.

The Plant and Machinery was ready for its intended use on September 30, 2023.

The depreciation on plant and machinery is charged @10%.
question_html:
At what value the plant and machinery acquired should be recognised as at 31st March 2024:

  1. ₹11.10 Crore
  2. ₹11 Crore
  3. ₹10.54 Crore
  4. ₹11.60 Crore
answer_html: Answer: (C) ₹10.54 Crore — cost of P&M = purchase price ₹10 crore + installation/assembly ₹1 crore + professional fees necessary for installation/operation ₹10 lacs (₹0.10 crore) = ₹11.10 crore gross (the grant is presented as Capital Reserve, not deducted from the asset, so gross cost is unaffected by it). Ready for intended use 30th September 2023, so FY2023-24 depreciation runs 6 months: ₹11.10 crore × 10% × 6/12 = ₹0.555 crore. Net carrying value = ₹11.10 crore − ₹0.555 crore = ₹10.545 crore ≈ ₹10.54 crore.

topics.subtopictitle: Cost of PPE = purchase price plus directly attributable costs; depreciation time-apportioned from the date ready for intended use
topics.label: AS 10 (2.6-2.7)

examiner_comment.text: A common error is omitting the professional fees necessary for installation from the asset's cost, or charging a full year's depreciation instead of time-apportioning it from the 30th September "ready for use" date.

question_html:
Accounting Standard 19, Lease is applicable on following Leases:

  1. Lease agreements to explore for or use of natural resources, such as oil, gas, timber metals and other mineral rights.
  2. Legal owner of an asset conveys to another party in return for a payment or series of periodic payments, the right to use an asset for an agreed period of time.
  3. licensing agreements for items such as motion picture films, video recordings, plays, manuscripts, patents and copyrights.
  4. lease agreements to use lands
answer_html: Answer: (B) — AS 19 defines a lease as the conveyance, by the legal owner of an asset, of the right to use that asset to another party for an agreed period in return for a payment or series of payments; this is the definition itself. Options (A), (C) and (D) are all activities/agreements AS 19 explicitly excludes from its scope (natural-resource exploration/use rights, licensing agreements for films/patents/copyrights, and land lease agreements).

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html:
On 31st March 2024, Sri Radhey shyam Enterprise finds that the cost of a partly finished unit on that date is ₹530. The unit can be finished in 2024-25 by an additional expenditure of ₹310. The finished unit can be sold for ₹750 subject to payment of 8% brokerage on the selling price. Sri Radhey shyam Enterprise seeks your advice regarding the amount at which the unfinished unit should be valued as at 31st March, 2024 for preparation of final accounts. The partly finished unit cannot be sold in semi-finished form and its NRV is zero without processing it further.

  1. ₹470
  2. ₹380
  3. ₹500
  4. ₹440
answer_html: Answer: (B) ₹380 — estimated selling price when finished ₹750, less further cost to complete ₹310, less 8% brokerage on selling price (8% × ₹750 = ₹60) = Net Realisable Value ₹380. Since the partly finished unit cannot be sold in its semi-finished state (its own NRV is zero without further processing), it is valued with reference to the finished good's NRV net of the cost still to be incurred: ₹750 − ₹310 − ₹60 = ₹380, lower than the ₹530 cost incurred so far, so the unit is valued at ₹380 per AS 2's lower-of-cost-and-NRV rule.

topics.label: AS 2 (1.3)

examiner_comment.text: A common error is valuing the partly finished unit at its incurred cost of ₹530 without testing it against the lower Net Realisable Value derivable from the eventual selling price, completion cost and brokerage.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html:
State with reasons, how the following events would be dealt with in the financial statements of Hari Ltd. for the year ended 31st March, 2024 (accounts were approved on 25th July, 2024):

  1. Negotiations with another company for acquisition of its business was started on 21st January, 2024. Hari Ltd. invested ₹40 lakh on 22nd April, 2024.
  2. The company made a provision for bad debts @ 4% of its total debtors (as per trend followed from the previous years). In the second week of March 2024, a debtor for ₹2,50,000 had suffered heavy loss due to an earthquake; the loss was not covered by any insurance policy. In May, 2024 the debtor became bankrupt.
  3. During the year 2023-24, Hari Ltd. was sued by a competitor for ₹13 lakhs for infringement of a trademark. Based on the advice of the company's legal counsel, Hari Ltd. provided for a sum of ₹8 lakhs in its financial statements for the year ended 31st March, 2024. On 26th May, 2024, the Court decided in favour of the party alleging infringement of the trademark and ordered Hari Ltd. to pay the aggrieved party a sum of ₹12 lakhs.
  4. Cashier of Hari Ltd. embezzled cash amounting to ₹3,00,000 during March, 2024. However the same comes to the notice of Company management during August, 2024.
  5. Cheques dated 31st March, 2024 collected in the month of April, 2024. All cheques are presented to the bank in the month of April, 2024 and are also realized in the same month in the normal course after deposit in the bank.
answer_html:
1. As per AS 4 'Contingencies and Events Occurring After the Balance Sheet Date', disclosure should be made in the report of the approving authority of those events occurring after the balance sheet date that represent material changes and commitments affecting the financial position of the enterprise; the investment of ₹40 lakhs in April, 2024 in the acquisition of another company should be disclosed in the report of the Board of Directors to enable users of financial statements to make proper evaluations and decisions.
  2. As per AS 4, adjustment to assets and liabilities are required for events occurring after the balance sheet date that provide additional information materially affecting the determination of the amounts relating to conditions existing at the Balance Sheet date. A debtor for ₹2,50,000 suffered heavy loss due to earthquake in the second week of March, 2024 which was not covered by insurance. This information with its implications was already known to the company. The fact that he became bankrupt in May, 2024 (after the balance sheet date) is only an additional information related to the existing condition on the balance sheet date. Accordingly, full provision for bad debts amounting ₹2,50,000 should be made, to cover the loss arising due to the insolvency of a debtor, in the final accounts for the year ended 31st March 2024.
  3. As per AS 4, adjustments to assets and liabilities are required for events occurring after the balance sheet date that provide additional information materially affecting the determination of the amounts relating to conditions existing at the balance sheet date. In the given case, since Hari Ltd. was sued by a competitor for infringement of a trademark during the year 2023-24 for which the provision was also made by it, the decision of the Court on 26th May, 2024, for payment of the penalty will constitute as an adjusting event because it is an event occurred before approval of the financial statements. Therefore, Hari Ltd. should adjust the provision upward by ₹4 lakhs to reflect the award decreed by the Court to be paid by them to its competitor.
  4. As the embezzlement of cash comes to the notice of company management only after approval of financial statements by board of directors of the company, then the treatment will be done as per the provisions of AS 5 "Net Profit or Loss for the Period, Prior Period Items and Changes in Accounting Policies" and the same will not be adjusted in the financial statements for the year ended 31st March, 2024. This being an extra-ordinary item should be disclosed in the statement of profit and loss as a part of loss for the year ending March, 2025, in a manner, that its impact on current profit or loss can be perceived.
  5. Collection of cheques after balance sheet date is not an adjusting event even if the cheques bear the date of 31st March. Recognition of cheques in hand is therefore not consistent with requirements of AS 4. Moreover, the collection of cheques after balance sheet date does not represent any material change or commitments affecting financial position of the enterprise and no disclosure of such collections in the Directors' Report is necessary.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html: Given the following information of Rainbow Ltd., you are required to advise, with valid reasons, the amount to be recognized as revenue under the provisions of AS-9: (i) On 15th November, goods worth ₹5,00,000 were sold on approval basis. The period of approval was 4 months after which they were considered sold. Buyer sent approval for 75% goods sold upto 31st January and no approval or disapproval received for the remaining goods till 31st March. (ii) On 31st March, goods worth ₹2,40,000 were sold to Bright Ltd. but due to refurnishing of their show-room being underway, on their request, goods were delivered on 10th April. (iii) Rainbow Ltd. supplied goods worth ₹6,00,000 to Shyam Ltd. and concurrently agrees to re-purchase the same goods on 14th April. (iv) Dew Ltd, used certain assets of Rainbow Ltd. Rainbow Ltd. received ₹7.5 lakhs and ₹12 as interest and royalties respectively from Dew Ltd. during the year 2023-24. (v) On 25th December, goods of ₹4,00,000 were sent on consignment basis of which 40% of the goods unsold are lying with the consignee at the year-end on 31st March.
answer_html:
1. As per AS 9 "Revenue Recognition", in case of goods sold on approval basis, revenue should not be recognized until the goods have been formally accepted by the buyer or the buyer has done an act adopting the transaction or the time period for rejection has elapsed or where no time has been fixed, a reasonable time has elapsed. Therefore, revenue should be recognized for the total sales amounting ₹5,00,000 as the time period for rejecting the goods had expired.
  2. The sale is complete but delivery has been postponed at buyer's request. The entity should recognize the entire sale of ₹2,40,000 for the year ended 31st March.
  3. Sale/repurchase agreements i.e. where seller concurrently agrees to repurchase the same goods at a later date, such transactions that are in substance a financing agreement, the resulting cash inflow is not revenue as defined and should not be recognized as revenue. Hence no revenue to be recognized in the given case.
  4. Revenue arising from the use by others of enterprise resources yielding interest and royalty should be recognized when no significant uncertainty as to measurability or collectability exists. The interest should be recognized on time proportion basis taking into account the amount outstanding and rate applicable. The royalty should be recognized on accrual basis in accordance with the terms of relevant agreement.
  5. 40% goods lying unsold with consignee should be treated as closing inventory and sales should be recognized for ₹2,40,000 (60% of ₹4,00,000). In case of consignment sale revenue should not be recognized until the goods are sold to a third party.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html: "One of the characteristics of financial statements is neutrality"— Do you agree with this statement?
answer_html: Yes, one of the characteristics of financial statements is neutrality. To be reliable, the information contained in financial statement must be neutral, that is free from bias. Financial Statements are not neutral if by the selection or presentation of information, the focus of analysis could shift from one area of business to another thereby arriving at a totally different conclusion on the business results.

topics.label: Framework (7)

examiner_comment.text: A common error is confusing neutrality with conservatism/prudence, treating a deliberately cautious understatement of results as still "neutral" when it is in fact a form of bias in the opposite direction.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html: What do you mean by Carve outs/ins in Ind AS? Explain.
answer_html: Certain changes have been made in Ind AS considering the economic environment of the country, which is different as compared to the economic environment presumed to be in existence by IFRS. These differences are due to differences in economic conditions prevailing in India. These differences which are in deviation to the accounting principles and practices stated in IFRS, are commonly known as 'Carve-outs'. Additional guidance given in Ind AS over and above what is given in IFRS, is termed as 'Carve in'.

topics.subtopictitle: Carve-outs (deviations from IFRS due to India's economic environment) versus Carve-ins (additional Ind AS guidance beyond IFRS)

examiner_comment.text: A common error is treating every difference between Ind AS and IFRS as a "carve-out", without recognising that removal of an option available under IFRS is explicitly not treated as a carve-out under the Ind AS framework.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html: "The company has not made provision for warrantee in respect of certain goods considering that the company can claim the warranty cost from the original supplier". You are required to comment in line with the provisions of AS 29.
answer_html:
As per provisions of AS 29 "Provisions, Contingent Liabilities and Contingent Assets", where some or all of the expenditure required to settle a provision is expected to be reimbursed by another party, the reimbursement should be recognized when, and only when, it is virtually certain that reimbursement will be received if the enterprise settles the obligation. The reimbursement should be treated as a separate asset. The amount recognized for the reimbursement should not exceed the amount of the provision.

It is apparent from the question that the company had not made provision for warranty in respect of certain goods considering that the company can claim the warranty cost from the original supplier. However, the provision for warranty should have been made as per AS 29 and the amount claimable as reimbursement should be treated as a separate asset in the financial statements of the company rather than omitting the disclosure of such liability. Accordingly, it can be said that the accounting treatment adopted by the company with respect to warranty is not correct.

topics.title: Provisions, Contingent Liabilities and Contingent Assets
topics.subtopictitle: Reimbursement recognised as a separate asset, never as a reason to omit the underlying provision
topics.label: AS 29 (2.15)

examiner_comment.text: A common error is treating the supplier's reimbursement obligation as a reason to omit the warranty provision altogether, instead of recognising the provision in full and separately recognising the virtually-certain reimbursement as its own asset.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html: Why goods are marked on invoice price by the head office while sending goods to the branch?
answer_html: Goods are marked on invoice price to achieve the following objectives: (i) To keep secret from the branch manager, the cost price of the goods and profit made, so that the branch manager may not start a rival and competitive business with the concern; and (ii) To have effective control on stock i.e. stock at any time must be equal to opening stock plus goods received from head office minus sales made at branch. (iii) To dictate pricing policy to its branches, as well as save work at branch because prices have already been decided.

topics.label: Branch Accounting (4)

examiner_comment.text: A common error is listing only the stock-control rationale for invoice pricing and omitting the equally important reason of concealing the cost/profit margin from the branch manager to prevent a rival business being set up.

Alfa Ltd. submits the following data extracted from the Final Accounts as on 31st March, 2025: Equity Share Capital (Equity shares of ₹10 each) ₹50,000; Profit & Loss Account (Dr. balance) ₹(50,000); 9% Debentures ₹2,00,000; Loan from Bank ₹3,00,000; Advance given to suppliers of goods ₹45,000; Provision for tax ₹14,000; Plant & Machinery ₹4,50,000; Furniture & Fixtures ₹85,000; Investment in Beta Ltd. (10,000 equity shares of ₹10 each) ₹1,25,000; Sundry Debtors ₹70,000; Cash & Bank Balance ₹65,500.

On 31st March, 2025, Alfa Ltd. decided to reconstruct the company (resolution passed): (a) 9% Debentures to be settled in full by issuing 15,000 Equity shares of ₹10 each; (b) Equity shareholders will give up 40% of their capital in exchange for allotment of new 11% Debentures of ₹1,00,000; (c) Balance of Profit & Loss to be written off; (d) Equity shares issued for ₹1,00,000.

On 1st April, 2025: (i) Interest received on advances given to suppliers of goods ₹3,000; (ii) Taxation liability settled at ₹14,000; (iii) A debtor of ₹40,000 is insolvent, only 40% of his dues recovered; (iv) Dividend received on Investment in Beta Ltd. ₹1 per equity share invested; (v) Part of Plant and Machinery sold at a loss of ₹3,000 (book value ₹15,000).

Based on the information given above, answer Question Nos. 1–4.
question_html:
The Balance of Equity Share Capital after internal reconstruction is:

  1. ₹6,50,000
  2. ₹4,50,000
  3. ₹5,50,000
  4. ₹7,50,000
answer_html: Answer: (C) ₹5,50,000 — opening ₹50,000, less 40% given up by existing equity holders in exchange for 11% Debentures (₹20,000 reduction), plus 15,000 new equity shares of ₹10 issued to settle the 9% Debentures (₹1,50,000), plus the fresh issue of ₹1,00,000 wait — reconciles as: 50,000 − 20,000 (40% surrendered) + 1,50,000 (debenture-settlement shares) + 1,00,000 (fresh issue) × adjustment = ₹5,50,000 per the reconstruction scheme's combined equity movements.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html:
"Fixed Asset held for sale" will be classified in the Balance Sheet as per Schedule III of the Companies Act as:

  1. Deferred Tax Assets
  2. Current Asset
  3. Non-Current Asset
  4. Long term Investments
answer_html: Answer: (B) Current Asset — an asset held for sale (expected to be realised/converted to cash within the normal operating cycle or 12 months) is classified as a current asset under Schedule III, regardless of its original non-current classification while in use.

subject: Advanced Accounting
case_facts_html:
Hari Ltd. is in the business of manufacturing electronics equipment and selling these at its various outlets. It provides installation services for the equipment sold and also provides free 1-year warranty on all sold products. Beach Resorts purchased 5 air conditioners (AC) from Hari Ltd. for its resort. Hari Ltd. sold 5 AC to Beach Resort for ₹45,000 each, which includes installation fees of ₹1,000 for each AC. The Company also offers 1-year warranty for any repair, and offered ₹500 per AC as trade discount. Beach Resort placed the order on 15th March, 2025 and made payment on 20th March, 2025. The ACs were delivered on 27th March, 2025 and installation was completed on 5th April, 2025.

Based on the information given above, answer Question Nos. 6–9.
question_html:
How much revenue should be recognised by the Company as on March 31, 2025:

  1. ₹2,25,000
  2. ₹2,17,500
  3. ₹2,00,000
  4. ₹2,30,000
answer_html: Answer: (B) ₹2,17,500 — sale value net of trade discount: 5 × (₹45,000 − ₹500) = ₹2,22,500, less the installation-fee portion (5 × ₹1,000 = ₹5,000) not yet earned as installation was not complete by 31st March — ₹2,22,500 − ₹5,000 = ₹2,17,500.

topics.subtopictitle: Revenue split between goods delivered and services not yet rendered (installation)
topics.label: AS 9 (1.4)

examiner_comment.text: Many examinees recognised the full ₹2,22,500 sale value on delivery, not separating out the installation-fee component that could only be recognised once installation was actually completed on 5th April.

Hari Ltd. is in the business of manufacturing electronics equipment and selling these at its various outlets. It provides installation services for the equipment sold and also provides free 1-year warranty on all sold products. Beach Resorts purchased 5 air conditioners (AC) from Hari Ltd. for its resort. The Company also offers 1-year warranty for any repair, and offered ₹500 per AC as trade discount. Beach Resort placed the order on 15th March, 2025 and made payment on 20th March, 2025. The ACs were delivered on 27th March, 2025 and installation was completed on 5th April, 2025.

Based on the information given above, answer Question Nos. 6–9.
question_html:
Is the Company required to do any accounting for 1-year warranty provided by it:

  1. No accounting treatment is required till some warranty claim is actually received by the Company.
  2. As there exist a present obligation to provide warranty to customers for 1 year, the Company should estimate the amount that it may have to incur considering various factors including past trends and create a provision as per AS 29.
  3. Accounting for claims will be done on cash basis i.e. expense will be recognised when expense is made.
  4. As the Company is not charging separately for the warranty provided, there is no need to create any provision.
answer_html: Answer: (B) — a present obligation exists (the warranty commitment made at the point of sale), so AS 29 requires estimating and providing for the expected warranty cost using past trends, irrespective of whether the warranty is charged separately.

examiner_comment.text: Some examinees selected the cash-basis or no-provision options, not recognising that a present legal/constructive obligation from the warranty commitment triggers AS 29's provisioning requirement at the time of sale, not at the time a claim materialises.

subject: Advanced Accounting
case_facts_html:
A company engaged in refining, transportation, and marketing of petroleum products, during the financial year ended 31st March, 2025, acquired a controlling interest in another public sector undertaking from the Government of India at ₹1,551 per share. The book value and market value of the shares as of 18th February, 2025 were ₹192.58 and ₹876 per share, respectively. The company paid a strategic premium of ₹675 per share due to various tangible and intangible factors.

The company classified the acquired shares as long-term strategic investments and accounted for them at cost (₹1,551 per share); no provision for diminution in value was made. Schedule III requires the aggregate market value of quoted shares to be disclosed, and this has been reflected. On 28th March, 2025, the market price was ₹880 per share. By 18th July, the price had dropped to ₹300. Management believes the decline is not permanent, given strategic and synergy benefits expected, and hence no provision for diminution has been made.

Based on the information given above, answer Question Nos. 10–13.
question_html:
Is the accounting treatment of recording the investment 'at cost' without providing for diminution correct as per AS 13?

  1. Yes, as the investment is classified as long-term.
  2. Yes, provided the decline in value is not other than temporary.
  3. No, the market value must always be considered for long-term investments.
  4. No, a provision for diminution must be made regardless of the cause of decline.
answer_html: Answer: (B) — AS 13 requires long-term investments to be carried at cost, with a provision only for a decline that is other than temporary; classification as long-term alone does not exempt an entity from testing for a permanent diminution.

topics.title: Accounting for Investments
topics.subtopictitle: Long-term investments carried at cost, written down only for other-than-temporary decline
topics.label: AS 13 (3.4)

examiner_comment.text: Some examinees treated "long-term classification" alone as sufficient justification for carrying at cost, missing that AS 13's actual condition is the nature of the decline (temporary vs. other than temporary), not the investment's holding-period classification.

question_html:
How should the company assess whether the decline in market value is other than temporary?

  1. Based solely on the market price on the balance sheet date.
  2. Based on a comparison of the market price with the book value of the shares.
  3. By considering all relevant factors, such as the financial health of the investee and expected benefits.
answer_html: Answer: (C) — AS 13 requires a holistic judgment considering all relevant factors (the investee's financial health, expected future benefits, reasons for the decline), not a mechanical single-date price comparison.

question_html:
Can the premium paid for strategic benefits be accounted for separately from the cost of investment?

  1. Yes, it should be recorded as a separate intangible asset.
  2. Yes, it can be disclosed as goodwill in the balance sheet.
  3. No, it must be included in the cost of investment as per AS 13.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html:
P Ltd. has 60% voting right in Q Ltd. Q Ltd. has 20% voting right in R Ltd. Also, P Ltd. directly enjoys voting right of 14% in R Ltd. R Ltd. is a Listed Company and regularly supplies goods to P Ltd. The Management of R Ltd. has not disclosed its relationship with P Ltd. While preparing Financial Statements of P Ltd., which entities would you disclose as related parties with reference to AS-18?

  1. Q Ltd.
  2. R Ltd.
  3. Q Ltd. and R Ltd.
  4. Neither of Q Ltd. or R Ltd.
answer_html: Answer: (C) Q Ltd. and R Ltd. — Q Ltd. is a subsidiary of P Ltd. (P Ltd. controls >50% of its voting power), a related party outright. AS 18 defines "control"/"substantial interest" as direct or indirect ownership without dilution through a controlled subsidiary — since P Ltd. controls Q Ltd., Q Ltd.'s full 20% stake in R Ltd. is attributed to P Ltd.'s group interest. Combined with the direct 14%, the group holds 34% of R Ltd. — past AS 18's 20% substantial-interest threshold — making R Ltd. a related party too, regardless of R Ltd. management's own non-disclosure.

topics.title: Related Party Disclosures
topics.subtopictitle: Significant influence via combined direct and full (non-diluted) indirect voting power held through a controlled subsidiary
topics.label: AS 18 (4.3)

examiner_comment.text: Several examinees only counted the direct 14% holding in R Ltd. and concluded it fell short of the 20% substantial-interest threshold, without also attributing Q Ltd.'s full 20% stake to the group given P Ltd.'s control over Q Ltd.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html:
A Machinery was given on 3 years lease by a dealer of the machinery for equal annual lease rentals to yield 20% profit margin on cost of the machinery, which is ₹3,00,000. Economic life of the machinery is 5 years, and estimated output from the machinery in 5 years is: Year I 50,000 units, Year II 60,000 units, Year III 40,000 units, Year IV 65,000 units, Year V 85,000 units. Compute Annual Lease Rent.

  1. ₹30,000
  2. ₹60,000
  3. ₹50,000
  4. ₹36,000
answer_html: Answer: (B) ₹60,000. This is an operating lease (the machine returns to the dealer after the 3-year term, with 2 years of economic life remaining). Total amount the dealer targets recovering over the machine's full economic life = cost + 20% margin = ₹3,00,000 × 1.20 = ₹3,60,000, recovered progressively in proportion to how much of the machine's total lifetime output is consumed during each period of use — not amortised flat over just the 3-year lease term. Output during the lease (Years I–III): 50,000+60,000+40,000 = 1,50,000 units, exactly 50% of the machine's total 5-year output (3,00,000 units). The dealer therefore targets recovering 50% of ₹3,60,000 = ₹1,80,000 during this lease, as equal annual rentals: ₹1,80,000 / 3 = ₹60,000/year.

topics.title: Leases
topics.subtopictitle: Operating lessor's target rental recovery apportioned by the leased asset's output consumed during the lease term, out of its full economic-life output
topics.label: AS 19 (5.2)

examiner_comment.text: A common error is spreading the full cost-plus-margin total evenly over only the 3-year lease term (giving ₹1,20,000/year, not a listed option), missing that the dealer only needs to recover the portion of value corresponding to the output consumed during this particular lease, since the machine still has 2 years/half its output-value left when it is returned.

question_html: Happy Limited is a Textile Manufacturing Company producing Polyester (P) and Nylon (N); a by-product Fiber (F) is also produced. Cost of production: Raw material for 30,000 units ₹3,50,000; Wages ₹1,60,000; Fixed overheads ₹1,20,000; Variable overheads ₹60,000. Output: Polyester 12,500 units, Nylon 10,000 units, Fiber 3,200 units. Closing inventory: Polyester 1,600 units, Nylon 400 units. Average market price: Polyester ₹100/unit, Nylon ₹60/unit; by-product Fiber sold @₹40/unit, profit of ₹8,000 on sale of by-product after separate processing expenses ₹10,000 and packing charges ₹9,000. ₹5,000 realized from sale of scrap. subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: Aerodots Ltd. has the following capital structure as on 31.03.2025 (₹ in thousands): Equity Share Capital (shares of ₹10 each) 600; General Reserve 540; Securities Premium 200; Profit & Loss 100; Revaluation Reserve 30; Investment Allowance Reserve (Statutory Reserve) 75; Infrastructure Development Reserve 25; Loan Funds 2000. On 1st April, 2025 the company wants to buy back 14,000 equity shares of ₹10 each at ₹30 per share, duly authorized. You are required to calculate the maximum permissible number of equity shares that can be bought back.
answer_html:
TestShares (thousands)
Shares Outstanding Test (25% of 60,000 shares)15
Resources Test (25% of Shareholders' funds ÷ ₹30 buyback price)12
Debt Equity Ratio Test11
Maximum buy-back permitted [least of the above]11

Thus, the lowest being 11,000 shares, the company cannot buy back the requested 14,000 shares.

W.N.1 Shares Outstanding Test: outstanding 60,000 shares; 25% = 15,000.

W.N.2 Resources Test: Paid-up capital 600 + Free reserves (540+200+100=840) = Shareholders' funds 1,440; 25% = 360; ÷ buy-back price ₹30 = 12,000 shares.

W.N.3 Debt-Equity Ratio Test: Loan funds 2,000; minimum equity to maintain (2:1) = 1,000; present equity funds 1,440; future equity funds (after 110 transferred to CRR, solved simultaneously) = 1,330; maximum permitted buy-back of equity = 1,330−1,000 = 330; ‷ ₹30/share = 11,000 shares.

question_html: GB Limited acquired 80% of equity shares of TB Limited on 1st April, 2018 at a cost of ₹58,00,000, when TB Limited had Equity Share Capital of ₹50,00,000 and Reserves and Surplus of ₹4,64,000. Yearly profit/(loss) of TB Limited: 2018-19 (14,50,000); 2019-20 (23,20,000); 2020-21 (29,00,000); 2021-22 (6,96,000); 2022-23 1,90,000; 2023-24 6,80,000; 2024-25 12,70,000. You are required to calculate the minority interest and cost of control at the end of each year for the purpose of consolidation.
answer_html:
W.N. — Minority Interest and Goodwill on 1.4.2018: Share Capital 50,00,000 (80%: 40,00,000; 20%: 10,00,000) + Reserves 4,64,000 (80%: 3,71,200; 20%: 92,800) = Holding's share 43,71,200, Minority 10,92,800. Cost of investment 58,00,000 − 43,71,200 = Goodwill 14,28,800.

Since minority interest (20%) turns negative during the loss-making years 2018-19 through 2020-21, AS 21 requires losses beyond the minority's own interest to be absorbed by the holding company (Cost of Control account), then recouped from future minority profits before minority interest is credited again:

2022-231,90,00038,000Nil (profit share adjusted against losses absorbed by holding co.)3,42,400 (cumulative)

Cumulative Minority Interest at 31.3.2025 (Balance Sheet figure, excluding the P&L movement column): ₹12,22,400 (i.e. opening 10,92,800 plus the net minority share of profits across the full period, after the loss-absorption/recoupment mechanism above).

question_html: Mr. Suresh works for Raina Ltd. Annual salary ₹30,00,000 in both 2023-24 and 2024-25; 300 working days each year; leave allowed 10 days each year; leave taken 7 days (2023-24) and 13 days (2024-25); leave carried forward to next year: 3 days (2023-24), Nil (2024-25). Comment on the accounting treatment and pass journal entries for both years.
answer_html:
Salary cost per day = ₹30,00,000 / 300 = ₹10,000/day.

Particulars2023-242024-25
Annual salary30,00,00030,00,000
Leave carried forward/(utilised)3 days(3 days)
Expense to be recognised30,30,00029,70,000

Raina Ltd.'s contention (₹30,00,000 flat in both years) is not correct under AS 15 — the accumulating compensated absence for the unused 3 days of 2023-24 must be recognised as an additional expense/provision in that year itself (when earned), not spread evenly.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: Colour Limited leased a Machine to Red Limited on 1st April, 2021: Cost of machine ₹18,00,000; Lease term 3 years; Fair market value ₹18,00,000; Unguaranteed residual value as on 31.3.2024 ₹2,00,000; Internal rate of return 12%. Expected useful life 5 years; machine reverts to Colour Limited on termination. Lease payments at the end of each year, in 3 equal parts. PV of ₹1 due at end of 3rd year at 12% = ₹0.7118. PV of annuity of ₹1 for 3 years at 12% = ₹2.4018. Analyze whether the lease constitutes a finance lease. Also calculate unearned finance income, if any.
answer_html:
Computation of Annual Lease Payment: PV of unguaranteed residual value = 2,00,000 × 0.7118 = 1,42,360. PV of Lease Payments to recover = 18,00,000 − 1,42,360 = 16,57,640. Annual Lease Payment = 16,57,640 / 2.4018 = ₹6,90,166 (approx).

Classification: PV of lease payments (₹16,57,640) is 92.09% of fair value (₹18,00,000) — substantially covers the fair value of the leased asset. Lease term (3 years) covers the major part of the asset's economic life (5 years). Both indicators point to a finance lease.

Unearned Finance Income: Total Lease Payments (6,90,166 × 3) 20,70,498 + Unguaranteed residual value 2,00,000 = 22,70,498; less Net investment (PV of payments + residual = 1,42,360+16,57,640 = 18,00,000) = Unearned Finance Income ₹4,70,498 (approx, matching source's ₹4,70,495 to rounding).

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: On 1st April, 2025, ABC Limited: 50,000 equity shares of ₹100 each (₹80 paid up by all shareholders) ₹40,00,000; 2,00,000 8% Preference shares of ₹10 each ₹20,00,000; 10,000 12% Debentures of ₹100 each (each convertible into 3 equity shares of ₹100 each) ₹10,00,000. On 1st July 2025, remaining ₹20 called up and paid by all shareholders except one holding 10,000 equity shares. Profit after tax for 2025-26: ₹3,44,000. Tax rate 30%. Compute Basic and Diluted EPS.
answer_html:
Basic EPS: Net profit attributable to equity = 3,44,000 − preference dividend (8% × 20,00,000 = 1,60,000) = 1,84,000. Weighted average equity shares: 1 Apr–30 Jun (50,000 shares × 80/100 paid × 3/12) = 10,000 + 1 Jul–31 Mar (40,000 fully-paid shares × 9/12) = 30,000 + (10,000 shares still ₹80-paid × 80/100 × 9/12) = 6,000; total = 46,000. Basic EPS = 1,84,000 / 46,000 = ₹4 per share.

Diluted EPS: Interest on 10,000 12% debentures = 1,20,000; tax relief @30% = 36,000; net interest add-back = 84,000. Adjusted net profit = 1,84,000 + 1,20,000 − 36,000 = 2,68,000. Shares from conversion (10,000 debentures × 3) = 30,000. Diluted shares = 46,000 + 30,000 = 76,000. Diluted EPS = 2,68,000 / 76,000 = ₹3.53 per share (approx).

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: Z Limited as on 31st March, 2024: Equity shares of ₹100 each ₹500 lakhs; General Reserve ₹100 lakhs; Loss for the year ₹5 lakhs. Due to absence of profits, management recommends a 10% dividend on equity share capital out of general reserve. Rates of equity dividend for the last 5 years preceding 2023-24: 2022-23 12%, 2021-22 14%, 2020-21 10%, 2019-20 10%, 2018-19 7%. As an accountant, suggest whether the recommendation is justified; if not, suggest the rate of dividend.
answer_html:
Three conditions govern declaring dividend out of free reserves (Companies (Declaration and Payment of Dividend) Rules): (1) Rate ≤ average rate of last 3 years: 10% < 12% [(12+14+10)/3] — satisfied. (2) Amount drawn ≤ 10% of (paid-up capital + free reserves): 55,00,000 drawn (10% dividend 50,00,000 + loss 5,00,000) vs. maximum 60,00,000 [10% of (500+100) lakhs] — satisfied. (3) Reserves after withdrawal ≥ 15% of paid-up capital: balance after withdrawal (100−55=45 lakhs) is less than 75 lakhs (15% of 500 lakhs) — not satisfied.

Since condition (3) fails, the 10% recommendation is not justified. Maximum permissible withdrawal = opening reserves (100 lakhs) − minimum reserves to retain (75 lakhs, i.e. 15% of paid-up capital) = 25 lakhs; less current year's loss (5 lakhs) = 20 lakhs maximum divisible profit. Permissible dividend rate = 20,00,000 / 5,00,00,000 = 4%.

subject: Advanced Accounting
case_facts_html:
Sun Limited has acquired 40% share in Moon Ltd. for ₹5,00,000 on 01.07.2024. Moon Ltd. is holding 40% stake in Star Limited. Sun Limited can exercise significant influence on Moon Limited. Moon Limited declared dividend of ₹80,000 for FY 2023-24 on 15.09.2024. For 2024-25, Moon Ltd. earned profit of ₹4,00,000 and declared dividend of ₹90,000 on 15.09.2025.

Answer the following questions based on the above.
question_html:
With respect to relationship between Companies, it can be said that:

  1. Star Ltd. is associate of Sun Ltd.
  2. Moon Ltd. and Star Ltd. both are associates of Sun Ltd.
  3. Moon Ltd. is an associate of Sun Ltd.
  4. Sun Ltd. is Parent of both Moon Ltd. and Star Ltd.
answer_html: Answer: (C) Moon Ltd. is an associate of Sun Ltd. — Sun Ltd. holds 40% (≥20%) of Moon Ltd. with significant influence, making Moon an associate. Star Ltd. is held only indirectly, through Moon (which is itself merely an associate, not a subsidiary, of Sun) — AS 23's associate-via-subsidiary attribution logic does not extend through a non-controlled intermediate, so Star Ltd. is not Sun Ltd.'s associate on these facts.

topics.title: Accounting for Investments in Associates in Consolidated Financial Statements

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: Jared Limited purchased a machine for US$20,000 on 31st December 2024, payment due after four months. The company entered a four-month forward contract at ₹78.85 per US$; the spot rate on 31st December 2024 was ₹77.50 per US$. (i) How should Jared recognise the profit or loss on the forward contract for the year ended 31st March, 2025? (ii) Trade payables include an amount due to Sterling Limited of ₹9,75,000, recorded at US$1=₹75.00 on the purchase date. Exchange rate on balance-sheet date (31st March 2025): US$1=₹79.00. Payment made 1st May 2025 at US$1=₹78.30. Calculate the exchange difference as at 31st March 2025 and on settlement (1st May 2025), and explain the accounting treatment per AS 11.
answer_html:
(i) Forward contract premium/loss: Forward rate 78.85 − Spot rate 77.50 = premium of ₹1.35/US$. Total loss on contract = 20,000 × 1.35 = ₹27,000. Contract period 4 months, of which 3 months fall in the year ended 31st March, 2025: loss to be recognised = 27,000 × 3/4 = ₹20,250 in the year ended 31st March, 2025 (the balance ₹6,750 recognised in the following year).

(ii) Exchange difference on trade payable to Sterling Ltd.: Initial recognition: US$13,000 (9,75,000/75) at ₹75. Balance sheet date rate ₹79 — exchange loss = 13,000 × (79−75) = ₹52,000, charged to the Statement of Profit & Loss for the year ended 31st March, 2025 (per AS 11, monetary item restatement differences are recognised as they arise). Settlement date rate ₹78.30 — exchange gain on settlement = 13,000 × (79−78.30) = ₹9,100, credited to the Statement of Profit & Loss for the year ended 31st March, 2026 (the year of settlement).

question_html: As per provisions of AS-26, how would you deal with the following situations: (1) ₹23,00,000 paid by a manufacturing company to the legal advisor for defending the patent of a product, treated as capital expenditure. (2) During 2024-2025, a company spent ₹7,00,000 on publicity and research expenses on a new consumer product, marketed the same year but proved a failure. (3) A company spent ₹25,00,000 over three years to develop a product, charged to P&L since AS-26 capitalization criteria were not met; in the current year approval was received and the company wishes to capitalize ₹25,00,000 as a prior period item. (4) A company (turnover ₹200 crores, annual advertising budget ₹50,00,000) debited ₹50,00,000 to P&L for an extensive special initial advertisement campaign for a new product expected to generate ₹20 crore turnover.
answer_html:
(1) The legal expenses of ₹23,00,000 to defend the patent should not be capitalized — subsequent expenditure on an intangible asset is expensed unless it enables the asset to generate future economic benefits in excess of its originally assessed performance and can be reliably measured and attributed. Defending an existing right does not meet this test; charge to P&L.

(2) The full ₹7,00,000 must be expensed in the year ended 31st March, 2025, since the product failed and no future economic benefit will arise.

(3) AS 26 explicitly prohibits reinstating expenditure on an intangible item that was previously recognised as an expense — the company cannot capitalize the ₹25,00,000 even with the current-year approval; it remains an expense already recognised, not a prior period item to be restated.

(4) Advertising and promotional expenditure is always charged to the Profit and Loss Account as incurred, regardless of expected future revenue benefit — the company's treatment of debiting the full ₹50,00,000 is correct.

examiner_comment.text: Some examinees allowed the ₹25,00,000 to be capitalized once approval was received, missing AS 26's explicit bar on reinstating expenditure once it has been recognised as an expense in an earlier period.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: Kumar Ltd. manufactures both passenger cars and commercial vehicles. Management has an informal long-term strategic vision to shift focus toward commercial vehicles over 5 years, reducing passenger car production by ~20% annually and establishing a new commercial-vehicle facility, with employees to be transferred in phases. However, no specific or approved plan exists for sale, closure, or discontinuance of the passenger car division; no formal disposal plan, no Board approval; the new factory has not commenced operations, no binding commitments made. Comment on whether this gradual scaling down, without a formal approved plan, can be regarded as a 'Discontinuing Operation' under AS 24.
answer_html:
Mere gradual phasing out is not considered a discontinuing operation as defined under AS 24. Examples of activities that do not necessarily satisfy the definition on their own (though they might in combination with other circumstances) include: gradual/evolutionary phasing out of a product line; discontinuing several products within an ongoing line of business; shifting production/marketing activities between locations; and closing a facility for productivity improvements or cost savings.

On these facts: the strategic plan has no final Board approval via resolution; there is no specific, time-bound plan for asset/employee transfer; and the new commercial-vehicle segment has not started operations. Kumar Ltd.'s passenger-car scale-down is therefore not a discontinuing operation under AS 24.

examiner_comment.text: Some examinees treated the mere existence of a strategic intention as sufficient for AS 24 classification, missing that a specific, Board-approved plan with a defined implementation timeline is required.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: Prem Ltd. holds 2,000, 15% Debentures of ₹100 each in Mehar Ltd. as on 1st April, 2024 at a cost of ₹2,50,000. Interest payable 30th June and 31st December each year. Transactions during 2024-25: 1st May 2024, 1,000 debentures purchased cum-interest at ₹1,05,000; 1st November 2024, 1,200 debentures sold ex-interest at ₹1,28,200; 30th November 2024, 500 debentures purchased ex-interest at ₹54,500; 31st December 2024, 900 debentures sold cum-interest for ₹1,18,000. Prepare the Investment Account showing holdings on 31st March, 2025 at cost, using FIFO.
answer_html:
15% Debentures (Investment) Account, FIFO basis — closing balance as on 31.3.25: 1,400 debentures, face value ₹1,40,000, cost ₹1,44,500 (900 from the opening 2,000 + 500 purchased 30.11.24: opening lot after the 1.11.24 sale of 1,200 leaves 800 of the original 2,000 plus the 1,000 bought 1.5.24 minus what's sold, reconciled via FIFO issue order; net closing units 1,400 as shown in the working note below).

W.N.1 — Loss on sale 1.11.24: Cost of 1,200 sold (FIFO, from opening lot) = 2,50,000/2,000 × 1,200 = ₹1,50,000. Sale proceeds ₹1,28,200. Loss = ₹21,800, charged to P&L.

W.N.2 — Profit on sale 31.12.24: Cost of 900 sold (FIFO: 800 remaining from opening lot + 100 from the 1.5.24 purchase) = (2,50,000/2,000 × 800) + (1,00,000/1,000 × 100) = 1,00,000 + 10,000 = ₹1,10,000. Sale proceeds (cum-interest, less accrued interest component) net to ₹1,11,250 principal. Profit = ₹1,250.

W.N.3 — Closing balance: 900 debentures remaining from the 1.5.24 purchase (1,000−100 sold) at ₹90,000 (proportionate cost) + 500 debentures from the 30.11.24 purchase at ₹54,500 = 1,400 debentures, ₹1,44,500.

question_html: Care, a retail business, opened a branch Omega on 1st January, 2025; all branch sales on credit. Goods supplied from Head Office, invoiced at 10% above cost. Transactions (Jan/Feb/March 2025): Goods sent to Branch (purchase price) 60,000 / 75,000 / 90,000; Sales as per branch monthly report 57,000 / 63,000 / 82,500; Cash received from debtors and remitted to HO 30,000 / 76,500 / 52,500; Returns to HO (invoice price) 1,800 / 900 / 3,600. Branch closing stock at 31st March, 2025: ₹80,100 at invoice-to-branch price. Record in HO books, showing balances as on 31st March, 2025 and the branch gross profit for the three months.
answer_html:
Branch Account (books of Care, Head Office): To Goods sent to Branch A/c (2,25,000 total invoice value: 60,000+75,000+90,000, at 10% above cost) 2,47,500; To Goods sent to Branch A/c — returns loading (6,300 × 10/110) 573; To Stock Reserve (80,100 × 10/110) 7,283; To Net Profit (balancing figure, transferred to General P&L) 56,045. By Goods sent to Branch — Loading 22,500; By Goods sent to Branch — Returns 6,300; By Bank (cash remitted, 30,000+76,500+52,500) 1,59,000; By Balance c/d — Closing Branch Assets: Stock 80,100, Debtors (Sales 2,02,500 − Collections 1,59,000 = 43,500) 1,23,600. Total both sides ₹3,11,400.

Memorandum Branch Debtors Account confirms Debtors closing balance ₹43,500 (Sales 2,02,500 − Cash received 1,59,000).

Branch gross profit for the three months: ₹56,045 (the loading on goods sent, net of returns and closing stock reserve, represents the branch's realised gross margin for the period).

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: Hari Ltd., OM Ltd. and Bhakti Ltd. jointly constructed a pipeline to transport gas manufactured by them (a jointly controlled asset under AS 27). Expenditure incurred: Buildings ₹18,00,000 (depreciate @5% p.a.); Pipeline ₹90,00,000 (@15% p.a.); Computers & electronics ₹4,50,000 (@40% p.a.); Vehicles ₹13,50,000 (@20% p.a.). They equally bear pipeline maintenance expenditure of ₹9,00,000 each year. Show the extract of the consolidated balance sheet and the extract of Statement of Profit & Loss and Balance Sheet for each venturer.
answer_html:
Each venturer records its own one-third share of each jointly-controlled asset directly in its own books, per AS 27's proportionate-consolidation treatment for a jointly controlled asset (no separate joint entity exists).

Per-venturer figures (identical for each of Hari/OM/Bhakti, one-third share each): Land & Building 6,00,000, less depreciation @5% (30,000) = 5,70,000. Plant & Machinery (Pipeline) 30,00,000, less depreciation @15% (4,50,000) = 25,50,000. Computers 1,50,000, less depreciation @40% (60,000) = 90,000. Vehicles 4,50,000, less depreciation @20% (90,000) = 3,60,000. Total PPE per venturer: ₹35,70,000. Depreciation and amortisation expense per venturer: 30,000+4,50,000+60,000+90,000 = ₹6,30,000. Other operating expenses (pipeline maintenance, one-third share) ₹3,00,000.

Consolidated (all three venturers combined) extract: PPE — Land & Building 3×5,70,000=17,10,000; Plant & Machinery 3×25,50,000=76,50,000; Computers 3×90,000=2,70,000; Vehicles 3×3,60,000=10,80,000; Total Consolidated PPE: ₹1,07,10,000.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: Indicate in each case whether revenue can be recognized and when, as per AS-9: (i) Delivery is delayed at buyer's request but buyer takes title and accepts billing. (ii) Instalment Sales. (iii) Trade discounts and volume rebates. (iv) Insurance agency commission for rendering services. (v) Advertising commission.
answer_html:
(i) Revenue is recognised notwithstanding the delayed physical delivery, so long as delivery is expected and the goods are on hand, identified, and ready for delivery at the time of sale recognition (not merely an intention to acquire/manufacture in time).

(ii) When consideration is receivable in instalments, revenue attributable to the sale price (excluding interest) is recognised at the date of sale; the interest element is recognised as revenue proportionately to the unpaid balance.

(iii) Trade discounts and volume rebates received are not revenue (they reduce cost); those given are deducted in determining revenue.

(iv) Insurance agency commissions are recognised on the effective commencement or renewal dates of the related policies.

(v) Advertising commission is recognised when the service is completed — media commission when the advertisement appears before the public (with the agency's intimation received); production commission when the project is completed.
