subject: advanced-accounting
question_html:
Glen Ltd. began construction of a new building on 1st January, 2022. On 1st April, 2022, following two loans were obtained to fund the construction cost:

(i) Loan of ₹60,00,000 from Data Bank Ltd. was taken at interest rate of 8% per annum. This loan was fully utilized for construction of the new building.

(ii) Loan of ₹20,00,000 from Satya Bank Ltd. Out of this, loan amount of ₹6,00,000 was utilized for working capital purpose. Total interest of ₹1,92,000 were paid to Satya Bank Ltd. for the financial year 2022-23.

Construction of the new building was completed on 31st January, 2023 and was ready for its intended use on the same date.

None of the loan was repaid during the year. The building is a qualifying asset for the purpose of AS-16.

Out of loan from Data Bank Ltd., surplus funds were temporarily invested for the short period of time. This temporary investment earned interest of ₹30,000.

You are required to calculate the amount of interest (a) to be capitalized, (b) to be charged to profit and loss account from the total interest incurred as borrowing cost during the year 2022-23 (as per AS-16). (5 Marks)
answer_html:
According to AS 16 “Borrowing Costs”, borrowing costs that are directly attributable to the acquisition, construction or production of a qualifying asset should be capitalized as part of the cost of that asset. The amount of borrowing costs eligible for capitalization should be determined in accordance with this Standard. Other borrowing costs should be recognised as an expense in the period in which they are incurred.

The standard also states that to the extent that funds are borrowed specifically for the purpose of obtaining a qualifying asset, the amount of borrowing costs eligible for capitalization on that asset should be determined as the actual borrowing costs incurred on that borrowing during the period less any income on the temporary investment of those borrowings.

Thus, eligible borrowing cost on Loan of Data Bank to be capitalized:

= ₹(60,00,000 × 8%) × 10/12 − ₹30,000
= ₹4,00,000 − ₹30,000
= ₹3,70,000

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html:
Karna Ltd., an Indian Company, has the following foreign currency transactions during the financial year 2022-23:

(i) On 1st July, 2022, imported goods from Try Ltd., a German based company, amounting to ₹30,96,000.

(ii) On 1st October, 2022, imported plant and machinery from Lucy Ltd., a German based company, for €18,500. The amount was paid on the date of import itself. (Ignore depreciation).

(iii) On 1st December, 2022, exported goods on credit to Cream Ltd., a German based company, amounting to ₹50,40,000.

All the above transactions were recorded in the books of account at the prevailing exchange rate on the date of the transactions. Ignore taxes and duty on the above transactions.

Payment due from Cream Ltd. and payment due to Try Ltd. is outstanding as on 31st March, 2023.

Rate of exchange between reporting currency (₹) and foreign currency (€) on different dates are as under:

Date₹/€

You are required, as per AS-11: (i) To show value at which above items will appear in Balance sheet as on 31st March, 2023; (ii) To calculate the amount of gain/loss on each of above transactions on account of exchange differences, if any. (5 Marks)
answer_html:
As per AS 11 “The Effects of Changes in Foreign Exchange Rates”, Foreign currency monetary items should be reported using the closing rate. Non-monetary items which are carried in terms of historical cost denominated in a foreign currency should be reported using the exchange rate at the date of the transaction. Exchange differences arising on the settlement of monetary items or on reporting an enterprise’s monetary items at rates different from those at which they were initially recorded during the period, or reported in previous financial statements, should be recognised as income or as expenses in the period in which they arise.

(i) Items given in the question will appear in the Balance Sheet at the following values:

(ii) Amount of gain/loss on each transaction on account of exchange difference:

Exchange loss on Transaction of import of goods from Try Ltd. = ₹(1,44,000) [36,000 German Currency × ₹4 (i.e. 90−86)]

Exchange gain on Transaction of export of goods to Cream Ltd = ₹3,60,000 [60,000 German Currency × ₹6 (i.e. 90−84)]

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html:
Discuss Disclosure requirements in following cases as per AS 1:

(i) Accountant of A Ltd. charges a probable loss of losing a suit in books of accounts and also disclosed the same fact in financial statements. The probability of losing the suit is 25%.

(ii) Accountant of A Ltd. capitalized all the revenue expenses of repair and maintenance during the year to Plant & Machinery and is also disclosing the same as company policy in financial statements.

(iii) A Ltd. has followed accrual basis of accounting since incorporation. The chief accountant also disclosed this fact in financial statements.

(iv) A Ltd. was providing for after sales expenses @ 2% of sales for covering expenses during the warranty period. Now A Ltd. observes that actual after sales expenses were much less as compared to provision because of better technology used in manufacturing of the products. Now, the Board of A Ltd. decides to account for these expenses as and when they occur. Sales during the period are ₹50 crores. (15 + 5 = 20 Marks)
answer_html:
(i) In this case, accountant of company created a provision for damages of probability of losing a suit by a charge against profits. Unless the probability of losing the suit is more than the probability of not losing it, there should not be any creation of provision for such probable losses. So there is no need to charge such loss against profit and disclosing the same in financial statements.

(ii) Repairs and maintenance are revenue expenditure and should not be added to the value of assets, as these expenses do not increase the capacity of asset. Hence such expenses should be charged to profit & loss statement. Further the chief accountant also disclosed its policy of adding repairs to value of assets by way of notes to accounts. As per AS 1 disclosure is not a method to correct the wrong treatments. So the contention of chief accountant is wrong.

(iii) Accrual is one of the Fundamental accounting assumptions. If fundamental accounting assumptions are followed properly then no specific disclosure is required. Disclosure is required only when there is deviation and the company is not following fundamental accounting assumptions. So the company need not disclose this in financial statements.

(iv) As per AS 1, any change in the accounting policies which has a material effect in the current period or which is reasonably expected to have a material effect in later periods should be disclosed. Accordingly, the notes on accounts should properly disclose the change and its effect.

Note: So far, the company has been providing 2% of sales for meeting after sales expenses during the warranty period. Now the company has improved the quality of its products with better technology and has been observing that actual expenses are very less than the provision, hence, the company has decided not to make provision for such expenses but to account for the same as and when expenses are incurred. Due to this change, the profit for the year is increased by ₹1 crore than would have been the case if the old policy were to continue.

examiner_comment.text: Some examinees, in part (i), incorrectly concluded that disclosing the probable loss in the financial statements was sufficient without first questioning whether a provision should have been recognised at all, given the disputed suit had only a 25% probability of being lost. In part (ii), several examinees accepted the chief accountant's own disclosure of the wrong capitalisation policy as adequate compliance, missing AS 1's rule that disclosure is never a substitute for correcting a treatment that is itself wrong. In part (iv), many examinees failed to recognise that a material change expected to affect future periods still requires disclosure of the change and its effect, even though no restatement of prior years was needed.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html:
Z Ltd. decides to increase its existing share capital by making right issue to its existing shareholders. The company is offering 2 new shares for every 5 existing shares held by the shareholders. The market value of shares is ₹420 per share. Company is offering each share at ₹245 per share.

Calculate the value of right and the ex-right market price of a share. (5 Marks)
answer_html:
Ex-right value of the shares = (Cum-right value of the existing shares + Rights shares × Issue Price) / (Existing Number of shares + No. of right shares)

= (₹420 × 5 Shares + ₹245 × 2 Shares) / (5 + 2) Shares

= ₹2,590 / 7 shares = ₹370 per share

Value of right = Cum-right value of the share − Ex-right value of the share = ₹420 − ₹370 = ₹50 per share

Note: In the question, the market value of share is given at ₹420 per share. It has been considered that this value is cum right.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html: List down the applicable criteria under the Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules, 2021, to classify a company as Small and Medium Sized Company (SMC).
answer_html:
Criteria for classification of Companies under the Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules, 2021 to classify a company as Small and Medium-Sized Company (SMC):

“Small and Medium Sized Company” (SMC) means, a company –

(i) whose equity or debt securities are not listed or are not in the process of listing on any stock exchange, whether in India or outside India;

(ii) which is not a bank, financial institution or an insurance company;

(iii) whose turnover (excluding other income) does not exceed rupees two-fifty crores in the immediately preceding accounting year;

(iv) which does not have borrowings (including public deposits) in excess of rupees fifty crores at any time during the immediately preceding accounting year; and

(v) which is not a holding or subsidiary company of a company which is not a small and medium-sized company.

subject: advanced-accounting
case_facts_html:
Mr. Vikram took a loan of ₹6,00,000 carrying interest @ 10% p.a. on 1st August, 2023 to purchase raw material. He purchased 4000 units of raw material @ ₹125 per unit. Replacement cost of raw material as on 31 March, 2024 is ₹100 per unit. Labour charges and variable overheads incurred are ₹1,00,000 to produce 1000 units of finished goods.

1000 units of Finished goods are produced with raw material (for every unit of finished goods produced, 2 units of raw material are required). Net realizable value of finished good is ₹300 per unit. All the finished goods produced are lying in stock as on 31 March, 2024.

There is no opening stock of raw material and finished goods.

Mr. Vikram used 1500 units of raw material to construct an Asset (Qualifying Asset). Labour and other overhead charges incurred on construction of asset are ₹90,000. Mr. Vikram also paid ₹15,000 to install the asset at Factory premises. Mr. Vikram used Balance of loan proceeds of ₹1,00,000 to invest in Equity Shares of P. Ltd. He purchased 9,000 Equity shares (Face Value ₹10 each) for ₹1,00,000 on 25th March, 2024.

The P. Ltd declared and paid dividend @ 20% on 30th March for the year 2023-24.

Based on the information given in above Case Scenario, answer the following Question No. 1-4:
question_html:
What would be the value of closing stock of Raw Material X and Finished Goods as on 31st March 2024?

  1. Closing Stock of Raw Material X ₹50,000 and closing stock of Finished Goods ₹3,50,000
  2. Closing Stock of Raw Material X ₹50,000 and closing stock of Finished Goods ₹3,00,000
  3. Closing Stock of Raw Material X ₹62,500 and closing stock of Finished Goods ₹3,50,000
  4. Closing Stock of Raw Material X ₹62,500 and closing stock of Finished Goods ₹3,00,000
answer_html: Answer: (B) Closing Stock of Raw Material X ₹50,000 and closing stock of Finished Goods ₹3,00,000 — of the 4,000 units of raw material purchased, 2,000 units went into the 1,000 finished-goods units and 1,500 units into the self-constructed asset, leaving 500 units as closing raw-material stock. Finished-goods cost = (2,000 units × ₹125 material) + ₹1,00,000 labour/overheads = ₹3,50,000 for 1,000 units, i.e. ₹350/unit, against an NRV of only ₹300/unit — since the finished goods will be sold below cost, AS 2's rule that "materials are not written down below cost if the finished products they will be incorporated into are expected to be sold at or above cost" no longer protects the raw material: it must instead be written down to its replacement cost of ₹100/unit as the best available measure of its NRV. Closing Raw Material = 500 × ₹100 = ₹50,000. Closing Finished Goods = 1,000 × lower of cost (₹350) and NRV (₹300) = 1,000 × ₹300 = ₹3,00,000.

case_facts_html:
Kay Ltd. sold goods of ₹22,00,000 to Mr. Ravi Kumar on 1st February, 2024 but at the request of the buyer, these goods were delivered on 10th April 2024.

Kay Ltd. also sold ₹2,00,000 goods on approval basis on 1st January, 2024 to Sheetal Enterprises. The period of approval is 3 months after which they were considered sold. Buyer sent disapproval for 25% of goods and approval for 50% of goods till 31 March, 2024.

Mr. Ravi Kumar has commenced legal action against Kay Ltd. for supply of faulty goods to claim damages. The lawyers of Kay Ltd. have advised that it is not remote yet that resources may be required to settle the claim. Legal cost to be incurred irrespective of the outcome of the case is ₹45,000. Settlement amount if the claim is required to be paid ₹5,00,000.

Sheetal Enterprises, a trade receivable of Kay Ltd. suffered a heavy loss due to an earthquake that occurred on 30th March, 2024. The loss was not covered by any insurance policy. In April, 2024, Sheetal Enterprises became bankrupt. The Balance due from Sheetal Enterprises as on 31 March, 2024 is ₹75,000.

Kay Ltd. makes provision for doubtful debts @ 5%.

Based on the information given in above Case Scenario, answer the following Question No. 5-7
question_html:
What is the amount to be recognized as Revenue as per AS 9 in the books of Kay Ltd. as on 31 March, 2024?

  1. ₹23,50,000
  2. ₹1,50,000
  3. ₹23,00,000
  4. ₹1,00,000
answer_html: Answer: (A) ₹23,50,000 — the sale to Mr. Ravi Kumar (₹22,00,000) qualifies as a "bill and hold" sale: delivery was deferred only at the buyer's own request, the goods were identified and ready for delivery, so revenue is recognised in full despite the delayed handover. On the approval sale to Sheetal Enterprises (₹2,00,000), the 3-month approval period runs from 1st January to 31st March, i.e. it has elapsed by the year end: the 50% (₹1,00,000) explicitly approved is revenue, the 25% (₹50,000) explicitly disapproved is not, and per AS 9 the remaining 25% (₹50,000) on which the buyer never responded is also recognised as revenue because the time period allowed for rejection has expired without rejection. Total revenue = ₹22,00,000 + ₹1,00,000 + ₹50,000 = ₹23,50,000.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html:
P Ltd. has 60% voting right in Q Ltd. Q Ltd. has 20% voting right in R Ltd. Also, P Ltd. directly enjoys voting right of 14% in R Ltd. R Ltd. is a Listed Company and regularly supplies goods to P Ltd. The Management of R Ltd. has not disclosed its relationship with P Ltd. While preparing Financial Statements of P Ltd., which entities would you disclose as related parties with reference to AS-18?

  1. Q Ltd.
  2. R Ltd.
  3. Q Ltd. and R Ltd.
  4. Neither of Q Ltd. or R Ltd.
answer_html: Answer: (C) Q Ltd. and R Ltd. — P Ltd. holds 60% of Q Ltd., making Q Ltd. a subsidiary and hence a related party by control. Since P Ltd. controls Q Ltd., Q Ltd.'s 20% voting power in R Ltd. is aggregated with P Ltd.'s own direct 14% holding: 20% + 14% = 34% combined voting power in R Ltd., well above the 20% threshold that gives rise to significant influence, making R Ltd. a related party too. R Ltd.'s own management not having disclosed the relationship does not change P Ltd.'s disclosure obligation, since AS 18 places the disclosure duty on the reporting enterprise regardless of the counterparty's conduct.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html:
A Machinery was given on 3 years lease by a dealer of the machinery for equal annual lease rentals to yield 20% profit margin on cost of the machinery, which is Rs. 3,00,000. Economic life of the machinery is 5 years, and estimated output from the machinery in 5 years is as follows: Year I 50,000 units; Year II 60,000 units; Year III 40,000 units; Year IV 65,000 units; Year V 85,000 units. Compute Annual Lease Rent.

  1. ₹30,000
  2. ₹60,000
  3. ₹50,000
  4. ₹36,000
answer_html: Answer: (B) ₹60,000 — as a dealer/manufacturer lessor, the fair value (normal selling price) built into the lease is cost plus the stated profit margin: ₹3,00,000 × 1.20 = ₹3,60,000. The 3-year lease covers only part of the machine's 5-year economic life, so only the portion of that value corresponding to the output actually consumed during the lease term is recoverable through rent: output in Years 1-3 (50,000+60,000+40,000 = 1,50,000 units) is exactly half of the machine's total 5-year output (50,000+60,000+40,000+65,000+85,000 = 3,00,000 units). Value to be recovered over the 3-year lease = 50% × ₹3,60,000 = ₹1,80,000, and equal annual rentals = ₹1,80,000 / 3 = ₹60,000.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html:
Aerodots Ltd. has the following capital structure as on 31.03.2024: Equity Share Capital (shares of ₹10 each) ₹6,00,000 [thousands]; Reserves: General Reserve ₹5,40,000; Securities Premium ₹2,00,000; Profit & Loss ₹1,00,000; Revaluation Reserve ₹30,000; Investment Allowance Reserve (Statutory Reserve) ₹75,000; Infrastructure Development Reserve ₹25,000; Loan Funds ₹20,00,000 (all figures ₹ in thousands, as printed).

On 1st April, 2024 the company wants to buy back 14,000 equity shares of ₹10 each at ₹30 per Equity share.

You are required to calculate maximum permissible number of equity shares that can be bought back.

Buy Back of shares is duly authorized by its articles and necessary resolution has been passed by the company.
answer_html:
Statement determining the maximum number of shares to be bought back (in thousands):

ParticularsNumber of shares
Shares Outstanding Test (W.N.1)15
Resources Test (W.N.2)12
Debt Equity Ratio Test (W.N.3)11
Maximum number of shares that can be bought back [least of the above]11

Thus, the lowest being 11,000 shares, the company cannot buy back 14,000 shares.

Working Notes:

1. Shares Outstanding Test: Number of shares outstanding 60 (thousand); 25% of the shares outstanding = 15 (thousand).

2. Resources Test: Paid up capital ₹600 (thousand); Free reserves (540+200+100) ₹840 (thousand); Shareholders' funds ₹1,440 (thousand); 25% of Shareholders fund ₹360 (thousand); Buy-back price per share ₹30; Number of shares that can be bought back = 12,000 shares.

3. Debt Equity Ratio Test (loans cannot exceed twice the Equity Funds post Buy-Back): Loan funds ₹2,000 (thousand); Minimum equity to be maintained after buy-back in the ratio of 2:1 (a/2) ₹1,000 (thousand); Present equity shareholders fund ₹1,440 (thousand); Future equity shareholders fund (see W.N.4) (1,440−110) = ₹1,330 (thousand); Maximum permitted buy-back of Equity [(d)−(b)] ₹330 (thousand); Maximum number of shares that can be bought back @ ₹30/share = 11,000 shares.

4. Amount transferred to CRR and maximum equity to be bought back, by simultaneous equation method – let amount transferred to CRR = x, maximum permitted buy-back of equity = y. Equation 1: (Present Equity − Transfer to CRR) − Minimum Equity to be maintained = Maximum Permitted Buy-Back ⇒ (1,440−x)−1,000 = y ⇒ 440−x = y. Equation 2: y/30 × 10 = x, i.e. 3x = y. Solving: x = ₹110 (thousand), y = ₹330 (thousand).

Alternatively, Maximum number of shares from debt equity ratio test may be worked out as: Buy-back price + Face value of equity shares = ₹30+₹10 = ₹40. Excess of equity fund over the minimum equity to be maintained = 1,440−1,000 = 440 (thousand). Number of Shares that can be bought back = 440/40 (thousand) = 11 (thousand).

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html: "In determining the cost of inventories, it is appropriate to exclude certain costs and recognise them as expenses in the period in which they are incurred." Provide examples of such costs as per AS 2 (Revised) 'Valuation of Inventories'.
answer_html:
In determining the cost of inventories, it is appropriate to exclude certain costs and recognise them as expenses in the period in which they are incurred. Examples of such costs are:

(a) Abnormal amounts of wasted materials, labour, or other production costs;

(b) Storage costs, unless the production process requires such storage.

(c) Administrative overheads that do not contribute to bringing the inventories to their present location and condition.

(d) Selling and distribution costs.

  2. ₹3,30,000
  3. ₹1,65,000

question_html:
Which is correct with reference to the subsidy received in the nature of promoters' contribution during 2024-2025: (i) It is not considered as a deferred income. (ii) It is not distributable as a dividend. (iii) It is treated as a capital reserve. (iv) It is not distributable as a dividend but considered as deferred income.

  1. (i), (ii) and (iii)
  2. (iii) and (iv)
  3. (ii) and (iii)
  4. (i) and (ii)
answer_html: Answer: (A) (i), (ii) and (iii) — per AS 12, a grant in the nature of promoters' contribution (given as a proportion of total investment, not related to specific fixed assets, and not in the ordinary course of business) is credited directly to Capital Reserve, treated as shareholders' funds — not as deferred income, and not distributable as a dividend.

As per AS-26, what is the correct accounting treatment for ₹18 lakhs spent on publicity and research expenses during 2024-2025?

  1. ₹18 lakhs is treated as an intangible asset and amortised equally over 5 years.
  2. ₹18 lakhs is treated as an intangible asset and amortised equally over 10 years.

On 1st July 2025 Capital Structure (₹ in lakhs): Equity Share Capital (₹100 each, fully paid) 45.00; General Reserve 74.00; Securities Premium 30.00; Profit & Loss 25.00; Revaluation Reserve 4.00; Statutory Reserve 6.50; Loan Funds 350.00. The company is considering reducing Loan Funds to ₹300 lakhs by paying ₹50 lakhs before 4th July 2025. Current market value ₹250/share; buy-back price offered at 20% premium over market value. Answer Question Nos. 11–14.
question_html:
What will be the maximum number of shares that can be bought back as per the Companies Act, 2013 according to the decision made on the basis of the above two questions?

  1. 11250 Shares
  2. 14500 Shares
  3. Nil Shares
  4. 6000 Shares
answer_html: Answer: (D) 6,000 Shares — since buy-back is only feasible at all (per Q11/Q12) once the company first reduces the loan to ₹300 lakhs, the company should pay down the ₹50 lakhs loan first, then proceed with the buy-back of 6,000 shares that becomes permissible at that lower debt level.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: SR Limited manufactures finished goods 'MP' from raw material 'RP'. Year ended 31st March 2025: Opening Inventory MP 4,000 units ₹1,20,000; RP 4,400 units ₹52,800. Purchase of RP 40,000 units ₹4,80,000. Labour ₹3,23,200. Fixed Overheads ₹3,15,000. Sales 40,200 units ₹11,20,000. Closing Inventory: MP 4,200 units; RP 4,000 units. Expected production 45,000 units of MP. Due to fall in market demand, sales price of MP fell to ₹22/unit; replacement cost of RP ₹11.50/unit on closing day. Calculate the value of Closing Stock of 'MP' and 'RP' as on 31st March 2025.
answer_html:
W.N.1 Actual production: Sales 40,200 + Closing FG 4,200 − Opening FG 4,000 = 40,400 units.

W.N.2 RP consumed: Opening RP 4,400 + Purchases 40,000 = 44,400 available; less Closing RP 4,000 = 40,400 units consumed (1 unit RP per unit MP produced).

W.N.3 Cost per unit RP (weighted average): (Opening value 52,800 + Purchases 4,80,000) / 44,400 units = 5,32,800/44,400 = ₹12.00/unit.

Cost of Material Consumed (40,400 × ₹12)4,84,800
Direct Labour3,23,200
Fixed Overhead (3,15,000 × 40,400/45,000 — based on normal/expected production, not actual)2,82,800
Cost of Production10,90,800
Cost per unit (10,90,800/40,400)₹27
Net Realisable Value per unit (selling price)₹22

Since NRV (₹22) is less than cost (₹27), the closing MP inventory is valued at NRV. Since finished goods NRV is below cost, the raw material RP feeding it is valued at replacement cost (₹11.50), per AS 2's write-down rule.

Value of closing inventory: MP (4,200 × ₹22) = ₹92,400. RP (4,000 × ₹11.50) = ₹46,000.

question_html: AB Limited purchased goods on credit from XY Limited for ₹150 lakhs for export. The export order was cancelled; AB Limited decided to sell the same goods locally with a price discount. XY Limited agreed to a 12% price discount requested by AB Limited. XY's chief accountant wants to adjust the sales figure to the extent of the discount. Discuss whether this treatment is as per the relevant Accounting Standard.
answer_html: Correct. Per AS 9, trade discounts given should be deducted in determining revenue. The 12% discount should be deducted from the turnover figure for revenue recognition purposes — XY Limited's adjustment of the sales figure to the extent of the discount is correct as per AS 9.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: XY Limited recognized dividend income of ₹10 lakhs on accrual basis on securities of face value ₹100 lakhs held at 31st March 2025. The dividend (10%) was declared on 30th April 2025, having been proposed on 30th March 2025. Comment.
answer_html: Incorrect. Dividends from investments in securities are not recognised in the Statement of Profit and Loss until the right to receive payment is established. Here, the dividend is proposed 30th March 2025 but declared only 30th April 2025 — the right to receive payment is established only on 30th April 2025. Recognising ₹10 lakhs on accrual basis at 31st March 2025 is not correct as per AS 9.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: XY Limited sold goods of ₹1,50,000 on approval basis on 15th December 2024; approval period 3 months, after which goods are considered sold. Buyer approved 60% of goods by 31st January 2025; no approval/disapproval received for the remainder by 31st March 2025. The accountant recognised ₹1,50,000 as revenue on 15th December, 2024. Comment.
answer_html: Incorrect as recognised. For goods sold on approval, revenue should not be recognised until formal acceptance, an act adopting the transaction, or expiry of the rejection period. Revenue for ₹90,000 (60%) should be recognised on 31st January, 2025 (date of approval); the remaining ₹60,000 should be recognised on 15th March, 2025, when the 3-month approval period lapsed without response (deemed acceptance) — not the full ₹1,50,000 on 15th December, 2024 as the accountant did.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: Grace Limited acquired the business (a cash-generating unit) of Venus Limited on 31st March 2023 for ₹8,000 lakhs: Fair value of identifiable assets ₹6,000 lakhs, Goodwill (amortised over 5 years) ₹2,000 lakhs. Anticipated useful life of acquired assets: 8 years, nil residual value, straight-line. On 31st March 2025, significant decline in production estimated due to government policy changes; net selling price of identifiable assets ₹3,000 lakhs. Cash flow forecast for next 6 years (₹ lakhs): 1,000/800/700/800/600/500. Discount rate 10% (PV factors: 0.909, 0.826, 0.751, 0.683, 0.621, 0.564). Calculate: (i) Value in use at 31 March 2025; (ii) Impairment loss for year ended 31 March 2025; (iii) Revised carrying amount of asset.
answer_html:
(i) Value in Use: 1,000×0.909=909.00 + 800×0.826=660.80 + 700×0.751=525.70 + 800×0.683=546.40 + 600×0.621=372.60 + 500×0.564=282.00 = ₹3,296.50 lakhs, rounded to ₹3,297 lakhs.

Carrying amount at 31.3.2025 (2 years post-acquisition): Goodwill 2,000 − amortisation (2,000/5×2=800) = 1,200. Identifiable assets 6,000 − depreciation (6,000/8×2=1,500) = 4,500. Total CGU carrying amount = 5,700.

Recoverable amount = higher of Value in Use (3,297) and net selling price of identifiable assets (3,000, no CGU-wide fair-value-less-costs-to-sell given) = 3,297 (since 3,297 > 3,000).

(ii) Impairment loss = Carrying amount (5,700) − Recoverable amount (3,297) = ₹2,403 lakhs.

(iii) Allocation: per AS 28, impairment is allocated first to goodwill (written down to zero: full 1,200 absorbed), then the remainder (2,403−1,200=1,203) to identifiable assets pro-rata: revised carrying amount of identifiable asset = 4,500−1,203 = ₹3,297 lakhs (goodwill: Nil).

question_html: Blue Limited and Yellow Limited Balance Sheets as at 31st March 2025 (₹ lakhs): Blue — Equity Shares of ₹100 40.000, 10% Debentures 15.000, General Reserves 1.500, Retirement Gratuity Fund 3.450, Trade Payables 7.400, Other current liabilities 1.240, Short-term provisions 0.710; Goodwill 8.750, PPE 35.650, Inventories 8.890, Trade Receivables 13.535, Cash in hand 0.485, Bank 1.990. Yellow — Equity Shares of ₹100 28.000, 8% Debentures 8.000, General Reserves 0.670, Retirement Gratuity Fund 1.300, Trade Payables 4.250, Other current liabilities 0.880, Short-term provisions 0.320; Goodwill 1.795, PPE 31.260, Inventories 4.800, Trade Receivables 4.650, Cash in hand 0.315, Bank 0.600. Blue absorbs Yellow's business on 31st March 2025: (i) 8% Debenture holders of Yellow paid at 10% discount via 10% Debentures at par in Blue. (ii) Unrecorded current asset ₹1,16,000 in Yellow's books, taken over. (iii) Yellow's Trade Payables include ₹1,50,000 payable to Blue. (iv) Yellow's Inventory taken over at 10% more than book value. (v) Yellow's Goodwill = 2 × simple average profits of 2021-22 (4,50,000), 2022-23 (3,90,000), 2023-24 (2,35,000); 2022-23 had a ₹50,000 cash embezzlement already adjusted in that year's profit. (vi) Yellow's PPE taken over at ₹36,44,500. (vii) Remaining assets/liabilities at book value. (viii) Yellow's equity shareholders issued Blue shares at 5% premium. Calculate the Purchase Consideration and prepare Blue's post-absorption Balance Sheet.
answer_html:
W.N.1 Goodwill of Yellow Ltd.: Adjusted profits: 2021-22: 4.50; 2022-23: 3.90+0.50 (add back embezzlement, a one-off/non-recurring item) = 4.40; 2023-24: 2.35. Total 11.25; average (i)/3 = 3.75; ×2 years' purchase = Goodwill ₹7.50 lakhs.

question_html: Seva Limited and subsidiary Meva Limited, Balance Sheets as at 31st March 2025 (₹ Lakh): Seva — Equity Shares of ₹10 6,000, General Reserve 1,500, P&L 2,000, 10% Debentures 1,180, Trade Payable 1,500; Land and Building 4,000, Plant & Machinery 1,460, Investments (Meva shares) 3,000, Inventories 1,400, Trade Receivable 1,420, Cash at Bank 550, Cash in Hand 350. Meva — Equity Shares of ₹10 4,000, General Reserve 1,200, P&L 1,500, 10% Debentures 820, Trade Payable 1,080; Land and Building 4,150, Plant & Machinery 1,650, Inventories 1,100, Trade Receivable 1,000, Cash at Bank 600, Cash in Hand 100. Seva acquired 80% of Meva on 1st April 2024 (Meva's General Reserve ₹2,000 lakh, P&L ₹800 lakh on that date). On 1st November 2024, Meva issued a 1:3 bonus share out of General Reserve (as at 31 March 2024 balance). On 31st March 2025, Seva's inventory includes goods purchased from Meva for ₹125 lakh, on which Meva made a profit of ₹25 lakh. Prepare the Consolidated Balance Sheet as per Schedule III.
answer_html:
W.N.9 Bonus shares: Meva's shares post-bonus 4,000 lakh (at ₹10 face value, i.e. 400 lakh shares) represent 4/3 of pre-bonus holding; pre-bonus = 4,000×3/4=3,000; bonus issued = 4,000−3,000=1,000 (lakh, i.e. ₹1,000 lakh face value), funded from General Reserve.

W.N.1 Meva's General Reserve movement: Opening 2,000 − Bonus 1,000 + transfer from P&L 200 = Closing 1,200.

W.N.2 Meva's P&L movement: Opening 800 − transfer to General Reserve 200 + Net profit for the year (balancing) 900 = Closing 1,500.

W.N.4 Capital profits (pre-acquisition): General Reserve at acquisition, net of the bonus issue (2,000−1,000=1,000) + P&L at acquisition (800) = 1,800. Seva's 80% share = 1,440; Minority's 20% = 360.

W.N.3 Revenue profits (post-acquisition): 900 (from W.N.2); Seva's 80% share: General Reserve 160 (80% of 200) + P&L 560 (80% of 700, i.e. profit after removing the amount already transferred to reserve) = 720; Minority's 20% = 180.

W.N.5 Capital Reserve: Paid-up value of shares held (80% of 4,000) 3,200 + share in capital profits 1,440 = 4,640; less cost of shares 3,000 = Capital Reserve ₹1,640 lakh.

W.N.6 Minority Interest: 20% of share capital (800) + share in revenue profits (180) + share in capital profits (360) = 1,340; less unrealised profit (20% of 25 = 5, Meva's share of the inter-company profit since Meva is the seller) = Minority Interest ₹1,335 lakh.

Consolidated Balance Sheet as at 31st March, 2025 (₹ Lakh): Share Capital 6,000 (Seva's own, unchanged); Reserves and Surplus 5,840 (Capital Reserve 1,640 + General Reserve 1,660 + P&L 2,540); Minority Interest 1,335; Long-term borrowings 2,000 (1,180+820); Trade payables 2,580 (1,500+1,080). Total 17,755. Assets: PPE 11,260 (Land&Building 8,150 [4,000+4,150] + Plant&Machinery 3,110 [1,460+1,650]); Inventories 2,475 (1,400+1,100−25 unrealised profit); Trade receivables 2,420 (1,420+1,000); Cash and cash equivalents 1,600 (Bank 1,150 + Cash in hand 450). Total 17,755.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: Sneha, an employee of Omre Limited, went on paid maternity leave for 9 months, 1st January 2024 to 30th September 2024, monthly pay ₹1,50,000. While preparing FY2023-24 financial statements, her salary for 3 months (Jan–Mar 2024) was omitted. When she joined 1st October 2024, the whole 9-month salary was paid. With reference to AS-5, determine if this is a prior period item and pass the FY2024-25 journal entry. Variant: Suppose Sneha was terminated 1st January 2024 and reinstated by court order on 30th September 2024, with the 9-month salary paid 1st October 2024 — what is the AS-5 treatment here, with journal entry?
answer_html:
Original scenario: Per AS 5, prior period items are income/expenses arising in the current period from errors or omissions in preparing prior periods' financial statements. The 3 months' salary (Jan–Mar 2024, ₹4,50,000) omitted from FY2023-24 is a prior period item in FY2024-25.

Journal entry (FY2024-25): Salary A/c (₹1,50,000×6) Dr. 9,00,000; Prior Period Item A/c (₹1,50,000×3) Dr. 4,50,000; To Bank A/c 13,50,000.

Variant (termination/reinstatement): AS 5 states "prior period items" does not include adjustments necessitated by circumstances that, though related to prior periods, are determined only in the current period. Since Sneha's reinstatement (with retrospective salary) was ordered by the court only in FY2024-25, the ₹4,50,000 (Jan–Mar 2024) is not a prior period item — the entire ₹13,50,000 is a current-year expense.

Journal entry (variant): Salary A/c (₹1,50,000×9) Dr. 13,50,000; To Bank A/c 13,50,000.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: What are the key elements of financial statements? Explain.
answer_html:
1. Assets: a resource controlled by the enterprise from past events, expected to bring future economic benefits (e.g. plant, patents, receivables).
  2. Liabilities: a present obligation arising from past events, settlement of which is expected to result in an outflow of economic benefits (e.g. borrowings, provisions).
  3. Equity: the residual interest in assets after deducting all liabilities — owners' claim (capital, reserves), distinct from liabilities (claims of parties other than owners); changes through contributions/distributions or income/expenses.
  4. Income/Gain: increases in economic benefits through inflow of assets or reduction of liabilities, increasing equity (includes revenue and gains).
  5. Expenses/Loss: decreases in economic benefits through outflows/depletion of assets or incurrence of liabilities, decreasing equity (other than distributions to owners) — expenses arise in the ordinary course (e.g. wages); losses may or may not (e.g. loss on PPE disposal), and are shown separately to aid performance assessment.

topics.title: Framework for Preparation and Presentation of Financial Statements
topics.subtopictitle: The five key elements - assets, liabilities, equity, income, expenses
topics.label: Framework (1.2)

examiner_comment.text: A direct theory recall question; common gaps include omitting the equity definition's distinction from liabilities, or failing to note that losses (unlike ordinary expenses) may fall outside the enterprise's normal activities.

question_html: Shanti Limited (Chennai), incorporated 1st April 2024, opened branches at Madurai and Tiruchi. Goods invoiced to branches at Cost + 25%. All branch expenses paid by HO; each branch has its own Sales Ledger, sends weekly statements, remits cash collections daily. Year ended 31st March 2025 (₹ lakhs): Madurai/Tiruchi — Credit Sales 1,25,200/1,10,000; Cash Sales 78,600/85,200; Sales Returns 2,300/1,200; Trade Receivable (closing) 34,500/23,600; Rent and Taxes 3,200/4,500; Bad Debts 6,000/—; Salaries 16,000/18,000; General Expenses 2,600/1,500; Goods Received from HO (at invoice price) 1,50,000/1,25,000; Advertisement 7,500/5,200; Closing Stock (at invoice price) 45,000/35,000. Prepare Branch Accounts as they would appear in HO's books, using the Debtors Method, for the year ended 31st March 2025.

Loading = 25% on cost = 1/5th on invoice price.

Memorandum Branch Debtors Account (both branches): To Sales (credit) 1,25,200/1,10,000; less Sales Returns 2,300/1,200, Bad Debts 6,000/—, Cash collected from debtors (balancing figure) 82,400/85,200 = Closing balance 34,500/23,600 (matches given closing Trade Receivable, confirming the collection figures).

Branch Account, Madurai / Tiruchi (₹ in lakhs, goods at invoice price):

Dr.MaduraiTiruchiCr.MaduraiTiruchi
To Goods sent to Branch (invoice price)1,50,0001,25,000By Cash (Cash Sales)78,60085,200
To Rent & Taxes3,2004,500By Cash (Collection from Debtors)82,40085,200
To Salaries16,00018,000By Debtors (closing)34,50023,600
To General Expenses2,6001,500By Closing Stock (invoice price)45,00035,000
To Advertisement7,5005,200By Goods sent to Branch (Stock Reserve, on returns loading)30,00025,000
To Stock Reserve (on closing stock loading)9,0007,000
To Net Profit transferred to General P&L82,20092,800

case_facts_html:
Surya Ltd. Has a two fixed asset, FA1 is being carried in the balance sheet for ₹600 lakhs and FA 2 is being carried at ₹300 lakhs.

As at 31st March 2024, the value in use for FA 1 is ₹500 lakhs and the net selling price is ₹550 lakhs. The Company did upward revaluation last year for ₹20 lakhs for FA 1.

As at 31st March 2024, the value in use for FA 2 is ₹350 lakhs and the net selling price is ₹320 lakhs.
question_html:
How much is the total Impairment loss for current year for FA 1:

  1. ₹100 Lakhs
  2. ₹50 Lakhs
  3. ₹30 lakhs
  4. Nil
answer_html: Answer: (ii) ₹50 Lakhs. Recoverable amount for FA 1 = higher of net selling price (₹550 lakhs) and value in use (₹500 lakhs) = ₹550 lakhs. Total impairment loss = carrying amount (₹600 lakhs) − recoverable amount (₹550 lakhs) = ₹50 lakhs.

topics.subtopictitle: Recoverable amount is the higher of net selling price and value in use; total impairment loss = carrying amount less recoverable amount
topics.label: AS 28 (7.4)

examiner_comment.text: A common error is comparing carrying amount only against value in use, ignoring that AS 28 defines recoverable amount as the higher of net selling price and value in use — using value in use alone here would overstate the impairment loss for FA 1.

question_html:
How much impairment loss will be charged to profit and loss for current year for FA1:

  1. ₹100 Lakhs
  2. ₹50 Lakhs
  3. ₹30 lakhs
  4. Nil
answer_html: Answer: (iii) ₹30 lakhs. FA 1's total impairment loss (₹50 lakhs, from Q1(a)) is first set off against the ₹20 lakhs revaluation reserve created by last year's upward revaluation of FA 1 (impairment of a revalued asset is treated as a revaluation decrease to the extent of the reserve balance available). The balance, ₹50 lakhs − ₹20 lakhs = ₹30 lakhs, is charged to the Statement of Profit and Loss.

question_html:
The debit or credit balance of "Foreign Currency Monetary Item Translation Difference Account"

  1. Is shown as "Miscellaneous Expenditure" in the Balance Sheet
  2. Is shown under "Reserves and Surplus" as a separate line item
  3. Is shown as "Other Non-current" in the Balance Sheet

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html:
ABC Ltd. was making provision for non-moving inventories based on no issues for the last 12 months up to 31.3.2023. The company wants to provide during the year ending 31.3.2024 based on technical evaluation:

Total value of inventory₹100 lakhs
Provision required based on 12 months issue₹3.5 lakhs
Provision required based on technical evaluation₹2.5 lakhs

Does this amount to change in Accounting Policy? Can the company change the method of provision?
answer_html:
The decision of making provision for non-moving inventories on the basis of technical evaluation does not amount to a change in accounting policy. Accounting policy of a company may require that provision for non-moving inventories should be made; the method of estimating the amount of provision may be changed in case a more prudent estimate can be made — this is a change in accounting estimate, not a change in accounting policy.

In the given case, considering the total value of inventory, the change in the amount of required provision of non-moving inventory from ₹3.5 lakhs to ₹2.5 lakhs is also not material. The disclosure can be made for such change in the following lines by way of notes to the accounts in the annual accounts of ABC Ltd. for the year 2023-24:

"The company has provided for non-moving inventories on the basis of technical evaluation unlike preceding years. Had the same method been followed as in the previous year, the profit for the year and the corresponding effect on the year end net assets would have been lower by ₹1 lakh."

examiner_comment.text: A common error is treating a switch to a more scientifically-grounded estimation basis (technical evaluation) for an existing provision as a change in accounting policy requiring restatement, rather than recognising it as a change in accounting estimate, applied prospectively with disclosure only if material.

question_html:
Classify the following activities as (1) Operating Activities, (2) Investing Activities, (3) Financing Activities (4) Cash Equivalents.

  1. Proceeds from long-term borrowings.
  2. Proceeds from Trade receivables.
  3. Trading Commission received.
  4. Redemption of Preference Shares.
  5. Proceeds from sale of investment
  6. Interim Dividend paid on equity shares.

  8. Dividend received on shares held as investments.
  9. Rent received on property held as investment.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html:
During the course of the last three years, a company owning and operating Helicopters lost four Helicopters. The company's accountant felt that after the crash, the maintenance provision created in respect of the respective helicopters was no longer required, and proposed to write it back to the Profit and Loss account as a prior period item.

Is the company's proposed accounting treatment correct? Discuss.
answer_html:
The balance amount of maintenance provision written back to profit and loss account, no longer required due to crash of the helicopters, is not a prior period item because there was no error in the preparation of previous periods' financial statements. The term "prior period items", as defined in AS 5 (revised) "Net Profit or Loss for the Period, Prior Period Items and Changes in Accounting Policies", refer only to income or expenses which arise in the current period as a result of errors or omissions in the preparation of the financial statements of one or more prior periods. The balance amount left in the provision created earlier is not as a result of error in the past. So it will not be considered as a prior period item. Such write back of provision is not an ordinary feature of the business; it shall be considered as an extra-ordinary item.

As per paragraph 8 of AS 5, extraordinary items should be disclosed in the Statement of Profit and Loss as a part of net profit or loss for the period. The nature and the amount of each extraordinary item should be separately disclosed in the Statement of Profit and Loss in a manner that its impact on current profit or loss can be perceived. Hence, the amount so written-back (if material) should be disclosed as an extraordinary item as per AS 5 rather than as a prior period item.

topics.title: Net Profit or Loss for the Period, Prior Period Items and Changes in Accounting Policies
topics.subtopictitle: Prior period items arise only from errors or omissions in preparing earlier financial statements - a provision write-back from a genuinely unusual event is an extraordinary item instead
topics.label: AS 5 (2.2)

examiner_comment.text: A common error is treating the reversal of a no-longer-required provision as a prior period item merely because the original provision was created in an earlier year, missing AS 5's requirement that prior period items arise specifically from errors or omissions in preparing earlier financial statements — a provision correctly created and later found unnecessary due to a genuinely unusual event is an extraordinary item, not a prior period correction.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html:
Rose Constructions undertake to construct a bridge for the Government of Uttar Pradesh. The construction commenced during the financial year ending 31.03.2024 and is likely to be completed by the next financial year. The contract is for a fixed price of ₹12 crore with an escalation clause. You are given the following information for the year ended 31.03.2024:

Cost incurred upto 31.03.2024₹4 crore
Cost estimated to complete the contract₹6 crore

Escalation in cost was by 5%. Hence, the contract price is also increased by 5%.

You are required to ascertain the stage of completion and compute the amount of revenue and profit to be recognized for the year as per AS 7.
answer_html:
Cost of construction of bridge incurred upto 31.3.2024₹4.00 crore
Add: Estimated future cost₹6.00 crore
Total estimated cost of construction₹10.00 crore
Contract Price (12 crore × 1.05)₹12.60 crore

Stage of completion: Percentage of completion till date to total estimated cost of construction = (4/10)×100 = 40%.

Revenue and Profit to be recognized for the year ended 31st March, 2024 as per AS 7:

Proportion of total contract value recognized as revenue = Contract price × percentage of completion = ₹12.60 crore × 40% = ₹5.04 crore.

Profit for the year ended 31st March, 2024 = ₹5.04 crore − ₹4 crore = ₹1.04 crore.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html: Mithya Ltd. entered into agreement with Satya Ltd. for sale of goods costing ₹8 lakh at a profit of 20% on cost. The sale transaction took place on 1st February, 2024. On the same day, Satya Ltd. entered into another agreement with Mithya Ltd. to resell the same goods at ₹10.80 lakh on 1st August, 2024. State the treatment of this transaction in the financial statements of Mithya Ltd. as on 31.03.2024. The predetermined re-selling price covers the holding cost of Satya Ltd. Give the Journal Entries as on 31.03.2024 in the books of Mithya Ltd.
answer_html:
In the given case, Mithya Ltd. concurrently agreed to repurchase the same goods from Satya Ltd. on 1st February, 2024. Also the re-selling price is pre-determined and covers purchasing and holding costs of Satya Ltd. Hence, the transaction between Mithya Ltd. and Satya Ltd. on 1st February, 2024 should be accounted for as financing rather than sale. The resulting cash flow of ₹9.60 lakh received by Mithya Ltd. cannot be considered as revenue as per AS 9 "Revenue Recognition".

question_html:

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html:
Bansal Company Ltd. imported raw material worth US Dollars 12,000 on 15th January, 2024 when the exchange rate was ₹68 per US Dollar. The payment for the transaction was made on 5th May, 2024 when exchange rate was ₹64 per US Dollar. At the year end, 31st March, 2024, the rate of exchange was ₹65 per US Dollar. The accountant of the company passed entry on 31st March, 2024 adjusting the cost of raw material consumed for the difference between ₹64 and ₹68 per US Dollar.

Discuss whether this treatment is justified as per the provisions of AS-11 (Revised).
answer_html:
As per AS 11, "The Effects of Changes in Foreign Exchange Rates", initial recognition of a foreign currency transaction is done in the reporting currency by applying the exchange rate at the date of the transaction. Accordingly, on 15th January, 2024, the raw material purchased and its creditors will be recorded at US dollar 12,000 × ₹68 = ₹8,16,000.

Also, on balance sheet date such transaction is reported at closing rate of exchange, hence it will be valued at the closing rate i.e. ₹65 per US dollar (USD 12,000 × ₹65 = ₹7,80,000) at 31st March, 2024, irrespective of the payment made for the same subsequently at a lower rate in the next financial year.

The difference of ₹3 (65 − 68) per US dollar i.e. ₹36,000 (USD 12,000 × ₹3) will be shown as an exchange gain in the profit and loss account for the year ended 31st March, 2024 and will not be adjusted against the cost of raw materials.

In the subsequent year on settlement date, the company would recognize or provide in the Profit and Loss account an exchange gain of ₹1 per US dollar, i.e. the difference from balance sheet date to the date of settlement between ₹65 and ₹64 per US dollar i.e. ₹12,000.

Hence, the accounting treatment adopted by the Accountant of the company is incorrect i.e. it is not in accordance with the provisions of AS 11.

topics.title: The Effects of Changes in Foreign Exchange Rates
topics.subtopictitle: Monetary items restated at the closing rate at each balance sheet date; the resulting exchange difference goes to profit and loss, never adjusted against the non-monetary cost already recorded
topics.label: AS 11 (3.4)

examiner_comment.text: A common error is adjusting the cost of raw material consumed for the exchange difference between the transaction-date and settlement-date rates, missing that AS 11 requires monetary items to be restated at the closing rate at each balance sheet date, with the resulting exchange difference recognised in the Statement of Profit and Loss, not adjusted against the non-monetary cost of raw material already recorded.

The payment made by the transferee company to discharge the Debenture holders and outside liabilities and cost of winding up of the transferor company shall not be considered as part of purchase consideration.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html:
How will interest be capitalized when qualifying assets are funded by borrowings in the nature of bonds that are issued at a discount?

X Ltd. issued in year 1, a 3 year 10% p.a. (interest paid annually) bond with a face value of ₹1,00,000 at a price of ₹90,000 to finance a qualifying asset which is ready for intended use at the end of year 2. Compute the amount of borrowings costs to be capitalized if the company uses for amortization of discount straight line basis.
answer_html:
As per AS 16, "Borrowing costs are interest and other costs incurred by an enterprise in connection with the borrowing of funds". Further, as per para 4(b) of the standard, "amortization of discounts or premiums relating to borrowings" is a component of borrowing costs. Thus, the borrowing costs comprise the periodic interest payable on the bonds in question and the amount of discount amortised during the period.

Paragraph 6 of the Statement, inter-alia, states that "Borrowing costs that are directly attributable to the acquisition, construction or production of a qualifying asset should be capitalized as part of the cost of that asset". Further, paragraph 19 states that "Capitalisation of borrowing costs should cease when substantially all the activities necessary to prepare the qualifying asset for its intended use or sale are complete". Thus, only that portion of the amortised discount should be capitalised as part of the cost of a qualifying asset which relates to the period during which acquisition, construction or production of the asset takes place.

Straight line basis (Amount in ₹)

YearsInterestAmortisation of discountTotal borrowing costs
Year 110,0003,33313,333
Year 210,0003,33313,333
Year 310,0003,33413,334

In the above case, the amount of borrowing costs capitalized would be ₹13,333 in Year 1 and Year 2. The borrowing costs of ₹13,334 incurred in Year 3 would be expensed since the asset is ready for its intended use at the end of Year 2.

topics.title: Borrowing Costs
topics.subtopictitle: Amortisation of a bond discount is a component of borrowing cost eligible for capitalisation only up to the period during which the qualifying asset is under construction
topics.label: AS 16 (4.4)

examiner_comment.text: A common error is capitalising the entire annual bond discount amortisation for all three years as a borrowing cost, missing that AS 16 requires capitalisation to cease once the qualifying asset is ready for its intended use — here, at the end of Year 2 — so the Year 3 amortised discount and interest must be expensed, not capitalised.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html:
A Company has an inter-segment transfer pricing policy of charging at cost less 5%. The market prices are generally 20% above cost.

You are required to examine whether the policy adopted by the company is correct or not?
answer_html: AS 17 "Segment Reporting" requires that inter-segment transfers should be measured on the basis that the enterprise actually used to price these transfers. The basis of pricing inter-segment transfers and any change therein should be disclosed in the financial statements. Hence, the enterprise can have its own policy for pricing inter-segment transfers and hence, inter-segment transfers may be based on cost, below cost or market price. However, whichever policy is followed, the same should be disclosed and applied consistently. Therefore, in the given case the inter-segment transfer pricing policy adopted by the company is correct if followed consistently.

topics.title: Segment Reporting
topics.subtopictitle: Inter-segment transfer pricing may be based on any consistently-applied and disclosed basis - cost, below cost, or market price
topics.label: AS 17 (3.6)

examiner_comment.text: A common error is concluding that any inter-segment transfer price other than market price is automatically non-compliant with AS 17, missing that the standard permits any consistently-applied and disclosed pricing basis, including cost, below cost, or market price.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html:
Will transactions with related parties, for services provided/received free of cost, be required to be disclosed?

A Limited has a corporate communications department, which centralises the public relations function for the whole group of A Limited and its subsidiaries. No charges are, however, levied by A Limited on its subsidiaries and accordingly, these transactions are not given accounting recognition. Would these constitute related party transactions requiring disclosure under AS 18 in the standalone financial statements of A Limited?
answer_html: These transactions would require disclosure under AS 18 in the standalone financial statements of A Limited. As per paragraph 10 of AS 18, a related party transaction is "a transfer of resources or obligations between related parties, regardless of whether or not a price is charged". In the given situation, there is a transfer of resources from A Limited to its subsidiaries, though no price is charged for the same. Hence, it will constitute a related party transaction and will require disclosure in the financial statements of A Ltd.

topics.title: Related Party Disclosures
topics.subtopictitle: A related party transaction requires disclosure whether or not a price is actually charged for the transfer of resources or obligations
topics.label: AS 18 (4.6)

examiner_comment.text: A common error is concluding that a related party transaction requires disclosure under AS 18 only if a price is actually charged, missing that the standard's own definition explicitly covers a transfer of resources or obligations between related parties regardless of whether or not a price is charged.

XYZ Limited has 5,00,000 shares outstanding as at 31st March, 2024. Further, it has granted options to issue equity shares as at that date. In respect of such options, 1,00,000 shares are considered to be the shares issued for no consideration. There are no changes in income or expenses that are expected from the issue of equity shares on exercise of these options.

Calculate Basic and Diluted EPS for XYZ Limited for separate financial statements and for the Group.

Computation of earnings per share

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html:
ABC Ltd. prepares its accounts annually on 31st March. On 1st April, 2022, it purchases a machine at a cost of ₹1,50,000. The machine has a useful life of three years and an expected scrap value of zero. Although it is eligible for a 100% first year depreciation allowance for tax purposes, the straight line method is considered appropriate for accounting purposes. ABC Ltd. has profits before depreciation and taxes of ₹2,00,000 each year and corporate tax rate is 40 percent each year.

The purchase of machine at a cost of ₹1,50,000 in 2022 gives rise to a tax saving of ₹60,000. The corporate tax rate has been assumed to be same in each of the three years. Calculate deferred tax and pass necessary journal entries.

What will be the amount of deferred tax, if the substantively enacted tax rates for 2022, 2023 and 2024 are 40%, 35% and 38% respectively.
answer_html:
If the cost of machine is spread over three years of its life for accounting purposes, the amount of the tax saving should also be spread over the same period as shown below:

Less: Depreciation for accounting purposes505050

In 2022, the amount of depreciation allowed for tax purposes exceeds the amount of depreciation charged for accounting purposes by ₹1,00,000 and, therefore, taxable income is lower than the accounting income — giving rise to a deferred tax liability of ₹40,000. In 2023 and 2024, accounting income is lower than taxable income because the amount of depreciation charged for accounting purposes exceeds the amount allowed for tax purposes by ₹50,000 each year; deferred tax liability is reduced by ₹20,000 in each of those years.

Journal Entries

The amount debited (credited) to the profit and loss account for each year is accordingly: 31st March, 2022 Debit ₹40,000; 31st March, 2023 (Credit) ₹(22,500); 31st March, 2024 (Credit) ₹(17,500).

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html: A Ltd. invested ₹1,00,000 to acquire 10% stake (Investment I) in B Ltd. and later invested ₹3,00,000 to acquire additional 20% (Investment II). The net asset value of the B Ltd. at the respective investment dates was ₹7,50,000 and ₹12,50,000 respectively. Determine whether B Ltd. is an associate of A Ltd. Also, calculate goodwill arising on the acquisition of the associate.
answer_html:
As per para 3 of AS 23, an associate is an enterprise in which the investor has significant influence and which is neither a subsidiary nor a joint venture of the investor. Significant influence may be gained by share ownership, statute or agreement. As regards share ownership, if an investor holds, directly or indirectly through subsidiary(ies), 20% or more of the voting power of the investee, it is presumed that the investor has significant influence, unless it can be clearly demonstrated that this is not the case. In this case, A Ltd. has invested 30% in B Ltd. so B Ltd. is to be considered as an associate of A Ltd.

The goodwill arising on the acquisition of the associate will be computed as follows:

Investment I1,00,000
Share of net assets (10 percent of ₹7,50,000)(75,000)
Goodwill (A)25,000
Investment II3,00,000
Share of net assets (20 percent of ₹12,50,000)(2,50,000)
Goodwill (B)50,000
Total goodwill (A + B)75,000

topics.title: Accounting for Investments in Associates in Consolidated Financial Statements
topics.subtopictitle: 20% voting-power presumption of significant influence; goodwill computed per-tranche against the investee's net asset value at each tranche's own acquisition date
topics.label: AS 23 (2.3)

examiner_comment.text: A common error is computing goodwill on the associate's acquisition as a single blended calculation across both tranches, missing that AS 23 requires each tranche of investment to be compared against the investee's net asset value at that tranche's own acquisition date, since intervening changes in net assets affect the goodwill computed on the later tranche.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html:
What are the disclosure and presentation requirements of AS 24 for discontinuing operations?

Give four examples of activities that do not necessarily satisfy criterion (a) of paragraph 3 of AS 24, but that might do so in combination with other circumstances.
answer_html:
(i) An enterprise should include the following information relating to a discontinuing operation in its financial statements beginning with the financial statements for the period in which the initial disclosure event (as defined in paragraph 15) occurs:

  1. a description of the discontinuing operation(s);
  2. the business or geographical segment(s) in which it is reported as per AS 17, Segment Reporting;
  3. the date and nature of the initial disclosure event;
  4. the date or period in which the discontinuance is expected to be completed if known or determinable;
  5. the carrying amounts, as of the balance sheet date, of the total assets to be disposed of and the total liabilities to be settled;
  6. the amounts of revenue and expenses in respect of the ordinary activities attributable to the discontinuing operation during the current financial reporting period;
  7. the amount of pre-tax profit or loss from ordinary activities attributable to the discontinuing operation during the current financial reporting period, and the income tax expense related thereto; and
  8. the amounts of net cash flows attributable to the operating, investing, and financing activities of the discontinuing operation during the current financial reporting period.

(ii) Para 3 of AS 24 "Discontinuing Operations" explains the criteria for determination of discontinuing operations. According to Paragraph 9 of AS 24, examples of activities that do not necessarily satisfy criterion (a) of paragraph 3, but that might do so in combination with other circumstances, include:

  1. Gradual or evolutionary phasing out of a product line or class of service;
  2. Discontinuing, even if relatively abruptly, several products within an ongoing line of business;
  3. Shifting of some production or marketing activities for a particular line of business from one location to another; and
  4. Closing of a facility to achieve productivity improvements or other cost savings.

An example in relation to consolidated financial statements is selling a subsidiary whose activities are similar to those of the parent or other subsidiaries.

topics.title: Discontinuing Operations
topics.subtopictitle: Disclosure and presentation requirements for a discontinuing operation, and activities that only satisfy the AS 24 criteria in combination with other circumstances
topics.label: AS 24 (6.5)

examiner_comment.text: A common error is treating any product-line phase-out or facility closure as an automatic discontinuing operation under AS 24, missing that paragraph 9's listed activities only qualify in combination with other circumstances that independently satisfy the AS 24 criteria for a distinct, separately identifiable major line of business or geographical area.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html:
During 2023-2024, an enterprise incurred costs to develop and produce a routine, low risk computer software product, as follows:

Completion of detailed programme and design (Phase 1)₹25,000
Coding and Testing for establishing technical feasibility (Phase 2)₹20,000
Other coding costs (Phase 3)₹42,000
Testing costs (Phase 4)₹12,000
Product masters for training materials (Phase 5)₹13,000
Duplication of computer software and training materials, from product masters (2,000 units) (Phase 6)₹40,000
Packing the product (1,000 units) (Phase 7)₹11,000

After completion of phase 2, it was established that the computer software is technically feasible for the market. What amount should be capitalized as software costs in the books of the company, on the Balance Sheet date?
answer_html:
As per para 44 of AS 26, costs incurred in creating a computer software product should be charged to research and development expense when incurred until technological feasibility/asset recognition criteria has been established for the product. Technological feasibility/asset recognition criteria have been established upon completion of detailed programme design or working model. In this case, ₹45,000 would be recorded as an expense (₹25,000 for completion of detailed programme design and ₹20,000 for coding and testing to establish technological feasibility/asset recognition criteria).

Cost incurred from the point of technological feasibility/asset recognition criteria until the time when product costs are incurred are capitalized as software cost (₹42,000 + ₹12,000 + ₹13,000) = ₹67,000. Duplication of computer software and training materials, from product masters and packing the products are costs incurred after the development phase. Hence, the same shall be expensed off during the year it is incurred.

topics.title: Intangible Assets
topics.subtopictitle: Costs incurred before technological feasibility is established are expensed (research phase); costs from that point until product-master completion are capitalised (development phase); post-development duplication/packing costs are expensed
topics.label: AS 26 (6.15)

examiner_comment.text: A common error is capitalising the cost of completing the detailed programme design and the coding/testing performed to establish technical feasibility, missing that AS 26 requires all costs incurred before technological feasibility is established to be expensed as research and development, with capitalisation beginning only from that point onward.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html:
During the year, QA Ltd. delivered manufactured products to customer K. The products were faulty and on 1st October, 2023 customer K commenced legal action against the Company claiming damages in respect of losses due to the supply of faulty product. Upon investigating the matter, QA Ltd. discovered that the products were faulty due to defective raw material procured from supplier F. Therefore, on 1st December, 2023, the Company commenced legal action against F claiming damages in respect of the supply of defective raw materials. QA Ltd. has estimated that its probability of success of both legal actions, the action of K against QA Ltd. and action of QA Ltd. against F, is very high.

On 1st October, 2023, QA Ltd. has estimated that the damages it would have to pay K would be ₹5 crore. This estimate was revised to ₹5.2 crore as on 31st March, 2024 and ₹5.25 crore as at 15th May, 2024. This case was eventually settled on 1st June, 2022, when the Company paid damages of ₹5.3 crore to K.

On 1st December, 2023, QA Ltd. had estimated that it would receive damages of ₹3.5 crore from F. This estimate was revised to ₹3.6 crore as at 31st March, 2024 and ₹3.7 crore as on 15th May, 2024. This case was eventually settled on 1st June, 2022 when F paid ₹3.75 crore to QA Ltd. QA Ltd. had, in its financial statements for the year ended 31st March, 2024, provided ₹3.6 crore as the financial statements were approved by the Board of Directors on 26th April, 2024.

(i) Whether the Company is required to make provision for the claim from customer K as per applicable AS? If yes, please give the rationale for the same.

(ii) If the answer to (i) above is yes, what is the entry to be passed in the books of account as on 31st March, 2024?

(iii) What will be the accounting treatment of the action of QA Ltd. against supplier F as per applicable AS?
answer_html:
(i) Yes, QA Ltd. is required to make provision for the claim from customer K as per AS 29, since the claim is a present obligation as a result of delivery of faulty goods manufactured. Also, it is probable that an outflow of resources embodying economic benefits will be required to settle the obligation. Further, a reliable estimate of ₹5.2 crore can be made of the amount of the obligation while preparing the financial statements as on 31st March, 2024.

(ii)

Statement of Profit and Loss A/c Dr.₹5.2 crore
  To Current Liability A/c₹5.2 crore

(iii) As per para 30 of AS 29, QA Ltd. shall not recognise a contingent asset. Here the probability of success of the legal action is very high but there is no concrete evidence which makes the inflow virtually certain. Hence, it will be considered as a contingent asset only and shall not be recognized.

topics.title: Provisions, Contingent Liabilities and Contingent Assets
topics.subtopictitle: Provision recognised for a present obligation with a probable, reliably estimable outflow
topics.label: AS 29 (2.4)

topics.title: Provisions, Contingent Liabilities and Contingent Assets
topics.subtopictitle: A contingent asset is not recognised, even where success is highly probable, until its realisation is virtually certain
topics.label: AS 29 (2.9-2.10)

examiner_comment.text: A common error is failing to distinguish the treatment of the two legal actions — provisioning is required for the probable, reliably estimable outflow to customer K under AS 29, while the claim against supplier F, however probable, remains an unrecognisable contingent asset until its realisation is virtually certain, not merely highly probable.

Both settlement dates are printed in the source as "1st June, 2022" (for the K claim and the F claim), which is chronologically impossible — every other date in this question falls in 2023/2024, and a settlement cannot pre-date the claims it settles (K's action commenced 1st October 2023; F's on 1st December 2023). This is an evident date error in the source's own suggested answer (very likely "2024" intended), reproduced verbatim rather than silently corrected, per this pipeline's flag-don't-fix policy. Kept as one connected record (parts (i)-(iii) all discuss the same fact pattern), not split.

case_facts_html:
Gases Ltd. is installing a 2,000 kms long gas pipeline for distribution of gasses (Project is a qualifying asset as per AS 16). For this purpose it borrowed funds for ₹700 Lakhs at subsidised rates and has to pay annually an interest of ₹70 Lakhs. The Company has also invested unused funds and is earning an income of ₹7 Lakhs annually. During the next year the Company used all funds and no income is now being earned. During the year 5, the Company has completed 1 stretch of 100 kms which is operational between two points and is capable of intended use.

Based on the information given above, answer Question No. 1 (a)–(d).
question_html:
For the year 1, how much borrowing cost should be capitalised to the project:

  1. ₹70 Lakhs
  2. ₹77 Lakhs
  3. ₹63 Lakhs
  4. ₹60 Lakhs

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html:
A dealer in machinery, Shakti Equipments Pvt. Ltd., leased out one of its machines to Delta Tools Ltd. on a 3-year operating lease, with equal annual lease rentals intended to yield a 20% profit margin on the cost of the machinery (₹3,00,000). Economic life of the machinery is 5 years; total expected output over its useful life: Year I 50,000 units, Year II 60,000, Year III 40,000, Year IV 65,000, Year V 85,000. Delta Tools will use the machine for Years I–III only, then return it. Compute the annual lease rent that provides the dealer a 20% profit margin on cost.

  1. ₹30,000
  2. ₹60,000
  3. ₹50,000
  4. ₹36,000
answer_html: Answer: (B) ₹60,000. Total amount the dealer targets recovering over the machine's full economic life = cost + 20% margin = ₹3,00,000 × 1.20 = ₹3,60,000. Since this is an operating lease, the dealer recovers this target progressively, in proportion to how much of the machine's total lifetime output/value is consumed during each period of use — not by amortising the full amount over just the 3-year lease term. Output during the 3-year lease (Years I–III): 50,000+60,000+40,000 = 1,50,000 units, exactly 50% of the machine's total 5-year output (3,00,000 units). The dealer therefore targets recovering 50% of ₹3,60,000 = ₹1,80,000 during this lease, as equal annual rentals over the 3 years: ₹1,80,000 / 3 = ₹60,000/year.

topics.title: Leases
topics.subtopictitle: Operating lessor's target rental recovery apportioned by the leased asset's output consumed during the lease term, out of its full economic-life output
topics.label: AS 19 (5.2)

examiner_comment.text: A common error is spreading the full cost-plus-margin total evenly over only the 3-year lease term (giving ₹1,20,000/year, not a listed option), missing that the dealer only needs to recover the portion of value corresponding to the output consumed during this particular lease, since the machine still has 2 years/half its output-value left when it is returned.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: A private limited company manufacturing fancy terry towels had valued its closing inventory of finished goods at realisable value, inclusive of profit and export cash incentives. Firm contracts had been received and goods were packed for export, but ownership had not been transferred to the foreign buyers. Comment on the valuation of the inventories by the company.
answer_html:
AS 2 requires inventories to be valued at the lower of historical cost and net realisable value. AS 9 permits valuing goods at net realisable value only in specific industries where performance is substantially complete prior to the transaction generating revenue — e.g. harvested agricultural crops or extracted mineral ores, where a sale is assured under forward contract/government guarantee or a ready market exists with negligible risk of failure to sell.

Fancy terry towels do not fall into the agricultural-crop or mineral-ore category. Since ownership had not transferred to the foreign buyers, the sale was not yet complete. The closing inventory should therefore have been valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value, not at net realisable value. Further, export cash incentives are recognised only in the year the export sale actually takes place, not accrued into inventory valuation ahead of the sale. The company's valuation policy is therefore not correct.

topics.title: Valuation of Inventories
topics.subtopictitle: Lower of cost and NRV - the NRV-only exception is limited to specific industries, not general manufacturing
topics.label: AS 2 (1.3)

examiner_comment.text: Some examinees accepted the NRV-inclusive-of-profit valuation on the basis of firm export contracts alone, not recognising that the AS 9 exception is limited to specific industries (agricultural/mineral) and does not extend to manufactured goods merely because a sale contract exists.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: Zenith Industries Ltd., preparing FY2024-25 financial statements. After year-end: (a) Fire on 10th April, 2025 destroyed uninsured stock worth ₹10,00,000, salvage recovered ₹2,00,000. (b) Legal claim filed 18th April, 2025 alleging misleading advertisement, damages claimed ₹20,00,000. (c) Cheques in Hand: company proposes recognising all cheques dated 31st March, 2025 or earlier received from stockists as "Cheques in Hand" under Cash and Cash Equivalents, reducing Trade Receivables — but two categories exist: (i) cheques physically collected by marketing personnel on/before 31st March, 2025; (ii) cheques sent by courier on/before 31st March but received only in April 2025. All cheques were deposited and realized in April 2025. Comment on the accounting treatment for each.
answer_html:
(a) Fire and loss of uninsured stock: occurred after the balance sheet date and does not relate to any condition existing on 31st March, 2025 — a non-adjusting event. Given its materiality (uninsured stock, future risk exposure), the fire and uninsured position must be disclosed, including its nature, estimated financial effect, and future vulnerability if determinable.

(b) Legal suit: initiated after the balance sheet date, no additional evidence of a pre-existing condition — also non-adjusting. Per AS 4 para 16, disclose as a contingent liability, including the nature of the contingency, estimated financial effect, and outcome uncertainties.

(c)(i) Cheques collected by marketing personnel: physically collected on or before 31st March, 2025 — since marketing personnel act as company representatives, this constitutes receipt by the company itself, discharging the stockist's liability. This is an adjusting event: reduce Trade Receivables and recognise as Cheques in Hand under Cash and Cash Equivalents, with appropriate accounting-policy disclosure.

(c)(ii) Cheques sent by courier, received only in April: though dated on/before 31st March, they were not in the company's possession until after the balance sheet date — a non-adjusting event. Account for these in the period actually received (April 2025), regardless of the cheque date; no disclosure needed since the event does not materially affect the financial position.

topics.title: Contingencies and Events occurring after the Balance Sheet Date
topics.subtopictitle: Adjusting vs non-adjusting events - physical possession vs mere date determines cheque treatment
topics.label: AS 4 (1.5)

examiner_comment.text: Some examinees treated all cheques dated on or before 31st March as adjusting events based on the cheque date alone, missing that physical possession by the company (or its representative) by the balance sheet date, not the cheque's date, is what actually determines adjusting vs. non-adjusting treatment.

question_html: Identify each of the following as Change in Accounting Policy / Change in Accounting Estimate / Extraordinary Item / Prior Period Item / Ordinary Activity: (i) Non-provision for salary already due in an earlier year. (ii) Attachment of the property of the enterprise. (iii) Introduction of a new pension scheme for employees. (iv) Change in Reserve for obsolete inventory. (v) Settlement of a litigation case. (vi) Legislative changes with long-term retrospective application. (vii) Change from Cost Model to Revaluation Model for PPE measurement. (viii) Government-sanctioned grant received this year for expenses incurred in a previous year.
answer_html:
1. Prior period item.
  2. Extraordinary item.
  3. Ordinary activity (not a change in accounting policy).
  4. Change in accounting estimate.
  5. Ordinary activity, but requires separate disclosure.
  6. Extraordinary item requiring separate disclosure.
  7. Change in accounting policy.
  8. Prior period item.
