subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: Best Ltd., a consultancy services provider, received a GST department demand notice of ₹2,50,000 on consultancy services provided; the company paid the demand and recorded it as extraordinary expenditure. Can this payment of a tax demand be recognised as an extraordinary item?
answer_html: No. Per AS 5, extraordinary items arise from events clearly distinct from ordinary activities and are not expected to recur frequently or regularly. Providing consultancy services is Best Ltd.'s ordinary business activity, and the GST liability arises directly from these ordinary transactions. Paying a tax demand raised by the taxation authority is part of normal business operations. Recording it as extraordinary is therefore not correct — it should be recognised as part of profit or loss from ordinary activities.

topics.label: AS 5 (2.4)

examiner_comment.text: Some examinees accepted the company's own extraordinary-item classification uncritically, not testing it against AS 5's actual definition (an event clearly distinct from, and not part of, the ordinary business activity).

question_html: A construction contractor entered a fixed-price contract of ₹18,000 lacs to construct a bridge within 3 years, with provisions for variations. (₹ in lacs): Year 1/2/3 — Initial revenue agreed 18,000/18,000/18,000; Variation in revenue (+)400/400 (Years 2,3); Contract costs incurred to date 4,186/12,336*/16,200**; Estimated profit for whole contract 1,900/2,000/2,000. *includes ₹200 lacs standard materials stored at site for use in Year 3. **excludes ₹200 lacs standard material brought forward from Year 2. subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: Class Ltd., a real-estate developer, purchased land for ₹225 crore in FY2025 intending a residential complex, then sold it a few months later for ₹360 crore due to a strategic reallocation and favourable market conditions. All legal formalities completed. Advise on revenue recognition for the year ended 31st March, 2025.
answer_html:
AS 9 recognises revenue when earned with reasonable certainty of collection, arising from the enterprise's ordinary activities. Class Ltd. is in the business of buying and selling properties; the land forms part of its inventory. The ₹360 crore sale is therefore a transaction arising from ordinary activities, and revenue is recognised when the sale is completed and collection is reasonably certain.

Per AS 5, this is not an extraordinary item, since it arises in the ordinary course of business — though given its size, its nature and amount should be separately disclosed if relevant to explaining the enterprise's performance. The ₹360 crore is recognised as revenue in the year the sale is completed.

topics.title: Revenue Recognition
topics.subtopictitle: Property sale by a real-estate dealer is ordinary-activity revenue, not extraordinary, even at unusual scale
topics.label: AS 9 (1.2)

examiner_comment.text: Some examinees treated the large, unusual sale as an extraordinary item given its size and the company's stated change in strategy, missing that dealing in land is Class Ltd.'s core ordinary business, so scale alone does not make a transaction extraordinary.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: Mediwell Hospitals Ltd. acquired 40 Doppler Scan Machines from Holiver Inc., USA, at US$1,65,100/unit at the start of FY2022-23, exchange rate ₹50/US$. Partly financed by a government grant of ₹5 crores (specific condition: refund on change in management/ownership control). In April 2025, 51% shareholding acquired by an overseas investor — management control changed, grant refund now due. Useful life 5 years, SLM at 20% p.a. Also: Bank charges US$4,000 (whole import), Sea freight ₹7,500/unit. No Capital Reserve or Deferred Income Account was maintained for the grant. Advise the accounting treatment for the grant refund per AS 12.
answer_html:
The grant was received towards a fixed asset; the capital (deduction-from-cost) approach was adopted (confirmed by the absence of a Capital Reserve or Deferred Income Account).

Cost of asset (1,65,100 × 40 units × ₹50)3,302 lakhs
Add: Freight and other charges (4,000×50 bank charges + 7,500×40 sea freight)5 lakhs
Total cost3,307 lakhs
Less: Grant received(500 lakhs)
Cost as per AS 10 (net of grant)2,807 lakhs
Less: Depreciation for 3 years (2,807 × 20% × 3)(1,684.2 lakhs)
Carrying amount as on 1.4.2025 (before refund)1,122.8 lakhs
Add: Grant refunded500 lakhs
Revised carrying amount1,622.8 lakhs

Per AS 12, when a grant that was deducted from an asset's cost becomes refundable, the amount refundable is added back to the carrying amount of the asset (or the gross book value increased), rather than expensed — increasing the future depreciation charge over the asset's remaining life.

topics.title: Accounting for Government Grants
topics.subtopictitle: Refund of a grant previously deducted from asset cost - added back to the asset's carrying amount
topics.label: AS 12 (1.7)

examiner_comment.text: Some examinees expensed the refunded grant amount directly to the P&L, not applying AS 12's specific rule that a refund of a grant deducted from asset cost is added back to the carrying amount of that asset.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: Mr. Rohan acquired 200 equity shares of Zeta Technologies Ltd. on a cum-right basis for ₹1,40,000 as a long-term investment. The company announced a 1:1 rights issue at ₹214/share. Mr. Rohan did not subscribe, instead selling his rights entitlement for ₹24,000. After the shares became ex-rights, the market value of his existing 200 shares fell to ₹1,20,000. State the appropriate accounting treatment for the sale of rights and the fall in market value, per AS 13.
answer_html:
Per AS 13, when investments are acquired cum-right and the market value immediately after becoming ex-rights is lower than cost, it may be appropriate to apply the rights sale proceeds to reduce the carrying amount of the investment to its (ex-rights) market value.

Here, cost ₹1,40,000; ex-rights market value ₹1,20,000 — a decline of ₹20,000. Of the ₹24,000 rights sale proceeds, ₹20,000 is applied to reduce the carrying amount from ₹1,40,000 to ₹1,20,000 (its ex-rights market value); the balance ₹4,000 (24,000−20,000) is credited to the Profit and Loss Account as income.

The investment in the 200 equity shares is shown at a carrying amount of ₹1,20,000 in Mr. Rohan's books.

topics.title: Accounting for Investments
topics.subtopictitle: Rights sale proceeds applied to reduce carrying amount to ex-rights market value, balance credited to P&L
topics.label: AS 13 (3.6)

examiner_comment.text: Some examinees credited the entire ₹24,000 rights sale proceeds to P&L as income, not applying AS 13's rule that the portion covering the decline to ex-rights market value should instead reduce the investment's carrying amount.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: Can interest be included in the cost of inventories?
answer_html:
As a general rule, AS 2 (para 12) provides that interest and other borrowing costs are usually not related to bringing inventories to their present location and condition, and are therefore usually excluded from inventory cost.

However, AS 16 (para 6) requires borrowing costs directly attributable to acquisition/construction/production of a qualifying asset to be capitalised, and para 5 specifically includes "inventories that require a substantial period of time to bring them to a saleable condition" as an example of a qualifying asset (e.g. liquor requiring 12+ months of maturation, per ASI 1). It is only in such exceptional cases — where time is a major factor in changing the condition of the inventory — that borrowing costs are included in inventory valuation. Routinely/repetitively manufactured inventory over a short period is never a qualifying asset, so its borrowing costs are never capitalised.

topics.title: Borrowing Costs
topics.subtopictitle: Interest capitalised into inventory cost only for the exceptional qualifying-asset case (substantial maturation period)
topics.label: AS 16 (4.2)

examiner_comment.text: Some examinees answered with a flat "no", missing the exceptional qualifying-asset case (e.g. maturing liquor) where AS 16 does require capitalisation into inventory cost.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: Garnet Limited has 4 operating segments (₹ in appropriate units): Fan — Inter-segment sales 3,200, External sales 10,900, Total assets 23,700; Light — 200, 1,400, 13,200; Lamp — 0, 1,500, 4,200; Printer — 1,100, 200, 3,400; Total — 4,500, 14,000, 44,500. How many reportable segments does Garnet Limited have per the Revenue and Assets criteria in AS 17? State reasons.
answer_html:
A segment is reportable if its revenue (external + inter-segment) is ≥10% of total revenue (external + internal, all segments), OR its assets are ≥10% of total assets.

Total revenue basis (external 14,000 + internal 4,500 = 18,500): 10% threshold = 1,850. Fan's total revenue (3,200+10,900=14,100) far exceeds 1,850 — Fan is reportable. (Light: 200+1,400=1,600, below threshold; Lamp: 0+1,500=1,500, below; Printer: 1,100+200=1,300, below.)

Assets basis (total 44,500): 10% threshold = 4,450. Fan (23,700) and Light (13,200) both exceed this — both are reportable on the assets criterion.

75% external-revenue test: reportable segments' external revenue must cover ≥75% of total external revenue (75% × 14,000 = 10,500). Fan and Light's combined external revenue (10,900+1,400=12,300) already exceeds 10,500, so no additional segments need to be added to meet the 75% threshold.

Conclusion: Garnet Limited has 2 reportable segments — Fan and Light (Fan qualifies on both revenue and assets; Light qualifies on assets only, but that alone is sufficient).

topics.title: Segment Reporting
topics.subtopictitle: Reportable segment thresholds - 10% revenue or assets test, plus the 75% external-revenue coverage check
topics.label: AS 17 (3.3)

examiner_comment.text: Some examinees tested the 10% revenue threshold against external sales alone, omitting inter-segment sales from the revenue base used for that specific test.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: Mr. Rajiv, a KMP of Raijada Limited, received a cheque of ₹70,000 towards reimbursement of expenses incurred on hotel stay, conference expenses, etc. while attending a meeting on behalf of the company. Is this transaction covered under AS-18?

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: On 1st April, 2024, Mansi Ltd. sold a plant for ₹8,52,800 (carrying amount ₹1,80,000) as part of a sale-and-leaseback package with Akash Ltd., leasing the asset back for an 8-year term. Economic life of the asset is 8 years. Minimum lease rents ₹1,60,000/year, payable annually from 31st March, 2025. Mansi Ltd.'s incremental borrowing rate is 10% p.a. Calculate the net effect on the Statement of Profit and Loss in Mansi Ltd.'s (the lessee's) books.
answer_html:
Lease classification: lease term (8 years) covers the entire economic life (8 years). PV of minimum lease payments = ₹1,60,000 × 5.335 (annuity factor @10% for 8 years) = ₹8,53,600, which substantially covers the fair value/sale price (₹8,52,800). This is therefore a finance lease.

Per AS 19 para 48, where a sale-and-leaseback results in a finance lease, the profit on sale (₹8,52,800−₹1,80,000 = ₹6,72,800) is not recognised immediately — it is deferred and amortised over the lease term in proportion to the depreciation of the leased asset.

Assuming straight-line depreciation: Depreciation = ₹8,52,800/8 = ₹1,06,600/year. Deferred profit amortised = ₹6,72,800/8 = ₹84,100/year. Net effect on Statement of P&L = ₹1,06,600 − ₹84,100 = ₹22,500 debit per annum, for each of the 8 years of the lease term.

topics.title: Leases
topics.subtopictitle: Sale-and-leaseback resulting in a finance lease - profit deferred and amortised in proportion to asset depreciation
topics.label: AS 19 (5.9)

examiner_comment.text: Some examinees recognised the full sale profit immediately in the year of sale, not applying AS 19's specific deferral-and-amortisation rule for a sale-and-leaseback that results in a finance lease.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: Should appropriation to mandatory reserves be excluded from net profit attributable to equity shareholders? AB Limited must, per an agreement with debenture holders, appropriate profits each year to a specific reserve such that, at redemption, the reserve equals at least half the debenture value. Since these appropriations aren't available for distribution to equity shareholders, AB Limited excluded them from the Basic EPS numerator. Is this correct?
answer_html:
The appropriation to such a mandatory reserve should be included in net profit attributable to equity shareholders for computing Basic EPS — AB Limited's treatment is not correct.

AS 20 para 11 defines the numerator as net profit/loss for the period "attributable to equity shareholders" — after deducting preference dividends and attributable tax, but nothing else. Emphasis on "attributable to equity shareholders" (not "available for distribution") means amounts appropriated to mandatory reserves, though not distributable as dividend, remain attributable to equity shareholders in substance (the reserve still belongs to them, merely earmarked). They should therefore be included in the Basic EPS computation.

topics.subtopictitle: Mandatory-reserve appropriations remain attributable to equity shareholders and are not excluded from the EPS numerator
topics.label: AS 20 (5.2)

examiner_comment.text: Some examinees conflated "attributable to equity shareholders" with "distributable to equity shareholders," incorrectly excluding non-distributable mandatory-reserve appropriations from the EPS numerator.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: Swift Limited acquired patent rights to manufacture Solar Roof Top Panels for ₹600 lacs. Product life cycle estimated at 5 years; amortization decided in the ratio of future cash flows: Year 1–5: 300, 300, 300, 150, 150 (₹ lacs). After Year 3, estimated balance future life revised to 3 years, with expected cash flow after Year 5 of ₹75 lacs. Determine the amortization cost of the patent for each year per AS 26.
answer_html:
Years 1–3, amortized in the ratio of the originally estimated future cash flows 300:300:300:150:150 (total 1,200): each of Years 1, 2, 3 = ₹600 × 300/1,200 = ₹150 lacs/year.

Unamortized patent cost after Year 3 = 600−450 = ₹150 lacs, now amortized over the revised remaining life of 3 years (Years 4, 5, 6) in the ratio of the revised estimated future cash flows: 150:150:75 (i.e. 2:2:1). Year 4 = 150×2/5=₹60 lacs; Year 5 = ₹60 lacs; Year 6 = 150×1/5=₹30 lacs.

Total amortized over the patent's full (revised) life: 150+150+150+60+60+30 = ₹600 lacs, fully recovering the original cost.

topics.subtopictitle: Amortization ratio revised mid-life when future-cash-flow estimates and remaining useful life change
topics.label: AS 26 (6.7)

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: Briefly explain the scope and forms of Joint Venture as per AS 27.
answer_html:
Scope: AS 27 applies to accounting for interests in joint ventures and reporting joint venture assets, liabilities, income, and expenses in the financial statements of venturers and investors, regardless of the structure/form under which the joint venture activities take place. Its consolidated-financial-statements provisions apply only when the venturer prepares and presents CFS.

Forms of Joint Venture: (i) Jointly controlled operations — no separate entity created; venturers use their own resources, raise their own funds, incur expenses, and realise sales individually, using shared assets/employees alongside their own business, with no separate books maintained for the joint venture. (ii) Jointly controlled assets — no separate legal entity, but the venturers jointly own assets used to generate economic benefit for each of them, taking up related expenses/liabilities per the contractual agreement. (iii) Jointly controlled entities — a new entity is created, pooling the venturers' resources; the entity purchases its own assets, incurs its own liabilities/expenses, and makes its own sales; the net result is shared per the contractual agreement, which also determines joint control; a separate set of books is maintained.

topics.subtopictitle: Three forms of joint venture - operations, assets, entities
topics.label: AS 27 (1.2)

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: X Ltd. purchased a fixed asset four years ago for ₹150 lakhs, depreciating at 10% p.a. SLM. At the end of the fourth year, it revalued the asset to ₹75 lakhs, writing off the revaluation loss to P&L. On the revaluation date, market price is ₹67.50 lakhs, expected disposal costs ₹3 lakhs, and value in use is estimated at ₹60 lakhs. What is the treatment of impairment loss, given fair value for revaluation is market-value-based?
answer_html:
W.N. — Carrying amount at revaluation: Purchase price 150.00, less depreciation for 4 years (150/10 × 4) 60.00 = carrying value before revaluation 90.00, less downward revaluation charged to P&L (90−75) 15.00 = revalued carrying amount 75.00 lakhs.

Recoverable amount = higher of net selling price and value in use. Net selling price = market price 67.50 − disposal costs 3.00 = 64.50 lakhs. Value in use = 60 lakhs. Recoverable amount = ₹64.50 lakhs (the higher of the two).

Impairment loss = carrying amount (75.00) − recoverable amount (64.50) = ₹10.50 lakhs, recognised as an expense in the Statement of Profit and Loss immediately (since the prior downward revaluation was already charged to P&L rather than to a revaluation reserve, there is no reserve balance to absorb this further impairment against).

topics.title: Impairment of Assets
topics.subtopictitle: Impairment loss = carrying amount less recoverable amount (higher of net selling price and value in use)
topics.label: AS 28 (7.4)

examiner_comment.text: Some examinees used the market price directly as net selling price without deducting disposal costs, or used net selling price as recoverable amount without comparing it against value in use to find the higher of the two.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: An oil company has been contaminating land for several years, not cleaning up since no legislation currently requires it. At 31st March, 2025, it is virtually certain that a law requiring clean-up of contaminated land will be enacted shortly after the year end. Is provisioning presently necessary?
answer_html:
Per AS 29 para 29, a past event creates a present obligation only when the enterprise has no realistic alternative to settling it. Environmental contamination alone does not create an obligation to remedy it unless a law requires the existing damage to be rectified — and where a proposed law's details are not yet finalised, an obligation arises only once enactment is virtually certain.

Here, it is virtually certain that a clean-up law will be enacted. The oil company must therefore provide for the clean-up cost in the year in which the legislation's enactment becomes virtually certain (the year ended 31st March, 2025) — not deferred until the law is actually enacted.

topics.title: Provisions, Contingent Liabilities and Contingent Assets
topics.subtopictitle: Obligation from prospective legislation arises once enactment is virtually certain, not upon actual enactment
topics.label: AS 29 (2.5)

examiner_comment.text: Some examinees concluded no provision was needed since the law had not yet been enacted at the balance sheet date, missing that "virtually certain" enactment is itself sufficient to trigger the obligation under AS 29.

subject: advanced-accounting
case_facts_html:
RTS Ltd, ("RTS" or the "Company"), is engaged in the business of manufacturing of equipment/components. The Company has a contract with the Indian Railways for a brake component which is structured such that:

  • The Company's obligation is to deliver the component to the Railways' stockyard, while the delivery terms are ex-works, the Company is responsible for engaging a transporter for delivery.
  • Railways sends an order for a defined quantity.
  • The Company manufactures the required quantity and informs Railways for carrying out the inspection.
  • Railways representatives visit the Company's factory and inspect the components and mark each component with a quality check sticker.
  • Goods once inspected by Railways are marked with a hologram sticker to earmark for delivery identification by the customer when they are delivered to the customer's location.
  • The Company raises an invoice once it dispatches the goods.

The management of RTS is under discussion with the auditors of the Company in respect of accounting of a critical matter as regards its accounting with respect subsequent events i.e. events after the reporting period. They have been checking as to which one of the following events after the reporting period provides evidence of conditions that existed at the end of the reporting period?

  1. Nationalisation or privatization by government
  2. Out of court settlement of a legal claim
  3. Rights issue of equity shares
  4. Strike by workforce
  5. Announcing a plan to discontinue an operation

The Company has received a grant of ₹8 crores from the Government for setting up a factory in a backward area. Out of this grant, the Company distributed ₹2 crores as dividend. The Company also received land, free of cost, from the State Government but it has not recorded this at all in the books as no money has been spent.

RTS has a subsidiary, A Ltd, which is evaluating its production process wherein normal waste is 5% of input. 5,000 MT of input were put in process resulting in wastage of 300 MT. Cost per MT of input was ₹1,000. The entire quantity of waste was on stock at the end of the financial year.
question_html:
When should RTS Ltd recognize revenue as per the Accounting Standards notified under the Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules, 2006? Would your answer be different if inspection is normally known to lead to no quality rejections?

  1. Revenue should be recognized on dispatch of components. The assessment would not change even in case where inspection is normally known to lead to no quality rejections.
  2. Revenue should be recognized on completion of inspection of components. The assessment would not change even in case where inspection is normally known to lead to no quality rejections.
  3. Revenue should be recognized on dispatch of components. The assessment would change where inspection is normally known to lead to no quality rejections.
  4. Revenue should be recognized on delivery of the component to the Railways' stockyard. The assessment would change where inspection is normally known to lead to no quality rejections.
answer_html: Answer: (B). Under AS 9, revenue on the sale of goods is recognised only once the seller has transferred the significant risks and rewards of ownership, and no significant uncertainty remains over the consideration or its collectability. Here, Railways' inspection and the affixing of the quality-check/hologram sticker is a substantive condition of the contract, not a formality — until inspection is complete, RTS still bears the risk that the components could be rejected. Revenue is therefore recognised only on completion of inspection, not on mere dispatch or delivery to the stockyard. This conclusion does not change even if inspection is normally known to result in no rejections, because the contractual right of inspection/rejection still exists as a matter of fact until it is actually exercised — a historical track record of passing inspection does not itself transfer the risk earlier.

topics.title: Revenue Recognition
topics.subtopictitle: Timing of revenue recognition on sale of goods - transfer of significant risks/rewards, inspection as a substantive condition of sale
topics.label: AS 9 — Revenue Recognition (2.4-2.5)

examiner_comment.text: A common error here is anchoring revenue recognition to the point of dispatch or delivery, treating the customer's post-delivery inspection as a mere formality rather than testing whether the contractual right of rejection has actually lapsed.

  5. Announcing a plan to discontinue an operation

The Company has received a grant of ₹8 crores from the Government for setting up a factory in a backward area. Out of this grant, the Company distributed ₹2 crores as dividend. The Company also received land, free of cost, from the State Government but it has not recorded this at all in the books as no money has been spent.

RTS has a subsidiary, A Ltd, which is evaluating its production process wherein normal waste is 5% of input. 5,000 MT of input were put in process resulting in wastage of 300 MT. Cost per MT of input was ₹1,000. The entire quantity of waste was on stock at the end of the financial year.
question_html:
In respect of A Ltd, state with reference to Accounting Standards notified under the Companies (Accounting Standards) Rules, 2006, what would be value of the inventory to be recorded in the books of accounts?

  1. ₹47,00,000.
  2. ₹50,00,000.
  3. ₹49,50,000.
  4. ₹49,47,368.
answer_html: Answer: (D) ₹49,47,368. Total process cost = 5,000 MT × ₹1,000 = ₹50,00,000. Normal waste = 5% of input = 250 MT, absorbed into the cost of good production (no separate value). Abnormal waste = actual waste 300 MT − normal waste 250 MT = 50 MT, valued separately at the normal-unit rate and excluded from inventory. Cost per unit of good output = ₹50,00,000 ÷ (5,000 − 250) = ₹50,00,000 ÷ 4,750 = ₹1,052.6316/MT. Good output = 5,000 − 300 = 4,700 MT. Value of inventory = 4,700 × ₹1,052.6316 = ₹49,47,368 (rounded).

topics.title: Valuation of Inventories
topics.subtopictitle: Normal loss absorbed into cost of good production; abnormal loss valued separately and excluded from inventory
topics.label: AS 2 — Valuation of Inventories (1.9)

examiner_comment.text: A common error here is spreading the entire cost of input over all 4,700 MT of good output without first separating normal loss (absorbed) from abnormal loss (excluded and valued separately), which produces one of the round, mathematically simpler distractor figures instead of the correct per-unit rate.

subject: advanced-accounting
case_facts_html:
RTS Ltd, ("RTS" or the "Company"), is engaged in the business of manufacturing of equipment/components. The Company has a contract with the Indian Railways for a brake component which is structured such that:

  • The Company's obligation is to deliver the component to the Railways' stockyard, while the delivery terms are ex-works, the Company is responsible for engaging a transporter for delivery.
  • Railways sends an order for a defined quantity.
  • The Company manufactures the required quantity and informs Railways for carrying out the inspection.
  • Railways representatives visit the Company's factory and inspect the components and mark each component with a quality check sticker.
  • Goods once inspected by Railways are marked with a hologram sticker to earmark for delivery identification by the customer when they are delivered to the customer's location.
  • The Company raises an invoice once it dispatches the goods.

The management of RTS is under discussion with the auditors of the Company in respect of accounting of a critical matter as regards its accounting with respect subsequent events i.e. events after the reporting period. They have been checking as to which one of the following events after the reporting period provides evidence of conditions that existed at the end of the reporting period?

  1. Nationalisation or privatization by government
  2. Out of court settlement of a legal claim
  3. Rights issue of equity shares
  4. Strike by workforce
  5. Announcing a plan to discontinue an operation

The Company has received a grant of ₹8 crores from the Government for setting up a factory in a backward area. Out of this grant, the Company distributed ₹2 crores as dividend. The Company also received land, free of cost, from the State Government but it has not recorded this at all in the books as no money has been spent.

RTS has a subsidiary, A Ltd, which is evaluating its production process wherein normal waste is 5% of input. 5,000 MT of input were put in process resulting in wastage of 300 MT. Cost per MT of input was ₹1,000. The entire quantity of waste was on stock at the end of the financial year.
question_html:
Please guide regarding the accounting treatment of both the grants mentioned above in line with the requirements of Accounting Standard 12.

  1. Distribution of dividend out of grant is correct. In the second case also not recording land in the books of accounts is correct.
  2. Distribution of dividend out of grant is incorrect. In the second case, not recording land in the books of accounts is correct.
  3. Distribution of dividend out of grant is correct. In the second case, land should be recorded in the books of accounts at a nominal value.
  4. Distribution of dividend out of grant is incorrect. In the second case, land should be recorded in the books of accounts at a nominal value.
answer_html: Answer: (D). The ₹8 crore grant for setting up a factory in a backward area is a grant in the nature of promoters' contribution — per AS 12 it must be credited directly to Capital Reserve and is neither available for distribution as dividend nor treated as deferred income; distributing ₹2 crore of it as dividend is therefore incorrect. Separately, land received free of cost from the State Government is a non-monetary government grant; AS 12 requires such assets to be recorded at their acquisition cost, or at a nominal value if received free of cost — it cannot simply be left off the books because no money was spent.

topics.title: Accounting for Government Grants
topics.subtopictitle: Grants of the nature of promoters' contribution go to Capital Reserve, not dividend; non-monetary grants received free are recorded at nominal value, not left unrecorded
topics.label: AS 12 — Accounting for Government Grants (1.5/1.8)

examiner_comment.text: A common error here is treating a capital-nature backward-area grant as ordinary distributable income once received in cash, and separately assuming a free non-monetary grant needs no accounting entry at all simply because no consideration was paid for it.

The explanation above is independently derived from AS 12's promoters'-contribution and non-monetary-grant rules and confirmed to land on option (D).

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html:
Gyan Ltd. borrowed ₹10 crore for construction of a plant at the rate of 10% per annum (interest paid annually ₹1 crore). The construction was being carried on and out of the borrowings, ₹4 crore was temporarily placed in a fixed deposit at the rate of 6% per annum (interest earned ₹24 lakh). At the year end, how much cost of borrowing Gyan Limited will capitalise?

  1. Interest paid on ₹10 crore i.e. ₹1 crore
  2. Interest paid on ₹6 crore as only this amount was utilized i.e. ₹60 Lakh.
  3. Interest paid less income on temporary investment i.e. ₹76 lakh
  4. Nothing will be capitalized
answer_html: Answer: (C) ₹76 lakh. Per AS 16, where funds are borrowed specifically for a qualifying asset, any income earned on temporary investment of those borrowed funds pending their use is deducted from the borrowing cost otherwise eligible for capitalisation. Interest paid = ₹1 crore (₹100 lakh); less income on the temporary investment of the unused ₹4 crore = ₹24 lakh; net eligible borrowing cost = ₹100 lakh − ₹24 lakh = ₹76 lakh.

topics.title: Borrowing Costs
topics.subtopictitle: Income on temporary investment of surplus borrowed funds is netted against interest paid to arrive at capitalisable borrowing cost
topics.label: AS 16 — Borrowing Costs (4.4)

examiner_comment.text: A common error here is capitalising the full interest paid on the entire borrowing without netting off the income earned on the temporarily-parked surplus funds, or alternatively capitalising interest only on the portion actually deployed in construction rather than on the full borrowing net of temporary-investment income.

extraction_note: Question and options verbatim from CAInter-AdvAcc-RTP-May2024-Q.pdf; source's suggested-answer hints table gives only "2. (c)" with no working shown. The explanation above is independently derived and confirmed: ₹100 lakh − ₹24 lakh = ₹76 lakh, matching option (C).

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html: What do you mean by Carve outs/ins in Ind AS? Explain.
answer_html: Certain changes have been made in Ind AS considering the economic environment of the country, which is different as compared to the economic environment presumed to be in existence by IFRS. These differences are due to differences in economic conditions prevailing in India. These differences which are in deviation to the accounting principles and practices stated in IFRS, are commonly known as 'Carve-outs'. Additional guidance given in Ind AS over and above what is given in IFRS, is termed as 'Carve in'.

topics.title: Introduction to Accounting Standards
topics.subtopictitle: Carve-outs (deviations from IFRS reflecting India's economic environment) vs Carve-ins (additional Ind AS guidance beyond IFRS)
topics.label: Introduction to Accounting Standards (9)

examiner_comment.text: A common error here is confusing a carve-out with the mere removal of an option available under IFRS, or omitting the distinction between a carve-out (a genuine deviation) and a carve-in (additional guidance beyond IFRS).

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html:
Based upon criteria for rating of non-corporate entity, categorize the following as Level I, Level II, Level III and Level IV entities for the purpose of compliance of Accounting Standards in India.

  1. Rama Textiles whose turnover (excluding other income) exceeds ten crore but does not exceed rupees fifty crore in the immediately preceding accounting year.
  2. Star Industries is having borrowings (including public deposits) in excess of rupees two crore but not in excess of rupees ten crore at any time during the immediately preceding accounting year.
  3. Newman Industries is having borrowings (including public deposits) less than rupees fifty lakh at any time during the immediately preceding accounting year.
  4. SS Finance is a financial institution carrying its business in India since last 10 years.
  5. DD Finance, holding company of SS Finance. (Entity mentioned at Point (v) above)
  6. Reliable Co-op Bank, a co-operative bank, carrying banking operations since last 15 years.
answer_html:
1. Level III Entity – Rama textiles, whose turnover (excluding other income) exceeds rupees ten crore but does not exceed rupees fifty crore in the immediately preceding accounting year.
  2. Level III Entity – Star industries is having borrowings (including public deposits) in excess of rupees two crore but not in excess of rupees ten crore at any time during the immediately preceding accounting year.
  3. Level IV Entity – Newman Industries is having borrowings (including public deposits) of less than rupees fifty lakhs at any time during the immediately preceding accounting year.
  4. Level I Entity – SS is a financial institution carrying its business in India since last 10 years.
  5. Level I Entity – DD finance, holding company of SS finance (Entity mentioned in point (d) above).
  6. Level I Entity – Reliable co-operative banks carrying on banking business for the last 15 years.

topics.title: Applicability of Accounting Standards

examiner_comment.text: A common error here is missing that a holding company of a Level I entity is itself automatically Level I regardless of its own size, and that banks/financial institutions/co-operative banks are Level I entities by their nature, not by a turnover or borrowings threshold.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html: A Ltd. enters into an agreement with Mr. Bhola for running a business for a fixed amount payable to the later every year. The contract states that the day-to-day management of the business will be handled by Mr. Bhola, while all financial and operating policy decisions are taken by the Board of Directors of the Company. Mr. Bhola does not have any voting power in A Limited. You are required to suggest how this transaction will be treated as at the closing date i.e. on 31st March, 2023 for the purposes of AS 18 'Related Party Disclosures'.
answer_html: Mr. Bhola will not be considered as a related party of A Ltd. in view of provisions of AS 18 "Related Party Disclosures" which states, "individuals owning, directly or indirectly, an interest in the voting power of the reporting enterprise that gives them control or significant influence over the enterprise, and relatives of any such individual are related parties". In the given case, in the absence of share ownership, Mr. Bhola would not be considered to exercise significant influence on A Limited, even though there is an agreement giving him the power to manage the company. Further, the fact that Mr Bhola does not have the ability to direct or instruct the board of directors does not qualify him as a key management personnel.

topics.title: Related Party Disclosures
topics.subtopictitle: Related-party status requires either a voting-power interest giving control/significant influence, or the ability to direct/instruct the board (key management personnel) - day-to-day management alone under a fee contract does not qualify
topics.label: AS 18 — Related Party Disclosures (4.3)

examiner_comment.text: A common error here is treating anyone contractually responsible for day-to-day management as automatically a related party, without checking for an actual voting-power interest or the ability to control the board's financial and operating policy decisions.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html: Shri Manoj a relative of key management personnel received remuneration of ₹3,50,000 for his services in the company for the period from 1st April, 2022 to 30th June, 2022. On 1st July, 2022, he left the service. You are required to suggest how this transaction will be treated as at the closing date i.e. on 31st March, 2023 for the purposes of AS 18 'Related Party Disclosures'.
answer_html: According to AS 18 on 'Related Party Disclosures', parties are considered to be related if at any time during the reporting period one party has the ability to control the other party or exercise significant influence over the other party in making financial and/or operating decisions. Hence, Shri Manoj, a relative of key management personnel should be identified as related party for disclosure in the financial statements for the year ended 31.3.2023 as he received remuneration for his services in the company for the period from 1st April, 2022 to 30th June, 2022.

topics.title: Related Party Disclosures
topics.subtopictitle: Related-party disclosure applies if the relationship existed at any time during the reporting period, even if it has since ended before year-end
topics.label: AS 18 — Related Party Disclosures (4.7)

examiner_comment.text: A common error here is excluding the transaction from disclosure on the reasoning that Shri Manoj was no longer employed as at the balance sheet date, missing that AS 18's "at any time during the reporting period" test is satisfied by the relationship having existed for even part of the year.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html: Arzoo Ltd. is in the business of manufacture of passenger cars and commercial vehicles. The company is working on a strategic plan to shift from the passenger car segment to the commercial vehicles segment over the coming 5 years. However, no specific plans have been drawn up for sale of neither the division nor its assets. As part of its plan, it has planned that it will reduce the production of passenger cars by 20% annually. It also plans to commence another new factory for the manufacture of commercial vehicles plus transfer of employees in a phased manner. These plans have not been approved from the Board of Directors and the new factory for manufacture of commercial vehicles has not yet started. You are required to comment if mere gradual phasing out in itself can be considered as a 'Discontinuing Operation' within the meaning of AS 24.
answer_html:
Mere gradual phasing out is not considered as discontinuing operation as defined under AS 24, 'Discontinuing Operations'. Examples of activities that do not necessarily satisfy criterion of the definition, but that might do so in combination with other circumstances, include:

  1. Gradual or evolutionary phasing out of a product line or class of service;
  2. Discontinuing, even if relatively abruptly, several products within an ongoing line of business;
  3. Shifting of some production or marketing activities for a particular line of business from one location to another; and
  4. Closing of a facility to achieve productivity improvements or other cost savings.

In view of the above, mere gradual phasing out in itself cannot be considered as discontinuing operation. The companies' strategic plan also has no final approval from the board through a resolution and there is no specific time bound activities like shifting of assets and employees. Moreover, the new segment, i.e. the commercial vehicle production line in a new factory has not started.

topics.title: Discontinuing Operations
topics.subtopictitle: Gradual/evolutionary phasing out of a product line does not by itself meet the definition of a discontinuing operation; needs a specific plan, board approval, and time-bound implementation
topics.label: AS 24 — Discontinuing Operations (6.2)

examiner_comment.text: A common error here is concluding that any strategic segment shift automatically meets AS 24's discontinuing-operation definition, without checking for a formally approved, specific, time-bound plan for disposal or discontinuance of the operation and its assets.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html: Sooraj Limited wishes to obtain a machine costing ₹30 lakhs by way of lease. The effective life of the machine is 14 years, but the company requires it only for the first 3 years. It enters into an agreement with Star Ltd., for a lease rental for ₹3 lakhs p.a. payable in arrears and the implicit rate of interest is 15%. The chief accountant of Sooraj Limited is not sure about the treatment of these lease rentals and seeks your advice. (Use annuity factor at @ 15% for 3 years as 2.28)
answer_html:
As per AS 19 'leases', a lease will be classified as finance lease if at the inception of the lease, the present value of minimum lease payment amounts to at least substantially all of the fair value of leased asset. In the given case, the implicit rate of interest is given at 15%. The present value of minimum lease payments at 15% using PV-Annuity Factor can be computed as:

Annuity Factor (Year 1 to Year 3)2.28
Present Value of minimum lease payments (₹3 lakhs each year)₹6.84 lakhs

Thus, the present value of minimum lease payments is ₹6.84 lakhs and the fair value of the machine is ₹30 lakhs. In a finance lease, the lease term should be for a major part of the economic life of the asset even if title is not transferred. However, in the given case, the effective useful life of the machine is 14 years while the lease is only for three years. Therefore, a lease agreement is an operating lease. Lease payments under an operating lease should be recognized as an expense in the statement of profit and loss on a straight-line basis over the lease term unless another systematic basis is more representative of the time pattern of the user's benefit.

examiner_comment.text: A common error here is classifying the lease as a finance lease purely because the present value of minimum lease payments is a large absolute number, without comparing it against the machine's fair value and separately checking whether the lease term covers a major part of the asset's economic life.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html: Hello Limited belongs to the manufacturing industry. The company received an actuarial valuation for the first time for its pension scheme which revealed a surplus of ₹12 lakhs. It wants to spread the same over the next 2 years by reducing the annual contribution to ₹4 lakhs instead of ₹10 lakhs. The average remaining life of the employees is estimated to be 6 years. You are required to advise the company on the following items from the viewpoint of finalization of accounts, taking note of the mandatory accounting standards.
answer_html: According to AS 15 (Revised 2005) 'Employee Benefits', actuarial gains and losses should be recognized immediately in the statement of profit and loss as income or expense. Therefore, a surplus amount of ₹12 lakhs is required to be credited to the profit and loss statement of the current year.

topics.title: Employee Benefits
topics.subtopictitle: Actuarial gains and losses are recognised immediately in the statement of profit and loss, not spread/deferred over future periods
topics.label: AS 15 — Employee Benefits (1.10)

examiner_comment.text: A common error here is accepting the company's proposal to spread the actuarial surplus over future years by reducing annual contributions, rather than recognising the full surplus immediately in the current year's profit and loss as AS 15 requires.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html: Surya Limited follows the financial year from April to March. A suit against the Company's Advertisement was filed by a party on 5th April, 2023, claiming damages of ₹5 lakhs. Keeping in view the provisions of AS-4, you are required to state with reasons whether the above event is to be treated as a Contingency, an Adjusting Event or a Non-Adjusting Event occurring after the Balance Sheet date.
answer_html: Suit filed against the company is a contingent liability, but it was not existing as on date of balance sheet date as the suit was filed on 5th April after the balance sheet date. As per AS 4, 'Contingencies' is restricted to conditions or situations at the balance sheet date, the financial effect of which is to be determined by future events which may or may not occur. However, it may be disclosed with the nature of contingency, being a contingent liability. This event does not pertain to conditions on the balance sheet date. Hence, it will have no effect on the financial statement and will be a non-adjusting event.

topics.title: Contingencies and Events Occurring After the Balance Sheet Date
topics.subtopictitle: A suit filed after the balance sheet date does not relate to a condition existing at that date - non-adjusting event, disclosable as a contingent liability
topics.label: AS 4 (1.2)

examiner_comment.text: A common error here is treating a suit filed after the balance sheet date as an adjusting event or an outright provision, rather than recognising it as a non-adjusting contingency arising from a post-year-end condition.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html: Surya Limited follows the financial year from April to March. Company sends a proposal to sell an immovable property for ₹45 lakhs in March 2023. The book value of the property is ₹30 lakhs as on year end date. However, the Deed was registered on 15th April, 2023. Keeping in view the provisions of AS-4, you are required to state with reasons whether the above event is to be treated as a Contingency, an Adjusting Event or a Non-Adjusting Event occurring after the Balance Sheet date.
answer_html: In this case, no adjustment to assets and liabilities is required as the event does not affect the determination and the condition of the amounts stated in the financial statements for the year ended 31st March, 2023. There was just a proposal before 31st March, 2023 and hence sale cannot be shown in the financial statements for the year ended 31st March, 2023. Sale of immovable property is an event occurring after the balance sheet date is a non-adjusting event.

topics.title: Contingencies and Events Occurring After the Balance Sheet Date
topics.subtopictitle: A mere sale proposal at year end, with the deed registered only after the balance sheet date, is a non-adjusting event - no adjustment to the financial statements
topics.label: AS 4 (1.5)

examiner_comment.text: A common error here is recognising the sale in the financial statements for the year ended 31st March on the basis that a proposal existed by that date, without checking whether the sale was actually completed (deed registered) before or after the balance sheet date.

question_html: On 15-01-2023 goods of ₹3,00,000 were sent on consignment basis, of which 20% of the goods unsold are lying with the consignee as on 31-03-2023. You are required to advise the accountant of BS Products Ltd., with valid reasons, the amount to be recognized as revenue in this case in the context of AS 9.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html: ₹4,00,000 worth of goods were sold on approval basis on 01-12-2022. The period of approval was 3 months after which they were considered as sold. Buyer sent approval for 75% goods upto 31-01-2023 and no approval or disapproval received for the remaining goods till 31-03-2023. You are required to advise the accountant of BS Products Ltd., with valid reasons, the amount to be recognized as revenue in this case in the context of AS 9.
answer_html: In case of goods sold on approval basis, revenue should not be recognized until the goods have been formally accepted by the buyer or the buyer has done an act adopting the transaction or the time period for rejection has elapsed or where no time has been fixed, a reasonable time has elapsed. Therefore, revenue should be recognized for the total sales amounting to ₹4,00,000 as the time period for rejecting the goods had expired.

topics.title: Revenue Recognition
topics.subtopictitle: Sale on approval basis - revenue recognised once formally accepted, an adopting act occurs, or the approval/rejection period has elapsed, whichever governs
topics.label: AS 9 (2.8)

examiner_comment.text: A common error here is recognising revenue only for the 75% expressly approved by the buyer and continuing to treat the remaining 25% as unsold, missing that the stated 3-month approval period had already lapsed for that portion by the year end, which itself triggers recognition.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html: Apart from the above, BS Products Ltd. sells goods to dealers also. One of the conditions of sale is that interest is payable @ 2% p.m. for delayed payments by dealers. The percentage of interest recovery is only 10% i.e. ₹50,000 on such overdue outstanding due to various reasons. During the year 2022-23, the company wants to recognize the entire interest receivable of ₹60,000. You are required to advise the accountant of BS Products Ltd., with valid reasons, the amount to be recognized as revenue in this case in the context of AS 9, and also determine the total revenue to be recognized for the year ending 31-03-2023.
answer_html:
As per the standard, "where the ability to assess the ultimate collection with reasonable certainty is lacking at the time of raising any claim, the revenue recognition is postponed to the extent of uncertainty involved. In such cases, the revenue is recognized only when it is reasonably certain that the ultimate collection will be made". In this case, interest should be recognized only if the ultimate collection is certain and the company expects to realize interest for the delayed payments for ₹50,000 only. Hence, based on the past experience, the realization of interest for the delayed payments by the agent is certain only to the extent of this amount and not ₹60,000. Therefore, the interest income of ₹50,000 should be recognized in the books for the year ended 31st March, 2023.

Thus, total revenue amounting ₹8,90,000 (2,00,000 + 2,40,000 + 4,00,000 + 50,000) will be recognized for the year ended 31st March, 2023 in the books of BS Products Ltd.

topics.title: Revenue Recognition
topics.subtopictitle: Effect of collection uncertainty on revenue recognition - recognised only to the extent collection is reasonably certain, based on past collection experience
topics.label: AS 9 (2.9)

examiner_comment.text: A common error here is recognising the full contractually-computed interest of ₹60,000 rather than limiting recognition to the ₹50,000 actually supported by past collection experience, and separately failing to aggregate all four cases into the single total revenue figure the question asks for.

As per para 13 of AS 21 any excess of the cost to the parent of its investment in a subsidiary over the parent's portion of equity of the subsidiary, at the date on which investment in the subsidiary is made, should be described as goodwill to be recognised as an asset in the consolidated financial statements. When the cost to the parent of its investment in a subsidiary is less than the parent's portion of equity of the subsidiary, at the date on which investment in the subsidiary is made, the difference should be treated as a capital reserve in the consolidated financial statements.

Since dividend is declared by Star Ltd. on the date of acquisition itself, it would be out of the divisible profits of Star Ltd. existing on the date of acquisition i.e., pre-acquisition profits from the perspective of Zoom Ltd. subject: advanced-accounting
question_html:
In the books of G Ltd., closing inventory as at 31.03.2024 amounts to ₹10,40,000 (on the basis of FIFO method). The company decides to change from FIFO method to weighted average method for ascertaining the cost of inventory for 31.3.2024. On the basis of weighted average method, closing inventory as on 31.03.2024 amounts to ₹8,80,000. Realisable value of the inventory as on 31.03.2024 amounts to ₹12,00,000. What will be the value of inventory in the books and what disclosure should be given in the financial statement on 31.3.2024?

  1. The value of inventory will be ₹8,80,000 and the fact that the valuation method has changed to be disclosed in the financial statement.
  2. The value of inventory will be ₹12,00,000, and full disclosure with the amount the valuation method has changed to be disclosed in the financial statement.
  3. The value of inventory will be ₹12,00,000, and the fact that valuation method has changed to be disclosed in the financial statement.
  4. The value of inventory will be ₹8,80,000, and full disclosure with the amount the valuation method has changed to be disclosed in the financial statement.
answer_html: Answer: (d) The value of inventory will be ₹8,80,000, and full disclosure with the amount the valuation method has changed to be disclosed in the financial statement. Per AS 2, inventory is valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value; once the company changes its costing method to weighted average, the "cost" figure to compare against NRV is the new weighted-average cost of ₹8,80,000, which is lower than the ₹12,00,000 NRV – so ₹8,80,000 is the value in the books. Separately, per AS 5, a change in the cost formula used for inventories is a change in accounting policy, which requires disclosure of both the fact of the change and, where the effect is material, the amount by which the change affects the financial statements.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html:
A Ltd. has a balance of ₹17,15,000 in the loan account with State Finance Corporation which is inclusive of ₹1,15,000 for interest accrued but not due. The loan is secured by hypothecation of the Plant and Machinery. As per Schedule III to the Companies Act, 2013 loan is to be disclosed in the balance sheet as follows:

  1. Disclosed ₹16,00,000 as a secured loan under long-term borrowings.
  2. Disclosed ₹16,00,000 as a secured loan under long-term borrowings and ₹1,15,000 under short-term borrowings.
  3. Disclosed ₹16,00,000 as a secured loan under long-term borrowings and ₹1,15,000 under other current liabilities.
  4. Disclosed ₹16,00,000 as a secured loan under long-term borrowings and no disclosure for ₹1,15,000.
answer_html: Answer: (c) Disclosed ₹16,00,000 as a secured loan under long-term borrowings and ₹1,15,000 under other current liabilities. The principal loan balance (₹17,15,000 − ₹1,15,000 interest accrued but not due = ₹16,00,000) is a long-term secured borrowing. Per Schedule III's format, "interest accrued but not due on borrowings" is not itself a borrowing (long-term or short-term) – it is separately classified under "Other current liabilities."

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html:
Most by-products as well as scrap or waste materials, by their nature, are immaterial. Thus, these are measured at:

  1. Cost
  2. Cost or Net Realisable Value whichever is lower
  3. Nil
  4. Net realisable value
answer_html: Answer: (d) Net realisable value. Per AS 2, because by-products, scrap and waste are immaterial by nature, they are measured at net realisable value, and this NRV is deducted from the cost of the main product(s) rather than being separately costed.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html: What do you mean by 'Accrual' in reference to AS-1? Also, specify any three reasons for 'Accrual Basis of Accounting'.
answer_html:
The term "Accrual" has been explained in AS 1 on Disclosure of Accounting Policies, as "Revenues and costs are accrued, that is, recognised as they are earned or incurred (and not as money is received or paid) and recorded in the financial statements of the periods to which they relate."

Reasons for Accrual Basis of Accounting (any three):

  1. Accrual basis of accounting attempts to record the financial effects of the transactions, events, and circumstances of an enterprise in the period in which they occur, rather than recording them in the period(s) in which cash is received or paid by the enterprise.
  2. Receipts and payments of the period will not coincide with the buying, producing or selling events and other economic events that affect entity performance.
  3. The goal of accrual basis of accounting is to follow the matching concept of income and expenditure so that reported net income measures an enterprise's performance during a period instead of merely listing its cash receipts and payments.
  4. Accrual basis of accounting recognizes assets, liabilities or components of revenues and expenses for amounts received or paid in cash in the past, and amounts expected to be received or paid in cash in the future.
  5. An important point of difference between accrual accounting and accounting based on cash receipts and outlay is the timing of recognition of revenues, expenses, gains and losses.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html:
Smart Ltd. closes its books of accounts every year on 31st March. The financial statements for the year ended 31st March, 2024 are to be approved by the approving authority on 30th June 2024. During the first quarter of 2024-2025, the following events/transactions have taken place. The accountant of the company seeks your guidance for the following:

  1. Smart Ltd. has an inventory of 50 stitching machines costing at ₹5,500 per machine as on 31st March, 2024. The company is expecting a heavy decline in the demand in next year. The inventories are valued at cost or net realisable value, whichever is lower. During the month of April 2024, due to fall in demand, the prices have gone down drastically. The company has sold 5 machines during this month at a price of ₹4,000 per machine.
  2. A fire has broken out in the company's godown on 15th April, 2024. The company has estimated a loss of ₹25 lakhs of which 75% is recoverable from the Insurance company.
  3. The company has entered into a sale agreement on 30th March, 2024 to sell a property for a consideration of ₹7,50,000 which is being carried in the books at ₹5,50,000 at the year end. The transfer of risk and reward and sale is complete in the month of May 2024 when conveyance and possession get completed.
  4. The company has received, during the year 2022-2023, a government grant of ₹15 lakhs for purchase of a machine. The company has received a notice for refund of the said grant on 15th June, 2024 due to violation of some of the conditions of grant during the year 2023-2024.

You are required to state with reasons, how the above transactions will be dealt with in the financial statement for the year ended 31st March 2024.
answer_html:
Events occurring after the balance sheet date are significant events, favourable or unfavourable, occurring between the balance sheet date and the date on which the financial statements are approved. Assets and liabilities should be adjusted for such events only if they provide additional evidence of conditions existing at the balance sheet date, or indicate the going-concern assumption is no longer appropriate. Here, the financial statements are approved on 30th June 2024.

  1. Since on 31st March 2024 Smart Ltd. was already expecting a heavy decline in demand, the price fall during April 2024 is considered an adjusting event, providing further evidence of the condition (declining net realisable value) existing at the balance sheet date. Inventory should be written down to ₹4,000 per machine: 50 machines × ₹4,000 = ₹2,00,000.
  2. The fire took place after the balance sheet date (during FY 2024-25), so the financials for FY 2023-24 are not adjusted for the fire loss. However, the going-concern assumption should be evaluated in light of the fire; if it remains appropriate, no disclosure is required in the financial statements.
  3. Since the transfer of risk and reward and completion of sale occurred only in May 2024 (conveyance and possession), no revenue should be recognised for this in the FY 2023-24 financial statements – this is a non-adjusting event, though disclosure of the agreement should be given.
  4. Since the refund notice was received after 31st March but before the 30th June 2024 approval date, and the violation of grant conditions took place during FY 2023-24 (a condition the company must have been aware of), the grant refund is an adjusting event and shall be adjusted in the FY 2023-24 financial statements.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html:
The Accountant of Heera Ltd. has sought your opinion with relevant reasons, whether the following transactions will be treated as change in Accounting Policy or not for the year ended 31st March, 2024. Please advise him in the following situations in accordance with the provisions of relevant Accounting Standard:

  1. Till the previous year the furniture was depreciated on straight line basis over a period of 5 years. From current year, the useful life of furniture has been changed to 3 years.
  2. Management decided to pay pension to those employees who have retired after completing 5 years of service in the organization. Such employees will get pension of ₹20,000 per month. Earlier there was no such scheme of pension in the organization.
  3. During the year ended 31st March, 2024, there was change in cost formula in measuring the cost of inventories.
answer_html:
1. Change in useful life of furniture from 5 years to 3 years is a change in accounting estimate, not a change in accounting policy.
  2. Adoption of a new accounting policy for events or transactions which did not occur previously (there was no pension scheme before) should not be treated as a change in an accounting policy. The introduction of the new pension scheme is therefore not a change in accounting policy.
  3. Change in the cost formula used in measuring the cost of inventories is a change in accounting policy.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html: AP Ltd., a construction contractor, undertakes the construction of a commercial complex for Kay Ltd. AP Ltd. submitted separate proposals for each of 3 units of the commercial complex. A single agreement is entered into between the two parties. The agreement lays down the value of each of the 3 units, i.e. ₹50 Lakh, ₹60 Lakh and ₹75 Lakh respectively. The agreement also lays down the completion time for each unit. Comment, with reference to AS-7, whether AP Ltd. should treat it as a single contract or three separate contracts.
answer_html:
As per AS 7 'Construction Contracts', when a contract covers a number of assets, the construction of each asset should be treated as a separate construction contract when: (a) separate proposals have been submitted for each asset; (b) each asset has been subject to separate negotiation and the contractor and customer have been able to accept or reject that part of the contract relating to each asset; and (c) the costs and revenues of each asset can be identified.

In the given case, AP Ltd. submitted separate proposals for each of the 3 units, the agreement lays down a separate value and separate completion time for each unit, and the costs/revenues of each unit are identifiable. Therefore, AP Ltd. is required to treat the construction of each unit as a separate construction contract, as the above-mentioned conditions of AS 7 are fulfilled in the given case – notwithstanding that a single agreement document was used.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html: On 1st December, 2023, GR Construction Co. Ltd. undertook a contract to construct a building for ₹45 lakhs. On 31st March, 2024, the company found that it had already spent ₹32.50 lakhs on the construction. Additional cost of completion is estimated at ₹15.10 lakhs. What amount should be charged to revenue in the final accounts for the year ended 31st March, 2024 as per provisions of AS-7?
answer_html:
₹ in lakhs
Cost of construction incurred till date32.50
Add: Estimated future cost15.10
Total estimated cost of construction47.60

Percentage of completion till date to total estimated cost of construction = (32.50/47.60) × 100 = 68.28%.

Proportion of total contract value recognised as revenue for the year ended 31st March, 2024 per AS 7 (Revised) = Contract price × percentage of completion = ₹45 lakh × 68.28% = ₹30.73 lakhs.

₹ in lakhs
Total cost of construction47.60
Less: Total contract price(45.00)
Total foreseeable loss to be recognized as expense2.60

According to AS 7, when it is probable that total contract costs will exceed total contract revenue, the expected loss should be recognized as an expense immediately (in full, not spread by percentage of completion).

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html:
Given below are the following information of B.S. Ltd.:

  1. Goods of ₹50,000 were sold on 18-03-2024 but at the request of the buyer these were delivered on 15-04-2024.
  2. On 13-01-2024 goods of ₹1,25,000 are sent on consignment basis, of which 20% of the goods unsold are lying with the consignee as on 31-03-2024.
  3. ₹1,00,000 worth of goods were sold on approval basis on 01-12-2023. The period of approval was 3 months after which they were considered sold. Buyer sent approval for 75% goods up to 31-01-2024 and no approval or disapproval received for the remaining goods till 31-03-2024.

You are required to advise the accountant of B.S. Ltd., with valid reasons, the amount to be recognized as revenue for the year ended 31st March, 2024 in the above cases in the context of AS-9.
answer_html:
As per AS 9 'Revenue Recognition', in a transaction involving the sale of goods, performance should be regarded as being achieved when: (a) the seller has transferred to the buyer the property in the goods for a price, or all significant risks and rewards of ownership have been transferred and the seller retains no effective control of the goods to a degree usually associated with ownership; and (b) no significant uncertainty exists regarding the amount of consideration to be derived from the sale.

Case (i): The sale is complete but delivery has been postponed at the buyer's request. B.S. Ltd. should recognize the entire sale of ₹50,000 for the year ended 31st March, 2024.

Case (ii): In case of a consignment sale, revenue should not be recognized until the goods are sold by the consignee to a third party. The 20% of goods lying unsold with the consignee should be treated as closing inventory, and sales should be recognized for ₹1,00,000 (80% of ₹1,25,000).

Case (iii): In case of goods sold on approval basis, revenue should not be recognized until the goods have been formally accepted by the buyer, or the buyer has done an act adopting the transaction, or the time period for rejection has elapsed (or, where no time has been fixed, a reasonable time has elapsed). Since the 3-month approval period had already expired by 31st March, 2024, revenue should be recognized for the full ₹1,00,000 (including the portion neither approved nor disapproved, since the approval window itself had lapsed).

Thus, total revenue amounting to ₹2,50,000 (50,000 + 1,00,000 + 1,00,000) will be recognized for the year ended 31st March, 2024 in the books of B.S. Ltd.

topics.title: Revenue Recognition
topics.subtopictitle: Revenue-recognition timing across delayed delivery, consignment sale, and sale-on-approval scenarios
topics.label: AS 9 — Revenue Recognition (2.8)

examiner_comment.text: A common error in case (iii) is withholding revenue recognition on the un-responded-to 25% of goods on the reasoning that no explicit acceptance was received, missing that AS 9 treats the mere expiry of the stated rejection period as itself sufficient for revenue recognition, with no separate acceptance needed.

Shrishti Ltd. contracted with a supplier to purchase machinery which is to be installed in its Department A in three months' time. The machine was purchased at ₹1,58,34,000 inclusive of IGST @ 12% for which input credit is available to Shrishti Ltd. ₹55,770 transportation charges were incurred to bring the machine to the factory site. An Architect was appointed at a fee of ₹30,000 to supervise machinery installation at the factory site.

Ascertain the amount at which the Machinery should be capitalized under AS 10, considering that IGST credit is availed by Shrishti Limited. Internally booked profits should be eliminated in arriving at the cost of machine.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html:
Legal Ltd. is engaged in the manufacturing of rubber. For its plant, it required machineries of latest technology. It usually resorts to Long Term Foreign Currency Borrowings for its fund requirements. On 1st April, 2023, it borrowed US $1 million from International Funding Agency, USA when the exchange rate was 1$ = ₹63. The funds were used for acquiring machineries, on the same date, to be used in three different plants. The useful life of the machineries is 10 years and their residual value is ₹30,00,000.

Earlier also the company used to purchase machineries out of foreign borrowings. The exchange differences arising on such borrowings were charged to profit and loss account and were not capitalized, even though the company had an option to capitalize it as per notified AS 11.

Now for this new purchase of machinery, Legal Ltd. is interested to avail the option of capitalizing the same to the cost of asset. Exchange rate on 31st March, 2024 is 1 US$ = ₹62. Assume that on 31st March, 2024, Legal Ltd. is not having any old long term foreign currency borrowings except for the amount borrowed for machinery purchased on 1st April, 2023.

Comment whether Legal Ltd. can capitalize the exchange difference to the cost of asset on 31st March, 2024. If yes, then calculate the depreciation amount on machineries as on 31st March, 2024.
answer_html:
As per paragraph 46A of AS 11, in respect of accounting periods commencing on or after 1st April, 2011, an enterprise (whether or not it had earlier exercised the option under paragraph 46, the option being irrevocable and applied to all such foreign currency monetary items) may add to or deduct from the cost of a depreciable capital asset the exchange differences arising on reporting long-term foreign currency monetary items relating to its acquisition, and depreciate this over the balance life of the asset.

Accordingly, though Legal Ltd. had not earlier exercised the option, it can still avail the option to capitalize the exchange difference to the cost of machinery by virtue of para 46A of AS 11. Further, since Legal Ltd. has no other long term foreign currency borrowings, it is not required to apply the capitalization option to any earlier borrowing.

Exchange difference to be capitalized and depreciation amount₹
Cost of the asset in $ (1 million); Exchange rate on 1st April, 2023 (₹63 = $1)—
Cost of the asset in ₹ (1 million × ₹63)63 million
Less: Exchange difference as on 31st March, 2024 – (63−62) × $1 million (Gain)(1 million)
Revised cost of asset62 million
Less: Depreciation for 2023-2024 – (62 million − 3 million) / 10 years(5.90 million)
Carrying amount as on 31st March, 202456.10 million

topics.title: The Effects of Changes in Foreign Exchange Rates
topics.subtopictitle: Para 46A option to capitalise exchange differences on long-term foreign-currency monetary items into a depreciable asset's cost
topics.label: AS 11 (3.5)

examiner_comment.text: A common error is assuming the para 46A option is unavailable to Legal Ltd. because it never exercised it in earlier years, missing that the option is available for this new borrowing on its own facts, since Legal Ltd. has no other long-term foreign-currency borrowings that would otherwise force the irrevocable-election issue.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html: XYZ Limited has set-up its business in a designated backward area which entitles the company to receive from the Government of India a subsidy of 20% of the cost of investment. Having fulfilled all the conditions under the scheme, the company on its investment of ₹75 crore received ₹15 crore as subsidy from the Government in January 2024. The company wants to treat this receipt as an item of revenue and thereby reduce the losses for the year ended on 31st March, 2024. Keeping in view the relevant Accounting Standard, examine whether this action is justified or not.
answer_html:
As per para 10 of AS 12 'Accounting for Government Grants', where government grants are in the nature of promoters' contribution – i.e. they are given with reference to the total investment in an undertaking, or by way of contribution towards its total capital outlay, and no repayment is ordinarily expected in respect thereof – the grants are treated as Capital Reserve, which can be neither distributed as dividend nor considered as deferred income.

In the given case, the subsidy received (20% of the cost of investment) is neither in relation to a specific fixed asset nor in relation to revenue – it is linked to the total investment made in the backward-area undertaking. It is therefore inappropriate to recognise this government grant in the profit and loss statement, since it is not earned but represents an incentive provided by the government without related costs.

The correct treatment is to credit the ₹15 crore subsidy to Capital Reserve. Therefore, the accounting treatment (treating it as revenue to reduce the reported loss) followed by the company is not proper.

topics.title: Accounting for Government Grants
topics.subtopictitle: Grants in the nature of promoters' contribution credited to Capital Reserve, never treated as revenue/deferred income
topics.label: AS 12 — Accounting for Government Grants (1.8)

examiner_comment.text: A common error is treating any cash subsidy received as revenue income by default, without first testing whether it meets AS 12's specific "promoters' contribution" characterisation (tied to total investment, not a specific asset or specific revenue item), which mandates Capital Reserve treatment instead.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html:
U Limited has obtained a term loan of ₹620 lacs for a complete renovation and modernisation of its Factory on 1st April, 2023. Plant and Machinery was acquired under the modernisation scheme and installation was completed on 30th April, 2024. An expenditure of ₹510 lacs was incurred on installation of Plant and Machinery, ₹54 lacs has been advanced to suppliers for additional assets which were also received and installed before 30th April, 2024 (additional asset has taken substantial period of time in its installation), and the balance loan of ₹56 lacs has been used for working capital purposes.

The company has paid total interest of ₹68.20 lacs during financial year 2023-2024 on the above loan. The accountant seeks your advice how to account for the interest paid in the books of accounts.
answer_html:
As per AS 16 'Borrowing Costs', borrowing costs directly attributable to the acquisition, construction or production of a qualifying asset should be capitalized as part of the cost of that asset; other borrowing costs should be recognized as an expense in the period in which they are incurred.

Qualifying Asset: an asset that necessarily takes a substantial period of time (ordinarily 12 months, unless a shorter or longer period is justified by the facts) to get ready for its intended use or sale.

Since construction of the asset completed only on 30th April, 2024 (after the year end), the treatment for the total borrowing cost of ₹68.20 lacs is:

PurposeNatureInterest to be capitalised (₹ lacs)Interest to be charged to P&L (₹ lacs)
Modernisation and renovation of plant and machineryQualifying asset68.20 × (510/620) = 56.10—
Advance to suppliers for additional assetsAssumed as qualifying asset (took substantial time to install)68.20 × (54/620) = 5.94—
Working CapitalNot a qualifying asset—68.20 × (56/620) = 6.16
Total62.046.16

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html: SP Hotels Limited enters into an agreement with Mr. A for running its hotel for a fixed return payable to the latter every year. The contract involves the day-to-day management of the hotel, while all financial and operating policy decisions are taken by the Board of Directors of the company. Mr. A does not own any voting power in SP Hotels Limited. Would he be considered as a related party of SP Hotels Limited?
answer_html: Mr. A will not be considered as a related party of SP Hotels Limited, in view of paragraph 3(c) of AS 18, which states: "individuals owning, directly or indirectly, an interest in the voting power of the reporting enterprise that gives them control or significant influence over the enterprise, and relatives of any such individual." In the given case, in the absence of share ownership, Mr. A would not be considered to exercise significant influence over SP Hotels Limited, even though there is an agreement giving him the power to manage the day-to-day operations of the company. Further, the fact that Mr. A does not have the ability to direct or instruct the Board of Directors (which retains all financial and operating policy decisions) means he does not qualify as a key management personnel either.
