subject: advanced-accounting
question_html: Sun Limited wishes to obtain a machine costing ₹30 lakhs by way of lease. The effective life of the machine is 14 years, but the company requires it only for the first 3 years. It enters into an agreement with Star Ltd. for a lease rental of ₹3 lakhs p.a. payable in arrears, and the implicit rate of interest is 15%. The chief accountant of Sun Limited is not sure about the treatment of these lease rentals and seeks your advice. (Use annuity factor at 15% for 3 years as 3.36.)
answer_html:
As per AS 19 'Leases', a lease will be classified as a finance lease if, at the inception of the lease, the present value of minimum lease payments amounts to at least substantially all of the fair value of the leased asset (discounted at the interest rate implicit in the lease).

Amount
Annuity Factor (Year 1 to Year 3) @ 15%3.36
Present Value of minimum lease payments (₹3 lakhs each year)₹10.08 lakhs (approx.)

The present value of minimum lease payments (₹10.08 lakhs) is far below the fair value of the machine (₹30 lakhs). Additionally, in a finance lease the lease term should cover the major part of the economic life of the asset even where title does not transfer – here the effective useful life of the machine is 14 years while the lease is only for 3 years. Both indicators point away from a finance lease.

The lease agreement is therefore an operating lease. Lease payments under an operating lease should be recognized as an expense in the statement of profit and loss on a straight line basis over the lease term, unless another systematic basis is more representative of the time pattern of the user's benefit – i.e. Sun Limited should expense ₹3 lakhs each year for the 3-year lease term.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html:
The following information relates to XYZ Limited for the year ended 31st March, 2024: Net Profit for the year after tax: ₹37,50,000. Number of Equity Shares of ₹10 each outstanding: 5,00,000. Convertible Debentures issued by the Company (at the beginning of the year):

ParticularsNos.
8% Convertible Debentures of ₹100 each50,000
Equity Shares to be issued on conversion55,000

The Rate of Income Tax: 30%. You are required to calculate Basic and Diluted Earnings Per Share (EPS).
answer_html:
Basic EPS = Net profit for the current year / Weighted average number of equity shares outstanding = ₹37,50,000 / 5,00,000 = ₹7.50 per share.

Diluted EPS = Adjusted net profit for the current year / Weighted average number of equity shares (including dilutive potential equity shares):

Adjusted net profit for the current year₹
Net profit for the current year37,50,000
Add: Interest expense for the current year (8% × ₹50,00,000 face value)4,00,000
Less: Tax relating to interest expense (30% of ₹4,00,000)(1,20,000)
Adjusted net profit for the current year40,30,000

Number of equity shares resulting from conversion of debentures = 55,000 (given in the question). Weighted average number of equity shares for diluted EPS = 5,00,000 + 55,000 = 5,55,000 shares.

Diluted EPS = ₹40,30,000 / 5,55,000 = ₹7.26 per share.

Note: Conversion of the convertible debentures into equity shares is a dilutive potential equity share. To compute the adjusted profit, the (post-tax) interest paid on the debentures is added back, since it would not be payable if the debentures were converted into equity shares.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html:
Saharsh Ltd. is engaged in manufacturing of electric home appliances. The company is in the process of finalizing its accounts for the year ended 31.3.2023 [as printed in source; see extraction-note] and needs your expert advice on the following issues:

  1. The company has its plants at 3 different locations. It has to shut down one of its plants due to internal reasons. The said plant site is under a rental agreement till 31.3.2024. The rent per month is ₹80,000. If the company cancels the agreement, it has to pay a penal amount equal to six months' rent. The company also has an option to sub-let the site at a rent of ₹45,000 per month.
  2. A case has been filed against the company in the consumer court and a notice for levy of a penalty of ₹20 lakhs has been received. The company has appointed a lawyer to defend the case for a fee of ₹2 lakhs. 50% of the fees has been paid and the balance 50% will be paid after finalisation of the case. There are 75% chances that the penalty may not be levied.
  3. The company had committed to supply a consignment worth ₹1 crore to one of its dealers by the year-end. As per the contract, if delivery is not made on time, a compensation of 15% of the value is to be paid. While the consignment was in transit, one of the trucks carrying goods worth ₹30 lakhs met with an accident. It was however covered by Insurance. According to the surveyor's report, the policy amount is collectable, subject to 10% deduction. Before closing the books of accounts, the company has received the information that the policy amount has been processed and the dealer has also claimed for the compensation.

Give your answers based on relevant Accounting Standard.
answer_html:
(i) As per AS 29, an 'onerous contract' is a contract in which the unavoidable costs of meeting the obligations under it exceed the economic benefits expected to be received under it; the unavoidable cost is the lower of the net cost of fulfilling the contract and any compensation/penalties from failing to fulfil it. Here: cost of cancelling the agreement = ₹80,000 × 6 months = ₹4,80,000. Cost of continuing the agreement while sub-letting = net of rent paid over rent collected from sub-tenant = (₹80,000 − ₹45,000) × 12 months = ₹4,20,000. The lower of the two, ₹4,20,000, is the amount to be provided for.

(ii) As per AS 29, an obligation is a present obligation only if, based on available evidence, its existence at the balance sheet date is probable (more likely than not). Here, there are 75% chances the penalty may not be levied – so the probability of an outflow is below the "more likely than not" threshold, and Saharsh Ltd. should not make a provision for the ₹20 lakh penalty. However, a provision should be made for the remaining 50% (unpaid) lawyer's fee, since that liability is not contingent on the outcome of the case.

(iii) Loss due to accident = ₹30,00,000. Insurance claim receivable by the company = ₹30,00,000 × 90% = ₹27,00,000 (10% deduction per the surveyor's report). Loss to be recognised in the books for 2023-24 = ₹30,00,000 − ₹27,00,000 = ₹3,00,000. Insurance claim receivable recorded in the books = ₹27,00,000 (virtually certain, per the processed policy amount). Compensation claim by the dealer, to be provided for in the books = ₹30,00,000 × 15% = ₹4,50,000.
Note (per source): alternatively, the 15% compensation can be computed on the whole ₹1 crore contract value, giving ₹15,00,000 (₹1 crore × 15%) instead.

topics.subtopictitle: Onerous-contract measurement, probability threshold for a present obligation, and insurance-claim/compensation provisioning across three scenarios for one company
topics.label: AS 29 (2.4)

examiner_comment.text: A common error in part (ii) is providing for the full ₹20 lakh penalty out of caution despite the stated 75% chance it will not be levied, missing that AS 29's "more likely than not" threshold is a specific probability test, not a general prudence override.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html: Write a short note on International Accounting Standard Board (IASB).
answer_html:
With a view of achieving the objective of setting global standards, the London based group namely the International Accounting Standards Committee (IASC), responsible for developing International Accounting Standards (IAS), was established in June, 1973.

  • It is presently known as International Accounting Standards Board (IASB).
  • Between 1973 and 2001, the IASC released IASs. Between 1997 and 1999, the IASC restructured their organisation, which resulted in formation of IASB. These changes came into effect on 1st April, 2001. Subsequently, IASB issued statements about current and future standards.
  • IASB publishes its Standards in a series of pronouncements called International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS).
  • The standards issued by IASC till 31.03.2001 are known as IASs and the standards issued by IASB since 01.04.2001 are known as IFRSs.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html:
Giant Ltd. has entered into a binding agreement with Tiny Ltd. to buy a custom-made machine of ₹1,00,000 at the end of 2024-25, before delivery of the machine, Giant Ltd. had to change its method of production. The new method will not require the machine ordered and it will be scrapped after delivery. The expected scrap value is nil.

You are required to advise the accounting treatment and give necessary journal entry in the year 2024-25.
answer_html:
A liability is recognized when outflow of economic resources in settlement of a present obligation can be anticipated and the value of outflow can be reliably measured.

When flow of economic benefit to the enterprise beyond the current accounting period is considered improbable, the expenditure incurred is recognised as an expense rather than as an asset.

In the given case, Giant Ltd. should recognise a liability of ₹1,00,000 to Tiny Ltd.

Also, the flow of future economic benefit from the machine to the enterprise is improbable.

Thus, the entire amount of purchase price of the machine should be recognised as an expense.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html: Virat Traders, an unlisted partnership firm, had a turnover of ₹249.99 crore and borrowings of ₹25.01 crore during the financial year 2023-24. It is not a bank, financial institution, or insurance company, and also not a subsidiary of any other entity. The firm wishes to avail MSME exemptions for FY 2024-25. Is it eligible?
answer_html:
Company qualifies as an MSME if following conditions are satisfied:

  1. whose equity or debt securities are not listed or are not in the process of listing on any stock exchange, whether in India or outside India;
  2. which is not a bank, financial institution or an insurance company;
  3. whose turnover (excluding other income) does not exceed 250 crore rupees in the immediately preceding accounting year;
  4. which does not have borrowings in excess of 50 crore rupees at any time during the immediately preceding accounting year; and
  5. which is not a holding or subsidiary of an entity which is not a MSME entity.

Yes, Virat Traders qualifies as an MSME since it meets all five criteria.

Further, it has been assumed that Virat Traders is not newly qualifying as an MSME in FY 2024-25 because a non-company entity that newly qualifies as an MSME can avail exemptions only after it remains as MSME for two consecutive years.

Until then, full AS compliance is required.

question_html: While preparing its financial statements for the year ended 31st March, 2025, B Limited has come across the following events which took place after 31st March, 2025. The financial statements of the company were approved by the Board of Directors on 30th May, 2025: B Limited started negotiations with S Limited during 2024-25 to acquire their Consumer Durables Business for ₹400 lakhs. The deal was finalized on 20th April, 2025 and B Limited invested ₹275 lakhs before 30th May, 2025. You are required to state with reasons, whether the aforesaid event is an adjusting or non-adjusting event as per the provisions of the relevant AS.
answer_html:
AS 4 (Revised) defines “Events Occurring after the Balance Sheet Date” as those significant events, both favourable and unfavourable, that occur between the balance sheet date and the date on which the financial statements are approved by the Approving Authority in the case of a company.

The acquisition of Consumer Durables Business of S Limited by B Limited is an event occurring after the balance sheet date. However, it is a non-adjusting event as it does not affect the determination and the condition of the amounts stated in the financial statements for the year ended 31st March, 2025. The disclosure should be made in the report of the approving authority about the investment of ₹275 lakhs to enable the users of financial statements to make proper evaluations and decisions.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html: During the course of audit for the year ended 31st March, 2025, the auditor discovered a fraud of ₹1,25,000 done by the accountant of the company. subject: advanced-accounting
question_html: Explain, in brief, the accounting treatment for an asset given under Operating Lease in the books of the Lessor.
answer_html:
The accounting treatment for an asset given under Operating Lease in the books of the lessor is given as under:

  1. The Lessor should present an asset given under Operating Lease as PPE in its balance sheet.
  2. Lease income from operating leases should be recognized in the Statement of Profit and Loss on a straight-line basis over the lease term, unless another systematic basis is more representative of the time pattern in which benefit derived from the use of the leased asset is diminished.
  3. Depreciation should be recognized in the books of the lessor. The depreciation of leased assets should be on a basis consistent with the normal accounting policy of the lessor for similar assets, and the depreciation charge should be calculated on the basis set out in AS 10.
  4. The impairment loss on assets given on operating leases are determined and treated as per AS 28.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html:
Arzoo Ltd. is in the business of manufacture of Passenger cars and commercial vehicles. The company is working on a strategic plan to shift from the Passenger car segment over the coming 5 years. However, no specific plans have been drawn up for sale of neither the division nor its assets. As part of its plan it will reduce the production of passenger cars by 20% annually. It also plans to commence another new factory for the manufacture of commercial vehicles plus transfer of employees in a phased manner.

(i) You are required to comment if mere gradual phasing out in itself can be considered as a ‘Discontinuing Operation' within the meaning of AS 24.

(ii) If the company passes a resolution to sell some of the assets in the passenger car division and also to transfer few other assets of the passenger car division to the new factory, does this trigger the application of AS 24?

(iii) Would your answer to the above be different if the company resolves to sell the assets of the Passenger Car Division in a phased but time bound manner?
answer_html:
Mere gradual phasing out is not considered as discontinuing operation as defined under para 3 of AS 24, ‘Discontinuing Operations'.

Examples of activities that do not necessarily satisfy criterion of the definition, but that might do so in combination with other circumstances, include: (1) Gradual or evolutionary phasing out of a product line or class of service; (2) Discontinuing, even if relatively abruptly, several products within an ongoing line of business; (3) Shifting of some production or marketing activities for a particular line of business from one location to another; and (4) Closing of a facility to achieve productivity improvements or other cost savings.

In view of the above the answers are:

(i) No, the companies' strategic plan has no final approval from the board through a resolution and there is no specific time bound activities like shifting of assets and employees. Above all, the new segment i.e. commercial vehicle production line in a new factory has not started.

(ii) No, the resolution is salient about stoppage of the Car segment in definite time period. Though, sale of some assets and some transfer proposal were passed through a resolution to the new factory, closure road map and new segment starting roadmap are missing. Hence, AS 24 will not be applicable.

(iii) Yes, phased and time bound programme resolved in the board clearly indicates the closure of the passenger car segment in a definite time frame and will constitute a clear roadmap. Hence, this action will attract compliance of AS 24.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html: A publisher owns 150 magazine titles of which 70 were purchased and 80 were self-created. The price paid for a purchased magazine title is recognised as an intangible asset. The costs of creating magazine titles and maintaining the existing titles are recognised as an expense when incurred. Cash inflows from direct sales and advertising are identifiable for each magazine title. Titles are managed by customer segments. The level of advertising income for a magazine title depends on the range of titles in the customer segment to which the magazine title relates. Management has a policy to abandon old titles before the end of their economic lives and replace them immediately with new titles for the same customer segment. Whether it will be a cash-generating unit as per AS 28?
answer_html: It is likely that the recoverable amount of an individual magazine title can be assessed. Even though the level of advertising income for a title is influenced, to a certain extent, by the other titles in the customer segment, cash inflows from direct sales and advertising are identifiable for each title. In addition, although titles are managed by customer segments, decisions to abandon titles are made on an individual title basis. Therefore, it is likely that individual magazine titles generate cash inflows that are largely independent one from another and that each magazine title is a separate cash-generating unit.

question_html: Galaxy Limited is in the process of finalization of its accounts for the year ended 31st March, 2025 and needs your advice on the following issue in line with the provisions of AS 29: Galaxy Limited is selling cosmetic products under its brand name “Angel” but is getting these products manufactured from X Limited. It has an understanding (enforceable agreement) with X Limited that if the company becomes liable for any damage claims, due to any injury or harm to the customer of the cosmetic products, 40% shall be reimbursed to it by X Limited. During the year 2024-25, an estimate of the claim of ₹25 lakhs may be payable to the customers by Galaxy Limited. How should Galaxy Limited account for the claim that becomes payable?
answer_html: Since the understanding results in an enforceable agreement, the reimbursement of ₹10,00,000 (40% of ₹25,00,000) shall be recognized as a reimbursement right and provision will be recognized for the full amount of the liability of ₹25,00,000. The reimbursement right shall be treated as a separate asset and shall not be offset with the provision. In the Statement of Profit and Loss, the expense may be presented as ₹15,00,000 after offsetting the reimbursement right.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html: Galaxy Limited has been sued by one of its competitor for alleged infringement of trademark and a notice for levy of penalty of ₹50 lakhs has been received by it. The company has appointed a law firm to defend its case for a fee of ₹5 lakhs. 60% of the fees has been paid in advance and the rest 40% would be paid after finalization of the case. There are 70% chances that the penalty may not be imposed.
answer_html: As per AS 29, an obligation is a present obligation if, based on the evidence available, its existence at the balance sheet date is considered probable, i.e. more likely than not. Liability is a present obligation of the enterprise arising from the past events, the settlement of which is expected to result in an outflow from the enterprise of resources embodying economic benefits. In the given case, there are 70% chances that the penalty may not be levied. Accordingly, Galaxy Limited should not make the provision for liability. The matter is disclosed as a contingent liability unless the probability of any outflow is considered as remote. However, a provision should be made for the remaining 40% fees of the law firm amounting to ₹2,00,000 in the financial statements for 2024-25.

topics.title: Provisions, Contingent Liabilities and Contingent Assets
topics.subtopictitle: Contingent liability disclosed, not recognised, where outflow is not probable (here, only 30% chance)
topics.label: AS 29 (2.9)

examiner_comment.text: Several examinees recognised a provision for the trademark-suit penalty itself, treating a 30% chance of levy as sufficient to be "probable," when AS 29 requires the outflow to be more likely than not before a provision (rather than mere contingent-liability disclosure) is warranted; many also missed the separate, unconditional obligation to provide for the remaining unpaid law-firm fee.

subject: advanced-accounting
case_facts_html:
Suman Ltd. is in the business of manufacturing electronics equipment and selling these at its various outlets. It provides installation services for the equipment sold and also provide free 1 year warranty on all the sold products.

Beach Resorts are leading resorts in the city. It purchased 5 air conditioners (AC) from Suman Ltd. for its resort. Suman Ltd. sold 5 AC to Beach resort for ₹45,000 each which includes installation fees of ₹1,000 for each AC. The Company also offers 1 year warranty for any repair etc. The Company also offered ₹500 per AC as trade discount. Beach resort placed order on March 15, 2024 and made payment on March 20, 2024. The ACs were delivered on March 27, 2024 and the installation was completed on April 5, 2024.
question_html:
How much revenue should be recognised by the Company as on March 31, 2024:

  1. ₹2,25,000
  2. ₹2,17,500
  3. ₹2,00,000
  4. ₹2,30,000
answer_html: Answer: (ii) ₹2,17,500. Per unit, the invoice price of ₹45,000 includes an installation fee of ₹1,000, so the equipment-sale component is ₹44,000; the ₹500 trade discount is deducted from this equipment price (trade discounts are deducted in determining revenue, not recognised separately — see Q1(c)), leaving ₹43,500 per AC. Delivery, and hence transfer of the significant risks and rewards of the AC itself, occurred on March 27, 2024, so ₹43,500 × 5 = ₹2,17,500 of equipment revenue is recognised as on March 31, 2024. The separately-priced installation fee is not yet recognised, since installation (a distinct service performed by Suman Ltd. itself) was not completed until April 5, 2024.

topics.subtopictitle: Goods subject to installation - deferral of the installation-linked portion of revenue until installation is complete

examiner_comment.text: A common error here is recognising the full ₹2,25,000 invoice value as on March 31, 2024, without splitting out the separately-priced installation fee that had not yet been earned, or without deducting the trade discount from the equipment price before arriving at the revenue figure.

The Company also offers 1 year warranty for any repair etc. The Company also offered ₹500 per AC as trade discount. Beach resort placed order on March 15, 2024 and made payment on March 20, 2024. The ACs were delivered on March 27, 2024 and the installation was completed on April 5, 2024.
question_html:
How much revenue should be recognised by the Company in the financial year 2024-25:

  1. ₹5000
  2. ₹2,20,000
  3. ₹10,000
  4. ₹2,40,000
answer_html: Answer: (i) ₹5,000. The installation fee of ₹1,000 per AC (unaffected by the trade discount, which applies to the equipment price) is recognised as revenue only once installation is actually complete — April 5, 2024, which falls in FY 2024-25. ₹1,000 × 5 ACs = ₹5,000.

topics.subtopictitle: Installation-fee revenue recognised in the period installation is actually completed
topics.label: AS 9 (2.8)

examiner_comment.text: A frequent mistake is carrying the full unrecognised balance forward into FY 2024-25, including the equipment portion that was already recognised in the prior year, instead of isolating just the deferred installation-fee component.

subject: advanced-accounting
case_facts_html:
Suman Ltd. is in the business of manufacturing electronics equipment and selling these at its various outlets. It provides installation services for the equipment sold and also provide free 1 year warranty on all the sold products.

Beach Resorts are leading resorts in the city. It purchased 5 air conditioners (AC) from Suman Ltd. for its resort. Suman Ltd. sold 5 AC to Beach resort for ₹45,000 each which includes installation fees of ₹1,000 for each AC. The Company also offers 1 year warranty for any repair etc. The Company also offered ₹500 per AC as trade discount. Beach resort placed order on March 15, 2024 and made payment on March 20, 2024. The ACs were delivered on March 27, 2024 and the installation was completed on April 5, 2024.
question_html:
What will be the accounting for trade discount:

  1. The same will be recognised separately in the profit and loss.
  2. The trade discounts are deducted in determining the revenue.
  3. Trade discount will be recognised after one year, when the warranty will be over.
  4. Trade discount will be recognised after installation is complete.
answer_html: Answer: (ii) The trade discounts are deducted in determining the revenue. Per AS 9, trade discounts and volume rebates are deducted in arriving at the revenue figure — they are never recognised as a separate profit and loss item, and have no connection to the warranty period or the installation date.

topics.title: Revenue Recognition
topics.subtopictitle: Trade discounts deducted in determining revenue, not recognised separately
topics.label: AS 9 (2.8)

examiner_comment.text: A common error is linking the trade discount's recognition timing to an unrelated event in the fact pattern, such as the warranty period or the installation date, instead of recognising that a trade discount is simply netted against revenue at the point of sale.

subject: advanced-accounting
case_facts_html:
Suman Ltd. is in the business of manufacturing electronics equipment and selling these at its various outlets. It provides installation services for the equipment sold and also provide free 1 year warranty on all the sold products.

Beach Resorts are leading resorts in the city. It purchased 5 air conditioners (AC) from Suman Ltd. for its resort. Suman Ltd. sold 5 AC to Beach resort for ₹45,000 each which includes installation fees of ₹1,000 for each AC. The Company also offers 1 year warranty for any repair etc. The Company also offered ₹500 per AC as trade discount. Beach resort placed order on March 15, 2024 and made payment on March 20, 2024. The ACs were delivered on March 27, 2024 and the installation was completed on April 5, 2024.
question_html:
Is the Company required to do any accounting for 1 year warranty provided by it:

  1. No accounting treatment is required till some warranty claim is actually received by the Company.
  2. As there exist a present obligation to provide warranty to customers for 1 year, the Company should estimate the amount that it may have to incur considering various factors including past trends and create a provision as per AS 29.
  3. Accounting for claims will be done on cash basis i.e. expense will be recognised when expense is made.
  4. As the Company is not charging separately for the warranty provided, there is no need to create any provision.
answer_html: Answer: (ii) As there exist a present obligation to provide warranty to customers for 1 year, the Company should estimate the amount that it may have to incur considering various factors including past trends and create a provision as per AS 29. The free 1-year warranty is a present obligation arising from a past event (the sale), with a probable outflow of resources and a reliable estimate obtainable from past claims experience — all three AS 29 recognition conditions are met, regardless of whether the warranty is priced separately or bundled into the sale price.

topics.title: Provisions, Contingent Liabilities and Contingent Assets
topics.subtopictitle: Present obligation from a past event triggers a provision, estimated using past trends
topics.label: AS 29 (2.4)

examiner_comment.text: A common error is waiting for an actual warranty claim before recognising anything (cash-basis thinking), rather than recognising that the obligation itself — and the probability of some claims occurring — already exists at the point of sale.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html:
As per AS 2, Inventories include materials awaiting use in production process, what should be included in Inventories from the following:

  1. Secondary Packing material required for transporting and forwarding the material.
  2. Spare parts, servicing equipment and standby equipment
  3. Primary packing material which is essential to bring an item of inventory to its saleable condition, for example, bottles, cans etc., in case of food and beverages industry.
  4. Publicity material
answer_html: Answer: (c) Primary packing material which is essential to bring an item of inventory to its saleable condition, for example, bottles, cans etc., in case of food and beverages industry. AS 2 includes in the cost of inventories all costs necessary to bring the item to its present location and saleable condition — primary packaging (e.g. the bottle/can itself) meets this test. Secondary packing (for onward transport) and publicity material are distribution/selling costs, expensed as incurred rather than inventoried; spare parts, servicing equipment and standby equipment are generally accounted for as property, plant and equipment under AS 10, not as inventory.

topics.title: Valuation of Inventories
topics.subtopictitle: Scope of inventories - primary packing material necessary to reach saleable condition is includible; spare parts/standby equipment and publicity/secondary-packing costs generally are not
topics.label: AS 2 (1.2)

examiner_comment.text: A common error is including spare parts and standby equipment as inventory by analogy with packing materials, without recognising that AS 10 (not AS 2) generally governs such items.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html:
Kirti Ltd. is in the business of manufacturing computers. During the year ended 31st March, 2024, the company manufactured 550 computers. It has the policy of valuing finished stock of goods at a standard cost of ₹1.8 lakh per computer. The details of the costs are as under:

(₹ in lakh)
Raw material consumed400
Direct Labour250
Variable production overheads150
Fixed production overheads (including interest of ₹100 lakh)290

Compute the value cost per computer for the purpose of closing stock.
answer_html:
As per para 9 of AS 2 ‘Valuation of Inventories’, for inclusion in the cost of inventory, allocation of fixed production overheads is based on the normal capacity of the production facilities.

In this case, finished stock has been valued at a standard cost of ₹1.8 lakh per computer which incidentally synchronizes with the value computed on the basis of absorption costing as under:

(₹ in lakh)
Materials400
Direct Labour250
Variable production overheads150
Fixed production overheads290
Less: Interest(100)190
Total cost990

Number of computers produced = 550 computers (Assumed to be normal production).

Cost per computer ₹990 lakh / 550 computers = ₹1.80 lakh.

topics.title: Valuation of Inventories
topics.subtopictitle: Fixed production overheads absorbed on normal capacity, excluding interest, for standard-cost/closing-stock valuation
topics.label: AS 2 (1.6)

examiner_comment.text: A common error is including the ₹100 lakh interest component within fixed production overheads when arriving at the cost of inventory, instead of excluding financing costs that are not part of bringing the inventory to its present location and condition.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html:
For five companies whose financial year ended on 31st March, 2023, the financial statements were approved by their approving authority on 15th June, 2023.

During 2023-2024, the following material events took place:

  1. A Ltd. sold a major property which was included in the balance sheet at ₹1,00,000 and for which contracts had been exchanged on 15th March, 2023. The sale was completed on 15th May, 2023 at a price of ₹2,50,000.
  2. On 30th April, 2023, a 100% subsidiary of B Ltd. declared a dividend of ₹3,00,000 in respect of its own shares for the year ended on 31st March, 2023.
  3. On 31st May, 2023, the mail order activities of C Ltd. (a retail trading group) were shut down with closure costs amounting to ₹2.5 million.
  4. On 1st July, 2023 the discovery of sand under D Ltd.'s major civil engineering contract site causes the cost of the contract to increase by 25% for which there would be no corresponding recovery from the customer.
  5. A fire, on 2nd April, 2023, completely destroyed a manufacturing plant of E Ltd. It was expected that the loss of ₹10 million would be fully covered by the insurance company.

You are required to state with reasons, how each of the above items numbered (a) to (e) should be dealt with in the financial statement of the various companies for the year ended 31st March, 2023.
answer_html:
Treatment as per AS 4 ‘Contingencies and Events Occurring After the Balance Sheet Date’

CompanyTreatment
(a)A Ltd.The sale of property should be treated as an adjusting event since contracts had been exchanged prior to the year-end. The effect of the sale would be reflected in the financial statements ended on 31.3.2023 and the profit on sale of property ₹1,50,000 would be treated as an extraordinary item.
(b)B Ltd.The declaration of dividend on 30th April, 2023 of ₹3,00,000 would be treated as a non-adjusting event in the financial statements of 2022-2023. This is because, the dividend has been declared after the balance sheet date and no conditions existed on the balance sheet date for such declaration of dividend. Further as per AS 9, right to receive dividend is established when it is declared and not before that.
(c)C Ltd.A closure not anticipated at the year-end would be treated as a non-adjusting event. Memorandum disclosure would be required for closure of mail order activities since non disclosure would affect user's understanding of the financial statements.
(d)D Ltd.The event took place after the financial statements were approved by the approving authority and is thus outside the purview of AS 4. However, in view of its significance of the transaction, the directors may consider publishing a separate financial statement/additional statement for the attention of the members in general meeting.
(e)E Ltd.The event is a non-adjusting event since it occurred after the year-end and does not relate to the conditions existing at the year-end. However, it is necessary to consider the validity of the going concern assumption having regard to the extent of insurance cover. Also, since it is said that the loss would be fully recovered by the insurance company, the fact should be disclosed by way of a note to the financial statements.

topics.title: Contingencies and Events Occurring After the Balance Sheet Date
topics.subtopictitle: Adjusting vs non-adjusting events after the balance sheet date across five illustrative scenarios
topics.label: AS 4 (1.4/1.5)

examiner_comment.text: A common error is treating D Ltd.'s scenario as a normal non-adjusting event requiring disclosure in the 2022-2023 financial statements, without recognising that the event occurred after the accounts were already approved and is therefore entirely outside AS 4's scope for that year's statements.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html:
Explain whether the following will constitute a change in accounting policy or not as per AS 5:

  1. Introduction of a formal retirement gratuity scheme by an employer in place of ad hoc ex-gratia payments to employees on retirement.
  2. Management decided to pay pension to those employees who have retired after completing 5 years of service in the organistaion. Such employees will get pension of ₹20,000 per month. Earlier there was no such scheme of pension in the organization.
answer_html:
As per para 31 of AS 5 ‘Net Profit or Loss for the Period, Prior Period Items and Changes in Accounting Policies’, the adoption of an accounting policy for events or transactions that differ in substance from previously occurring events or transactions, will not be considered as a change in accounting policy.

  1. Accordingly, introduction of a formal retirement gratuity scheme by an employer in place of ad hoc ex-gratia payments to employees on retirement is not a change in an accounting policy.
  2. Similarly, the adoption of a new accounting policy of paying pension to retired employees is a policy for events or transactions which did not occur previously. Hence, it will not be treated as a change in an accounting policy.

topics.title: Net Profit or Loss for the Period, Prior Period Items and Changes in Accounting Policies
topics.subtopictitle: Adoption of a policy for events/transactions that did not previously occur is not a change in accounting policy
topics.label: AS 5 (2.5)

examiner_comment.text: A common error is treating both scenarios as changes in accounting policy simply because the amount charged to profit or loss will differ going forward, without checking whether the underlying event or transaction itself is genuinely new rather than merely a change in the treatment of the same recurring event.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html: When will the revenue be recognized in the case of inter divisional transfers?
answer_html: The Accounting Standard Board of ICAI has come up with an announcement in the earlier years wherein it clarified that the inter-divisional transfers/sales are not revenue as per AS 9 "Revenue Recognition". According to it, in case of inter-divisional transfers, risks and rewards remain within the enterprise and also there is no consideration from the point of view of the enterprise as a whole. Therefore, the recognition criteria for revenue recognition are also not fulfilled in respect of inter-divisional transfers. Hence, no revenue is recognized in the case of inter-divisional transfers.

topics.label: AS 9 (2.2)

examiner_comment.text: A common error is treating an inter-divisional transfer priced at a notional transfer price as genuine revenue, without recognising that the enterprise as a whole has not transacted with any outside party.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html: Alfa Ltd. purchased an item of property, plant and equipment for US $ 50 lakh on 01.04.2023 and the same was fully financed by the foreign currency loan [i.e. US $] repayment in five equal instalments annually. (Exchange rate at the time of purchase was 1 US $ = ₹60]. As on 31.03.2024 the first instalment was paid when 1 US $ fetched ₹62.00. The entire loss on exchange was included in cost of goods sold. Alfa Ltd. normally provides depreciation on an item of property, plant and equipment at 20% on WDV basis and exercised the option to adjust the cost of asset for exchange difference arising out of loan restatement and payment. Calculate the amount of exchange loss and its treatment and depreciation.
answer_html:
Exchange differences arising on restatement or repayment of liabilities incurred for the purpose of acquiring an item of property, plant and equipment should be adjusted in the carrying amount of the respective item of property, plant and equipment as Alfa Ltd. has exercised the option and it is long term foreign currency monetary item.

Thus, the entire exchange loss due to variation of ₹20 lakh on 31.03.2023 on payment of US $ 10 lakh, should be added to the carrying amount of an item of property, plant and equipment and not to the cost of goods sold. Further, depreciation on the unamortized depreciable amount should also be provided.

Calculation of Exchange loss:

Foreign currency loan (in ₹) = (50 lakh $ × ₹60) = ₹3,000 lakh

Exchange loss on outstanding loan on 31.03.2024 = ₹40 lakh US $ × (62.00−60.00) = ₹80 lakh.

So, ₹80 lakh should also be added to cost of an item of property, plant and equipment with corresponding credit to outstanding loan in addition to ₹20 lakh on account of exchange loss on payment of instalment. The total cost of an item of property, plant and equipment to be increased by ₹100 lakh.

Total depreciation to be provided for the year 2023-2024 = 20% of (₹3,000 lakh + 100 lakh) = ₹620 lakh.

topics.title: The Effects of Changes in Foreign Exchange Rates
topics.subtopictitle: Exchange differences on restatement/repayment of a long-term foreign-currency loan financing PPE, capitalised into the asset's carrying amount
topics.label: AS 11 (3.5)

examiner_comment.text: A common error is leaving the exchange loss in the cost of goods sold (as the company's own initial treatment had done) rather than capitalising it into the carrying amount of the property, plant and equipment once the long-term-monetary-item option has been exercised, and consequently missing the resulting increase in the depreciation charge.

(a)" even though no corresponding "(b)" sub-part is ever printed anywhere in the paper — treated as one single, unsplit record since no second sub-part exists. The answer's own text also dates the ₹20 lakh instalment exchange loss "on 31.03.2023," which is inconsistent with the question's own facts (loan taken 01.04.2023, first instalment paid "As on 31.03.2024") — almost certainly a typo in the source for 31.03.2024, reproduced here exactly as printed rather than silently corrected. The arithmetic itself (₹20 lakh + ₹80 lakh = ₹100 lakh; 20% × ₹3,100 lakh = ₹620 lakh) was independently re-derived and confirmed correct regardless of the date typo.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html:
Energy Ltd. has acquired a generator on 1.4.2023 for ₹100 lakh. On 2.4.2023, it applied to Indian Renewal Energy Development Authority (IREDA) for a subsidy. The subsidy was granted in June, 2024 after the accounts for 2023-2024 were finalized. The company has not accounted for the subsidy for the year ended 31.3.2024.

State

  1. Is this a prior period item?
  2. How should the subsidy be accounted in the accounting year 2024-2025?
answer_html:
The answer is in para 13 of AS 12 "Accounting for Government Grants" which permits recognition of grant only when there is reasonable assurance that –

  1. the enterprise will comply with the conditions attached to them and
  2. the subsidy will be received.

Mere making of an application does not provide the reasonable assurance that the subsidy will be received. Letter of sanction from IREDA is required to provide this assurance. Since, the subsidy was granted in June, 2024 after approval of accounts, non-recognition of grant in 2023-2024 will not be considered as an error. Hence, this is not a prior period item. Therefore, the company was right in not recognizing the grant.

Further, AS 4 requires adjustment of events occurring after the balance sheet date only upto the date of approval of accounts by the Board of Directors. In view of this, the company is correct in not adjusting the same in the accounts in the year 2023-2024.

(ii) The subsidy should be deducted from the cost of the generator. The revised unamortised amount of generator should be written off over the remaining useful life.

Alternatively, the same may be treated as ‘deferred income’ and allocated over the remaining useful life in the proportion in which depreciation is charged.

topics.title: Accounting for Government Grants
topics.subtopictitle: Recognition of a government grant requires reasonable assurance of both compliance and receipt - mere application is insufficient
topics.label: AS 12 (1.4)

examiner_comment.text: A common error is treating the mere filing of a subsidy application as sufficient grounds to recognize the grant, or alternatively treating the later grant of the subsidy as a prior period item requiring restatement of the already-approved 2023-2024 accounts.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html:
A company is engaged in the business of refining, transportation and marketing of petroleum products. During the financial year ended 31st March, 2024, the company acquired controlling interest from Government of India in another public sector undertaking @ ₹1,551 per share as against the book value of ₹192.58 per share and market value of ₹876 per share as on 18th February, 2024.

Thus, the strategic premium of ₹675 per share has been paid considering various tangible and intangible factors.

The above investment in the shares of the acquired company has been considered as long term strategic investment and, therefore, has been accounted for at cost, i.e. at ₹1,551 per share in the financial statements. No provision for diminution in value has been made in the books of account.

As per the requirement of Schedule III to the Companies Act, 2013, the aggregate market value of the quoted shares has been properly reflected in the financial statements.

On 28th March, 2024, the acquired shares were quoted at ₹880 per share on BSE and the current market price as on 18th July was around ₹300.

Considering the tangible and intangible benefits the Management is of the view that there is no permanent diminution in the value of the strategic investment in the acquired company, as the same has been considered as a long-term investment. Therefore, there is no need for provision for diminution in the value of the shares of the acquired company.

Required:

  1. Whether the accounting treatment 'at cost' under the head ‘Long Term Investments’ without providing for any diminution in value is correct and in accordance with the provisions of AS 13.
  2. If any provision for diminution in the value is to be made, whether such provision should be charged to the profit and loss account or whether same can be considered as deferred expenditure and amortised over a period of 5 years. Whether it is open for the company to charge off such diminution in the value in the books of account instead of creating provision.
  3. Whether the premium paid for strategic benefits for investment described in facts of the case, can be accounted for separately in the books of account keeping in view that AS 13 specifies that long term investments should be recorded at cost and there is no specific provision in the standard in respect of accounting for premium paid for strategic benefits.
answer_html:
1. The accounting treatment 'at cost' under the head ‘Long Term Investment’ in the separate financial statements of the company without providing for any diminution in value is correct and is in accordance with the provisions of AS 13 provided that there is no decline, other than temporary, in the value of investment.
  2. The provision for diminution in the value of investment should be a charge to the profit and loss statement. As per the requirements of AS 13, the diminution in the value of investment can neither be accounted for as deferred revenue expenditure nor it can be written off in the statement of profit and loss.
  3. The long-term investments should be carried at cost as per the requirements of AS 13. The amount paid over and above the market price should be treated as cost and cannot be accounted for separately.

topics.title: Accounting for Investments
topics.subtopictitle: Long-term investments carried at cost unless there is a decline other than temporary; a strategic-benefit premium forms part of cost and is not separately accounted for or amortised
topics.label: AS 13 (3.6)

examiner_comment.text: A common error is proposing to amortise the diminution in value as deferred revenue expenditure over several years, rather than recognising that AS 13 requires any genuine, other-than-temporary decline to be charged immediately to profit and loss, with no deferred-expenditure treatment available.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html: Hill Ltd. has a share capital of 50,000 shares @ ₹100 per share. Sun Ltd. acquired 15% shares in Hill Ltd. on 1.4.2024. It also acquired all the 5,000, 12% convertible debentures of ₹100 each of Hill Ltd. These debentures will be converted at par into equity shares of Hill Ltd. after 3 years. State whether, as per AS 23, Hill Ltd. is an Associate of Sun Ltd. or not with reasons?
answer_html:
As per para 3 of AS 23 ‘Accounting for Investments in Associates in Consolidated Financial Statements’, an associate is an enterprise in which the investor has significant influence and which is neither a subsidiary nor a joint venture of the investor.

Standard further explains in para 4 that as regards share ownership, if an investor holds, directly or indirectly through subsidiary (ies), 20% or more of the voting power of the investee, it is presumed that the investor has significant influence, unless it can be clearly demonstrated that this is not the case. Conversely, if the investor holds, directly or indirectly through subsidiary (ies), less than 20% of the voting power of the investee, it is presumed that the investor does not have significant influence, unless such influence can be clearly demonstrated.

Further as per an explanation to para 4 of the standard, for the purpose of classification of associate, the potential equity shares of the investee held by the investor will not be taken into account for determining the voting power of the investor. In other words, the voting power should be determined on the basis of the current outstanding securities with voting rights.

As per the information given in the question, Sun Ltd. presently holds indirectly 22.7% shares (with and without voting rights) (Refer W.N.) in Hill Ltd. However, the current outstanding securities with voting rights in Hill Ltd. is only 15% and the remaining holding is on account of potential equity shares. Since potential equity shares do not have voting rights they will not be taken into consideration while determining the significant influence of Sun Ltd. on Hill Ltd. Hence, Hill Ltd. is not an associate of Sun Ltd.

Working Note: Calculation of percentage of holding of shares after conversion

₹
Current holding is 15% i.e. 7,500 shares of ₹100 each7,50,000
Potential equity shares i.e. 5,000 shares of ₹100 each5,00,000
Total12,50,000

Total share capital of Hill Ltd. after conversion of debentures into equity shares will be = ₹50,00,000 + ₹5,00,000 = ₹55,00,000

Percentage of holding = ₹(12,50,000/55,00,000) × 100 = 22.7% approx.

topics.title: Accounting for Investments in Associates in Consolidated Financial Statements
topics.subtopictitle: Potential equity shares (e.g. convertible debentures) excluded when determining voting power for associate classification
topics.label: AS 23 (2.10)

examiner_comment.text: A common error is computing the combined 22.7% effective holding (current shares plus convertible debentures) and concluding significant influence exists purely because that combined figure exceeds 20%, without recognising that potential equity shares (the convertible debentures, before conversion) carry no voting rights and must be excluded from the voting-power test.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html:
Arzoo Ltd. is in the business of manufacture of Passenger cars and commercial vehicles. The company is working on a strategic plan to shift from the Passenger car segment over the coming 5 years. However, no specific plans have been drawn up for sale of neither the division nor its assets. As part of its plan it will reduce the production of passenger cars by 20% annually. It also plans to commence another new factory for the manufacture of commercial vehicles plus transfer of employees in a phased manner.

  1. You are required to comment if mere gradual phasing out in itself can be considered as a ‘Discontinuing Operation' within the meaning of AS 24.
  2. If the company passes a resolution to sell some of the assets in the passenger car division and also to transfer few other assets of the passenger car division to the new factory, does this trigger the application of AS 24?
  3. Would your answer to the above be different if the company resolves to sell the assets of the Passenger Car Division in a phased but time bound manner?
answer_html:
Mere gradual phasing out is not considered as discontinuing operation as defined under para 3 of AS 24, ‘Discontinuing Operations’.

Examples of activities that do not necessarily satisfy criterion of the definition, but that might do so in combination with other circumstances, include:

  1. Gradual or evolutionary phasing out of a product line or class of service;
  2. Discontinuing, even if relatively abruptly, several products within an ongoing line of business;
  3. Shifting of some production or marketing activities for a particular line of business from one location to another; and
  4. Closing of a facility to achieve productivity improvements or other cost savings.

In view of the above the answers are:

  1. No, the companies' strategic plan has no final approval from the board through a resolution and there is no specific time bound activities like shifting of assets and employees. Above all, the new segment i.e. commercial vehicle production line in a new factory has not started.
  2. No, the resolution is salient about stoppage of the Car segment in definite time period. Though, sale of some assets and some transfer proposal were passed through a resolution to the new factory, closure road map and new segment starting roadmap are missing. Hence, AS 24 will not be applicable.
  3. Yes, phased and time bound programme resolved in the board clearly indicates the closure of the passenger car segment in a definite time frame and will constitute a clear roadmap. Hence, this action will attract compliance of AS 24.

topics.title: Discontinuing Operations
topics.subtopictitle: Mere gradual/evolutionary phasing out, without a definite time-bound board resolution, is not a discontinuing operation
topics.label: AS 24 (6.2)

examiner_comment.text: A common error is treating the mere existence of a strategic plan and a board resolution touching some assets as sufficient to trigger AS 24, without checking whether the resolution actually sets out a definite, time-bound closure roadmap for the whole segment.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html:
A publisher owns 150 magazine titles of which 70 were purchased and 80 were self-created. The price paid for a purchased magazine title is recognised as an intangible asset. The costs of creating magazine titles and maintaining the existing titles are recognised as an expense when incurred. Cash inflows from direct sales and advertising are identifiable for each magazine title. Titles are managed by customer segments. The level of advertising income for a magazine title depends on the range of titles in the customer segment to which the magazine title relates. Management has a policy to abandon old titles before the end of their economic lives and replace them immediately with new titles for the same customer segment.

Whether it will be a cash-generating unit as per AS 28?
answer_html:
It is likely that the recoverable amount of an individual magazine title can be assessed. Even though the level of advertising income for a title is influenced, to a certain extent, by the other titles in the customer segment, cash inflows from direct sales and advertising are identifiable for each title. In addition, although titles are managed by customer segments, decisions to abandon titles are made on an individual title basis.

Therefore, it is likely that individual magazine titles generate cash inflows that are largely independent one from another and that each magazine title is a separate cash-generating unit.

topics.title: Impairment of Assets
topics.subtopictitle: Identification of a cash-generating unit - independent, identifiable cash inflows determine separate CGU status even where some influence between related assets exists
topics.label: AS 28 (7.8)

examiner_comment.text: A common error is treating the whole customer segment as a single cash-generating unit because advertising income is partly influenced by the range of titles in that segment, without recognising that direct sales and advertising cash inflows are still separately identifiable per title, and abandonment decisions are made per title.

subject: advanced-accounting
question_html:
A company incorporated under Section 8 of the Companies Act, 2013, have main objective to promote the trade by organizing trade fairs / exhibitions. When company was organizing the trade fair and exhibitions it decided to charge 5% contingency charges for the participants/outside agencies on the income received from them by the company, while in the case of fairs organized by outside agencies, 5% contingency charges are levied separately in the invoice, the contingency charges in respect of fairs organized by the company itself are inbuilt in the space rent charged from the participants. Both are credited to Income and Expenditure Account of the company.

The intention of levying these charges is to meet any unforeseen liability, which may arise in future. The instances of such unforeseen liabilities could be on account of injury/loss of life to visitors/exhibitors, etc., due to fire, terrorist attack, stampede, natural calamities and other public and third party liability. The chances of occurrence of these events are high because of large crowds visiting the fair. The decision to levy 5% contingency charges was based on assessment only as actual liability on this account cannot be estimated.

The following accounting treatment and disclosure was made by the company in its financial statements:

  1. 5% contingency charges are treated as income and matching provision for the same is also being made in accounts.
  2. A suitable disclosure to this effect is also made in the notes forming part of accounts.

Required:

  1. Whether creation of provision for contingencies under the facts and circumstances of the case is in conformity with AS 29.
  2. If the answer of (i) is "No" then what should be the treatment of the provision which is already created in the balance sheet.
answer_html:
(i) Para 14 of AS 29 "Provisions, Contingent Liabilities and Contingent Assets" states that a provision should be recognised when (a) An enterprise has a present obligation as a result of a past event and (b) It is probable that an outflow of resources embodying economic benefits will be required to settle the obligation and (c) A reliable estimate can be made of the amount of the obligation. If these conditions are not met, no provision should be recognised.

From the above, it is clear that in the contingencies considered by the company, neither a present obligation exists as a result of past event, nor a reliable estimate can be made of the amount of the obligation. Accordingly, a provision cannot be recognised for such contingencies under the facts and circumstances of the case.

(ii) "Provision" is the amount retained by the way of providing for any known liability. Since the contingencies stipulated by the company are not known at the balance sheet date, the provision in this regard cannot be created. Therefore, the provision so created by the company shall be treated as a ‘Reserve’.

topics.title: Provisions, Contingent Liabilities and Contingent Assets
topics.subtopictitle: No provision where neither a present obligation nor a reliable estimate exists; an amount already provided under such circumstances is treated as a reserve
topics.label: AS 29 (2.4)

examiner_comment.text: A common error is accepting a self-assessed contingency charge as a valid provision simply because the company has a genuine, high-probability risk exposure, without testing whether a present obligation from a past event and a reliable estimate actually exist as required by AS 29.

question_html:
In G Ltd.'s books, closing inventory at 31.03.2024 was ₹10,40,000 (FIFO method). The company changes to weighted average method for 31.3.2024: closing inventory becomes ₹8,80,000. Realisable value at 31.03.2024 is ₹12,00,000. What will be the value of inventory in the books and what disclosure should be given?

  1. The value will be ₹8,80,000 and the fact that the valuation method has changed to be disclosed.
  2. The value will be ₹12,00,000, and full disclosure with the amount the valuation method has changed to be disclosed.
  3. The value will be ₹12,00,000, and the fact that the valuation method has changed to be disclosed.
  4. The value will be ₹8,80,000, and full disclosure with the amount the valuation method has changed to be disclosed.
answer_html: Answer: (iv) — inventory is valued at the lower of cost and net realisable value; the weighted-average cost (₹8,80,000) is lower than NRV (₹12,00,000), so ₹8,80,000 is the book value. Since this is a change in accounting policy (costing formula) with a material effect, AS 1/AS 2 require full disclosure, including the quantified amount of the effect of the change (not merely the fact of the change).

topics.subtopictitle: Change in cost formula requires full disclosure of the change and its quantified financial effect
topics.label: AS 2 (1.2)

examiner_comment.text: Some examinees selected the "fact only" disclosure option instead of the "full disclosure with amount" option, understating the disclosure actually required for a material accounting policy change.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html:
Cost of a current investment acquired was ₹1000 but fair value was ₹800; recorded at ₹800. Now fair value of the investment is ₹1200. At what value should it be recorded, and how much gain credited to profit and loss?

  1. No change required; continues at ₹800.
  2. Recorded at ₹1000 and gain of ₹200 credited to P&L.
  3. Recorded at ₹1200 and gain of ₹400 credited to P&L.
  4. Recorded at ₹1200 but no gain credited to P&L.
answer_html: Answer: (ii) — current investments are carried at the lower of cost and fair value; even though fair value has now risen to ₹1,200 (above cost), the investment cannot be marked up beyond its original cost of ₹1,000. The carrying value is restored from ₹800 to ₹1,000 (the ceiling), recognising a gain of ₹200 (1,000−800) — the further rise from 1,000 to 1,200 is unrealised and not recognised.

topics.title: Accounting for Investments
topics.subtopictitle: Current investments carried at the lower of cost and fair value - never marked up beyond original cost
topics.label: AS 13 (3.3)

examiner_comment.text: Some examinees recorded the investment at the full current fair value of ₹1,200, not applying the cost ceiling that governs current-investment valuation under AS 13.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: As per the revised scheme effective from accounting periods commencing on or after 1st April, 2024, classify non-company entities for the purpose of applicability of Accounting Standards. Briefly explain the criteria for each category.
answer_html:
Non-company entities are classified into two categories: Micro, Small and Medium Sized Entities (MSMEs) and Large entities.

A non-company entity qualifies as an MSME if it satisfies all of: (i) its equity/debt securities are not listed or in the process of listing on any stock exchange (in India or abroad); (ii) it is not a bank, financial institution, or insurance company; (iii) turnover (excluding other income) does not exceed ₹250 crore in the immediately preceding accounting year; (iv) it does not have borrowings exceeding ₹50 crore at any time during the immediately preceding accounting year; and (v) it is not a holding or subsidiary of an entity that is not itself an MSME. These conditions are assessed as at the end of the relevant accounting period. A Large entity is any non-company entity that does not meet the MSME definition, and must comply in full with all Accounting Standards; MSMEs receive certain exemptions/relaxations.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: Lion Ltd. (manufacturing/construction contracts), FY ended 31st March 2025, follows historical cost, FIFO, and percentage-of-completion. During the year, management changes: (i) inventory valuation FIFO→Weighted Average (citing raw-material price volatility); (ii) depreciation SLM→WDV (citing better usage reflection). The company discloses the inventory-method change in notes but not the depreciation-method change (calling it immaterial), and has not disclosed its accounting policy on government grants despite receiving a significant subsidy this year. (a) Identify AS 1 violations, if any. (b) Critically evaluate whether "materiality" justifies non-disclosure of a change in accounting policy. (c) Is the FIFO→Weighted Average change an estimate or policy change under AS 1?
answer_html:
(a) AS 1 requires all significant accounting policies to be disclosed, and any material change in policy to be disclosed along with its nature and reasons (with the effect indicated if ascertainable). Applying this: (1) Inventory method change (FIFO→Weighted Average) is a change in accounting policy, correctly disclosed with justification — compliant, provided the quantified effect is also disclosed or noted as unascertainable. (2) Depreciation method change (SLM→WDV) is technically a change in accounting estimate under AS 10, but AS 1 still requires disclosure of material items affecting the financial statements — depreciation affects profit, asset values, and return ratios; non-disclosure on unsubstantiated "immateriality" grounds is not appropriate without clear quantitative evidence. (3) Government grants policy non-disclosure: AS 1 requires disclosure of all significant accounting policies, including for government grants received — non-disclosure here is a violation of AS 1.

(b) Materiality is assessed by an item's potential to influence users' economic decisions. A depreciation-method change affects profit, asset values, and tax, and even a quantitatively modest impact may carry qualitative significance for comparability/trend analysis. The company's blanket reliance on "materiality" to justify non-disclosure is not valid unless supported by concrete evidence that the impact is immaterial both quantitatively and qualitatively.

(c) The change from FIFO to Weighted Average is a change in accounting policy (not a change in accounting estimate) — it is a change in the cost formula used to measure inventory, and its nature and financial impact should be properly disclosed.

topics.subtopictitle: Disclosure requirements for accounting policy changes and the limits of a materiality-based non-disclosure defence
topics.label: AS 1 (1.5)

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: Zing Ltd., 2024-25: Raw Material closing stock 700 units, cost ₹35/unit, replacement cost ₹20/unit. Finished products FP1/FP2: Production 3,000/1,600 units; Closing stock 500/300 units. Material consumed ₹3,20,000; Direct labour ₹1,60,000; Direct expenses ₹78,000 (these three cost figures pertain to combined joint production). Fixed overhead ₹95,000, including ₹15,000 godown rent (for storing finished products, not a production cost). 1,000 units of by-product BY also emerged, sold @₹12/unit after ₹2,500 expense; ₹4,800 realized from scrap sale. Average market price: FP1 ₹160/unit, FP2 ₹100/unit. Calculate the value of closing stock per AS 2.
answer_html:
Per AS 2, most by-products/scrap are measured at NRV, deducted from the cost of the main product.

NRV of by-product BY: Selling price (1,000×₹12) 12,000, less separate processing charges 2,500 = ₹9,500.

Joint cost to allocate: Raw material 3,20,000 + Labour 1,60,000 + Direct expenses 78,000 + Fixed overhead (95,000−15,000 godown rent, excluded as unrelated to production) 80,000 = 6,38,000; less NRV of BY (9,500) and scrap sale value (4,800) = ₹6,23,700 to allocate between FP1 and FP2.

FP1FP2
Output (units)3,0001,600
Sales price/unit₹160₹100
Sales value4,80,0001,60,000
Allocation ratio31
Joint cost allocated (3:1)4,67,7751,55,925
Cost per unit₹155.93₹97.45

Since both FP1 (₹155.93 cost vs ₹160 selling price) and FP2 (₹97.45 vs ₹100) sell above cost, both finished goods are valued at cost, and the raw material feeding them is valued at its own cost (₹35/unit, not written down to the ₹20 replacement cost).

Closing inventory: FP1 (500×₹155.93) = ₹77,965. FP2 (300×₹97.45) = ₹29,235. Raw material (700×₹35) = ₹24,500. Total closing inventory = ₹77,965 + ₹29,235 + ₹24,500 = ₹1,31,700.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: Kiran Ltd. Balance Sheets (2024/2025): Share capital 12,00,000/12,00,000; P&L A/c 8,50,000/10,00,000; Long Term Loans 10,00,000/10,60,000; Trade payables 3,50,000/4,00,000; Fixed Assets 17,00,000/20,00,000; Investment in shares 2,00,000/2,00,000; Inventory 6,80,000/7,00,000; Trade receivables 7,20,000/6,60,000; Cash 60,000/70,000; Bills Receivable 40,000/30,000. Income Statement 2025: Sales 40,80,000; Cost of sales 27,20,000; Gross Profit 13,60,000; Admin expenses 4,60,000; Depreciation 2,20,000; Operating Profit 6,80,000; Dividend received 50,000; Interest paid 1,40,000; PBT 5,90,000; Tax 2,60,000; PAT 3,30,000. Retained earnings: Opening 8,50,000 + Profit 3,30,000 − Dividend paid 1,80,000 = Closing 10,00,000. Prepare the Cash Flow Statement using the indirect method.
answer_html:
(i) Cash flows from operating activities: PBT 5,90,000 + Depreciation 2,20,000 + Interest (non-operating) 1,40,000 = 9,50,000; less Dividend received (non-operating) (50,000) = Operating Profit before WC changes 9,00,000; add Decrease in Bills Receivable 10,000, Decrease in Trade receivables 60,000, Increase in Trade payables 50,000 = 10,20,000; less Increase in inventory (20,000) = Cash flow from operations before tax 10,00,000; less Tax paid (2,60,000) = Cash flow from operating activities: ₹7,40,000.

(ii) Cash flows from investing activities: Purchase of fixed assets (20,00,000+2,20,000 depreciation−17,00,000 opening = 5,20,000) outflow (5,20,000); Dividend on investments received 50,000 = Cash used in investing activities: ₹(4,70,000).

(iii) Cash flows from financing activities: Long term loan taken 60,000; Interest paid (1,40,000); Dividend paid (1,80,000) = Cash used in financing activities: ₹(2,60,000).

Net increase in cash: ₹10,000 (7,40,000−4,70,000−2,60,000). Opening cash 60,000 + 10,000 = Closing cash balance ₹70,000 (matches given).

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: Garden Ltd. acquired plant and machinery for ₹20 lakhs and sold furniture and fixtures for ₹5 lakhs in the same year. Can the company disclose net cash outflow towards purchase of fixed assets in the cash flow statement per AS 3?
answer_html: No. Per AS 3 para 21, major classes of gross cash receipts and gross cash payments from investing and financing activities must be reported separately, except for the specific items permitted to be reported net under paras 22 and 24 — acquisition and disposal of fixed assets is not among those permitted items. The company cannot net the ₹20 lakh purchase against the ₹5 lakh disposal; both must be shown as separate gross cash flow lines.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: When can an item qualify to be a prior period item as per AS 5?
answer_html: Per AS 5 para 16, prior period items are income or expenses that arise in the current period as a result of errors or omissions in the preparation of financial statements of one or more prior periods. The term does not include other adjustments necessitated by circumstances that, though related to prior periods, are determined only in the current period (e.g. arrears payable to workers from a retrospective wage revision).

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: A Ltd. finds that the stock sheets of 31.3.2024 did not include two pages containing details of inventory worth ₹20 lakhs. How should this be dealt with in the accounts for the year ended 31st March, 2025, per AS 5?
answer_html: This omission is a prior period item under AS 5 para 16. Per para 19, prior period items are normally included in determining the current period's net profit or loss — so ₹20 lakhs should be added to the opening stock as at 1.4.2024. Alternatively, such items may be shown in the statement of profit and loss after the current period's net profit/loss has been determined. Either presentation must clearly indicate the effect of the item on the current period's profit or loss.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: A company took a construction contract for ₹100 lakhs in January 2024; 80% completed at cost ₹92 lakhs by 31.3.2025; further ₹23 lakhs estimated to complete; expected loss ₹15 lakhs. Can the company recognise the loss in the FY2024-25 financial statements?
answer_html: Yes. Per AS 7 paras 31 and 35, an expected loss on a construction contract must be recognised as an expense immediately, regardless of (i) whether work has commenced; (ii) the stage of completion; or (iii) profits expected on other contracts. The company must recognise the ₹15 lakh loss immediately in the year ended 31.3.2025.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: Tonk Tanners (leather shoes): On 31st December, 2024, shoes worth ₹3,20,000 were sent to Mohan Shoes for sale on consignment; 25% remained unsold with Mohan Shoes as on 31st March, 2025. Advise when revenue is recognised in 2024-25 per AS 9.
answer_html: Mohan Shoes is a consignee (agent), not a buyer — risk and reward remain with Tonk Tanners until Mohan Shoes sells to a third party. Revenue is recognised only for the goods actually sold by the consignee: ₹3,20,000 × 75% = ₹2,40,000 recognised as revenue in 2024-25; the remaining 25% (unsold) stays as Tonk Tanners' closing inventory.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: On 10th January, 2025, Tonk Tanners supplied shoes worth ₹4,50,000 to Shani Shoes and concurrently agreed to repurchase the same goods on 11th April, 2025. Advise on revenue recognition.
answer_html: A sale with a concurrent agreement to repurchase the same goods is, in substance, a financing arrangement, not a genuine sale. The resulting cash inflow is not revenue and should not be recognised as revenue in 2024-25.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: On 21st March, 2025, shoes worth ₹1,60,000 were sold to Shoe Shine, but due to their showroom refurbishment, delivery was made on 12th April, 2025 at their request. Advise on revenue recognition.
answer_html: If, on 21st March 2025, Shoe Shine took title and accepted billing for the goods, the sale is complete and all risks/rewards of ownership have transferred, even though physical delivery was delayed at the buyer's own request. subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: On 1st December 2024, Precision Tools Ltd. replaced the motor of an old machine with a new one costing ₹1,20,000, improving output capacity by 15%. The old motor had cost ₹50,000 and accumulated depreciation ₹35,000. Calculate the amount to be capitalized.
answer_html: Carrying amount of the old motor = 50,000−35,000 = ₹15,000, which is derecognised (written off) since it is being replaced. The new motor's acquisition cost of ₹1,20,000 is capitalised as a separate component (component accounting under AS 10). Net effect: ₹1,20,000 capitalised, ₹15,000 carrying amount of the old motor removed/expensed.

question_html: Zenith Industries Ltd. received ₹65 lakhs from a local authority to develop medical facilities for employees at its new township. Explain the accounting treatment per AS 12.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: Zenith Industries Ltd. also received ₹82 lakhs as a Central Government subsidy for establishing a new production unit in a notified backward area, classified as being in the nature of promoters' contribution, intended to support long-term development. Explain the treatment per AS 12.
answer_html: Per AS 12, grants in the nature of promoters' contribution — given with reference to total investment/capital outlay, with no repayment ordinarily expected — are treated as Capital Reserve, which can neither be distributed as dividend nor treated as deferred income. Since this ₹82 lakh subsidy is neither tied to a specific fixed asset nor to revenue, the full amount should be credited to Capital Reserve.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: On 1st April 2024, Kesar held 75,000 equity shares of Beta Ltd. at book value ₹15/share (nominal ₹10 each). Transactions: 20th June 2024, purchased 15,000 additional shares at ₹16/share. 1st August 2024, Beta Ltd. declared a 1:6 bonus issue. 31st October 2024, rights issue of 3-for-7 held at ₹15/share; Kesar sold one-third of his rights entitlement to Megha at ₹2/share and subscribed to the remainder on 5th November 2024. Prepare the Investment Account in Kesar's books for the year ending 31st March 2025.
answer_html:
W.N.1 Bonus shares: (75,000+15,000)/6 = 15,000 bonus shares (holding at bonus date: 90,000).

W.N.2 Rights entitlement: (75,000+15,000+15,000)/7 × 3 = 45,000 rights shares entitlement (on a holding of 1,05,000 post-bonus).

W.N.3 Sale of rights: One-third of 45,000 = 15,000 shares' worth of entitlement sold × ₹2/share = ₹30,000, credited to Statement of Profit and Loss (proceeds from renouncing rights, not adding to the investment's cost).

W.N.4 Rights subscribed: Remaining two-thirds of 45,000 = 30,000 shares subscribed × ₹15/share = ₹4,50,000.

Investment Account (Equity shares in Beta Ltd.): Dr: To Balance b/d 75,000 shares ₹11,25,000; To Bank A/c (20.6.24 purchase) 15,000 shares ₹2,40,000; To Bonus issue (W.N.1) 15,000 shares — Nil cost; To Bank A/c (rights subscribed, W.N.4) 30,000 shares ₹4,50,000. Total: 1,35,000 shares, ₹18,15,000. Cr: By Balance c/d (balancing figure) 1,35,000 shares ₹18,15,000.

subject: Advanced Accounting
question_html: X Co. Ltd. (share capital ₹50 lakhs, equity shares of ₹10 each) was taken over by Y Co. Ltd. X Co. Ltd. has General Reserve ₹10,00,000 and Profit and Loss account Cr. ₹5,00,000. Y Co. Ltd. issued 11 equity shares of ₹10 each for every 10 shares of X Co. Ltd. Pass the journal entries in Y Co. Ltd.'s books for the shares issued under the Pooling of Interests method.
answer_html:
Purchase consideration = 50,00,000 × 11/10 = ₹55,00,000.

Journal entries (books of Y Co. Ltd.):

  1. Business Purchase A/c Dr. 55,00,000; To Liquidator of X Co. Ltd. 55,00,000 (business of X Co. Ltd. purchased).
  2. Assets A/c (balancing figure) Dr. 65,00,000; To Business Purchase A/c 55,00,000; To General Reserve A/c 5,00,000; To Profit and Loss A/c 5,00,000 (assets and reserves/surplus taken over — under Pooling of Interests, X's reserves are carried forward at their existing book figures, not merged into goodwill).
  3. Liquidator of X Co. Ltd. Dr. 55,00,000; To Equity Share Capital A/c 55,00,000 (purchase consideration discharged via equity shares of Y Co. Ltd.).

W.N.: Purchase consideration ₹55,00,000 − Share capital of X Co. Ltd. ₹50,00,000 = ₹5,00,000 to be adjusted from (i.e., absorbed into) General Reserve.

topics.title: Amalgamation of Companies
topics.subtopictitle: Pooling of Interests method - reserves carried forward at book value, purchase-consideration excess/shortfall adjusted against reserves
topics.label: Amalgamation of Companies (1)

examiner_comment.text: Some examinees computed goodwill for the excess of purchase consideration over share capital, applying the Purchase Method's logic instead of the Pooling of Interests method's requirement to adjust the difference directly against reserves.
